item.title: [Investing] Hedge funds bought tech at the fastest pace since 2022, one week after the flush
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Amazon crossed $3 trillion for the first time and SpaceX hit an all-time low on the same tape, while Bank of America's Bull and Bear indicator printed one of the strongest sell signals of the century.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon crossed $3 trillion for the first time and SpaceX hit an all-time low on the same tape, while Bank of America's Bull and Bear indicator printed one of the strongest sell signals of the century.

Yesterday the question was whether a closed strait and a VIX at 15.99 could stay on the same page. Today the market answered by buying tech with both hands, and the flows tell you the cleansing everyone celebrated lasted about five sessions.

Market context. The morning started at the line that mattered. Per the Financial Markets list, $QQQ backtested the June lows at 686 near the open and bounced from there, with EliteOptionsTrader's August 5 692 calls going from roughly $4.75 to $8.50 inside ninety minutes.

Then the split tape. Per the Kalshi list, Amazon crossed $3 trillion of market value for the first time while SpaceX printed an all-time low, one day before its first earnings report in company history. Tesla ran 4 percent. Stocks climbed as oil fell, with Trump telling oil companies to get prices down now and separately claiming the United States "completely controls" the Strait of Hormuz. Iran showed no interest in resuming negotiations.

The flow data is the part to sit with.

SignalReading
Hedge fund tech buyingfastest pace since 2022
Tech fund inflowslargest 5-week total on record
BofA Bull and Bear indicatorone of the strongest sell signals of the century
Korean market volatilityexceeds the 2008 financial crisis

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, and it was mine to publish. I put $TSLA on the watchlist yesterday off the weekly candle closing entirely outside its lower Bollinger band. It opened up 4 percent. Heisenberg, whose setup it was, called it before I did.
  • Against, inside a day. I went 65/35 that oil is higher two weeks out. Crude fell today and the president is publicly jawboning it lower. Two weeks is the horizon and the first session went the wrong way.
  • Resolved, and not mine. The Bessent notepad reading "buy Japanese yen $5-10 bil" was real. Japan spent more than $50 billion in one day defending the yen at its weakest since 1986, and the Treasury and New York Fed bought alongside Tokyo the next day.
  • Dead. No CLARITY Act vote is scheduled, no cloture motion is filed, and the bill sits at number 423 on the calendar with the Senate leaving August 8.
  • Due tomorrow. $AMD reports, and SpaceX reports for the first time ever into an all-time low, two days before its unlock.

1. The memory trade flipped inside twenty-four hours, and the hyperscalers took the other side. Yesterday UBS had memory spending doubling to $761 billion by 2027 and Micron re-rating from 5 times earnings toward 12. Today the trade broke the other way. Per the Stocks list, Reuters reports CXMT is considering a second Beijing DRAM fab in the Yizhuang district on top of the Shanghai and Hefei plants already under construction, taking its capacity to more than double current levels and past 600,000 wafers a month.

Memory sold off. The hyperscalers rallied. Kyle Reidhead argues that is not a coincidence and the arithmetic is his best work in weeks. Memory is now roughly 35 percent of hyperscaler hardware spend against 8 percent in 2023, and Apple spent its earnings call complaining that memory costs are squeezing margins. AWS already says its server investments break even in under three years at today's inflated component prices.

So run it forward. If memory and chip supply loosen, every data centre gets cheaper, every server pays back faster, and the $860 billion of capex going out this year buys more compute per dollar. Falling input costs speed the buildout up rather than slowing it down.

He supplies his own caveat and it is the right one. The new Chinese supply is commodity DRAM, not the high-bandwidth memory that is sold out through 2026, so the selloff is probably overblown. I am revising to 55/45 that memory multiples expand before they compress, down from 65/35, because a second fab announcement inside a week is a supply signal and UBS's re-rating case was always a bet on scarcity being structural.

2. The re-grossing already happened, and that is the problem. Six days ago Goldman's crowded-position index had its worst month against the S&P since 2001 and Jordi Visser called it a cleansing event. Cleansing events are supposed to leave positioning light for a while.

Instead, per the Kalshi list, hedge funds have bought tech at the fastest pace since 2022 and tech funds just took their largest five-week inflow on record. The money that was force-sold in July came back in under a week, and it came back into the same names.

Shay Boloor has the bull reading on the People to follow list, and it is the clearest statement of what the flows imply. He expects the Lag 7 to turn back into the Mag 7, and says "all of the bottleneck bros are going to start wondering, why aren't we catching a bid anymore. It's because the generals are back in action." Ryan Detrick adds on the Financial Markets list that six sectors gained more than 1 percent in July and a declining savings rate is what an expansion looks like when net wealth rises.

Against them sits Bank of America's Bull and Bear indicator at one of the strongest sell signals of the century, and Bloomberg's James Seyffart on the People to follow list: "The amount of gambling coming to the ETF market is crazy." REX Shares is launching 2X daily long ETFs on Akamai, DigitalOcean and Penguin Solutions. That is what the top of a speculation cycle sounds like when it files paperwork.

My lean, and it is a downgrade. I go to 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August, back from 70/30 yesterday. Visser's argument for a bottom rested on hedge funds hedging rather than liquidating and coming back slowly. They came back immediately, at size, into a sell signal. That is a weaker setup than the one I upgraded on.

3. Warsh and Bessent are running the same trade from two desks. Per Capital Flows, the most useful framing of the week. Warsh spent his July press conference on capital spending rather than inflation. His words: "The most striking feature of the economy is the strong growth of business investment." He put a number on it, saying AI-related high-tech equipment and software shows four-quarter growth rates of nearly 20 percent, and told Congress two weeks earlier that "it seems inevitable that what is now called AI investment will soon be called just investment."

Then his description of his own posture. "We haven't done much in 42 days. The markets have done quite a bit."

Bessent's half runs through Japan. Cross-border yen borrowing is roughly a quarter trillion dollars directly and near a trillion once derivatives are counted, and that is the funding pipe for dollar assets. So the yen hitting a 1986 low, Japan's record single-day defence, and the Treasury buying alongside it are not three stories. They are one, and the thing being protected is the liquidity the buildout runs on.

Why it is urgent now: Anthropic went from a $9 billion revenue run rate to nearly $50 billion in about five months and has filed confidentially to go public, while OpenAI runs near $25 billion and still loses more than a dollar for every dollar it earns. Those companies need public markets at the exact moment SpaceX trades 20 percent below its offer price. Warsh also put Marc Andreessen on the Fed's new AI task force.

Treat the coordination claim as a frame rather than a finding, because the author supports the policy he is describing and sells access to the thesis. The quotes and the intervention sequence are checkable and they are the durable part.

4. Goldman found the earnings asterisk, and then found the half that cuts the other way. Per zerohedge on the Financial Markets list, S&P 500 earnings growth is tracking 45 percent year over year in the second quarter against a 22 percent consensus coming in. Nineteen points of that is Alphabet and Amazon's combined $151 billion of "other income" on equity investments.

Here is the part the bears will skip. Strip those gains and growth is still tracking 26 percent, an acceleration against the first quarter and the fastest pace since 2021.

That number damages both sides of the argument I have been running. Ed Yardeni's asterisk and Jim Chanos's profit-inflation mechanism are both real and now quantified at nineteen points. And the underlying business is accelerating anyway. Anyone telling you this quarter is fake has to explain 26 percent.

5. The Coldcard hack is far bigger than one unlucky holder. Yesterday I carried one man losing 18.25 Bitcoin. Per Anthony Pompliano, the real number is more than $100 million from over 5,000 wallets, and Bloomberg's headline calls the attack ongoing.

The mechanism matters for how you price it. Bitcoin itself was not touched. The flaw sits in Coinkite's random number generator, so it is a vendor failure rather than a protocol failure. Pompliano's forecast is that this pushes money toward ETFs and third-party multi-sig, and he runs a bitcoin treasury company, so weigh the forecast accordingly.

Scott Melker has the sentence that lands. Over a million retail traders were liquidated last October, and this week the losses hit people who did everything right and held in self custody. The believers are the ones getting destroyed.

6. The two loudest bitcoin holders in the market went opposite ways today. Michael Saylor's Strategy sold $102 million of Bitcoin, buying STRC with it. Jim Cramer said he is selling all of his on quantum risk, and told viewers to buy the Amazon dip in the same session. Tom Lee's BitMine bought $19 million of Ethereum, with Lee personally adding $20 million last week, and BlackRock launched a tokenized money-market fund on Ethereum.

The price backdrop is worse than the flow. Per Milk Road on the Stocks list, Bitcoin trades near $63,900, about 49 percent below its October 2025 high of $126,198, and Polymarket had 2026 CLARITY passage at 28 percent on July 30 against 82 percent in February. Kalshi's traders now forecast Ethereum crashes to $1,390 this year.

Saylor selling and Cramer capitulating on the same day the legislative catalyst dies is the cleanest sentiment washout crypto has produced this cycle. That is a reason to look rather than a reason to buy, and I am 55/45 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before it sees $75,000.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SPCX. All-time low today, first earnings report in company history tomorrow, and the insider unlock two days later. It trades 20 percent under an offer price set seven weeks ago and nearly half off its peak. Asked whether the stock is a big opportunity here, Elon Musk answered "I think so," which is the only bid on the tape and also the least disinterested one.
  • $AMD. Reports tomorrow into a complex where memory is the swing input on cost. Per wafer.ai, Kimi K3 serves at 3.8 times the throughput and 71 percent lower cost on MI355x than on Nvidia's B200, and if AMD echoes anything like that on the call it reframes the name.
  • $MU. The CXMT second-fab report is the first genuine supply headline since the shortage narrative took hold. High-bandwidth memory is still sold out through 2026, so the thesis survives, but the crowding does not survive a doubling of Chinese commodity capacity without a fight.
  • $AMZN. Three trillion dollars, and Cramer says buy the dip. AWS at a $169 billion run rate growing 37 percent is the reason, and $220 billion of 2026 capex against already-negative free cash flow is the argument on the other side.
  • $INDI. John Galt is long it as the only Western supplier into Unitree's August 10 listing, priced near $5.9 billion at about 71 times trailing earnings. His broader read on the tape is the honest one: fugly, very tough, sit on your hands if you can.

item.title: [Investing] The AI trade broke on its financing, and Nvidia's credit market called it first
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Hyperscaler credit default swaps hit records while Nvidia guaranteed up to $750 billion of OpenAI's debt, Meta borrowed $24.9 billion instead of buying back stock, and a levered fund lost 67 percent in a month.
item.content:encoded:
Hyperscaler credit default swaps hit records while Nvidia guaranteed up to $750 billion of OpenAI's debt, Meta borrowed $24.9 billion instead of buying back stock, and a levered fund lost 67 percent in a month.

Last Sunday I wrote that the memory thesis was under attack and surviving on price while losing ground on argument. It survived. What broke this week was the money underneath the entire buildout, and it broke in the one place equity investors do not look. Here is the arc, the plumbing, the accounting, both cases, what I would do, and the week's scoreboard.

The arc of the week. Monday opened on Alphabet. Per Ticker Symbol: YOU, its filing showed $811 billion of future purchase agreements against $332 billion three months earlier, about $200 billion of it due inside twelve months, with some energy contracts running to 2054. Free cash flow was negative $5.9 billion against positive $24.6 billion two quarters ago, long-term debt more than doubled in six months, the interest bill roughly quintupled, and buybacks stopped for the first time since 2017.

The same morning, per the Market list, Nvidia was in talks to guarantee up to $250 billion of financing for a 10-gigawatt OpenAI campus in southern Ohio. By Tuesday the reported figure was above $750 billion, and the cost of insuring Nvidia's own debt surged to a record. That instrument is a credit default swap, a contract that pays out if the borrower fails, so its price is the market's live quote on how safe the company's paper is.

Tuesday is when it stopped being one name. Per the Financial Markets list, zerohedge reported "unprecedented carnage in AI IG CDS" with the hyperscaler basket another 3 basis points wider to a fresh record. The thirty-year Treasury closed the prior week at 5.17 percent, its highest weekly close since July 2007. And BlackRock closed a $12.5 billion bond sale against a Meta data centre in Texas, the 2048 notes priced 287.5 basis points over Treasuries with roughly $20 billion of demand, BlackRock-backed entities owning 80 percent and Meta 20, lease-backed so the debt never touches Meta's balance sheet.

Wednesday the Fed held on a 9 to 3 vote, the most dissents since 2016 and every one of them wanting rates higher, Kevin Warsh said there is no soft inflation target because the target is 2 percent, and the thirty-year broke through the 5.2 percent ceiling it had been testing since October 2023.

Thursday the forced seller got a name. Per Diet TBPN, Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness sold its entire public book, longs and shorts, in a single block to Citadel. Per the Financial Markets list, the Journal put the month at down 67 percent against a fund up 439 percent after fees through June 30. Everything he owned ripped the moment the selling stopped: Bloom Energy up 26 percent, Nebius 25, IREN 25, SanDisk 20, CoreWeave 20, Micron 15.

Friday closed the ledger. July finished red on the S&P 500, ending eleven straight green Julys, with the Nasdaq 100 posting its worst July in 22 years and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index its worst month since 2008. The thirty-year hit 5.27 percent and TLT posted its lowest monthly close since the fund launched in 2002.

How the money actually moves. Three separate channels got welded into one scary word this week, and they carry different risks. Separating them is most of the work.

The first is vendor financing. Nvidia is guaranteeing the debt of the customer buying its chips. Per Jose Najarro, a guarantee is not funding and Nvidia pays only if OpenAI misses, and his bull read is that prior backstops ran $3 billion to $6 billion, so a number this size is an existential commitment nobody fakes.

The bear read, from Douglas Swift on the Stocks list, is the sentence of the week. This is how Lucent and Nortel financed the CLECs that bought their switches, and "when the supplier underwrites the demand, the demand signal stops being independent information." The pattern is not one deal either. It runs $1 billion into Nokia, $2 billion into Marvell, $1 billion into Naver, equity in Lumentum and Coherent, above $500 billion with SK Group and $30 billion already in OpenAI.

The second is off balance sheet. Per Prof G Markets, Nikkei Asia counts roughly $1.65 trillion of off-balance-sheet obligations across Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Oracle against about $1.35 trillion of reported debt, with Bloomberg nearer $1.8 trillion. Meta's alone is $420 billion, three times what it reports. Per the clip, Scott Galloway called it concealment rather than accounting. Ed Elson supplied the correction that matters: these vehicles are genuine risk transfer rather than hidden recourse, and the party holding the risk is the private credit funds. That is a different failure mode from the vendor-financing one, and both can run at once.

The third is plain corporate borrowing, and this is where the market actually voted. Per the People to follow list, Meta bought back zero stock last quarter and borrowed $24.9 billion instead, taking long-term debt from $58.7 billion at year end to $83.7 billion. A year ago the same quarter carried $10.2 billion of buybacks and no new debt. Microsoft, on the same day, held its 2026 capex guidance flat and rose 15 percent. The distinction the tape priced was funded from cash against funded from the bond market, at a nineteen-year high in the long end.

The accounting got looser in the same week, and that is not a coincidence. Per Prof G Markets, Jim Chanos makes an accounting-identity argument rather than a valuation one. Capex spenders capitalise the outlay and depreciate it over five to ten years. The receivers, Nvidia and Caterpillar and the utilities, book the revenue and the profit immediately. The same dollar therefore inflates aggregate profits, he sizes the mismatch in the hundreds of billions a year, and his arithmetic is that S&P profits should be growing 8 or 9 percent against a reported 28 or 29.

Ed Yardeni found the same asterisk from the other end. Per his note, three companies added $9 per share of earnings growth through accounting gains on venture investments, and stripping those takes blended growth from 37.9 percent to 22.

Then Microsoft changed two policies on one call. Per a reading of the transcript, it is extending the estimated useful life of data centres and office buildings from 15 to 25 years starting in fiscal 2027, which lowers depreciation and lifts operating profit. The second change got almost no coverage: "more of our future data center leases will shift from finance leases to operating leases as a result of this update. Finance leases are included in capital expenditures while operating leases are not." Reported free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capex, so moving lease spend out of capex mechanically raises it.

Amazon's quarter reads the same way under the hood. Per a line-item read of the filing, stripping the Anthropic mark leaves earnings of $1.68 per share against $1.82 of guidance, a miss and flat year over year, and the reported 33 percent rise in operating cash flow rests on an income tax deferral that, undone, leaves roughly $27.7 billion and a 15 percent decline. Purchases of non-marketable securities ran $24.4 billion in the quarter and $39.8 billion across the first half, against $4.8 billion for all of 2025.

The bull case. Start with the strongest version, and it comes from the man who wrote the bear headline. Per Prof G Markets, Apollo's Torsten Slok points out these are among the most profitable companies alive, so record credit default swap prices on Oracle, SpaceX, Google, Amazon and Nvidia are not a default signal. They are the market repricing when the AI payoff arrives. Slower future cash flow means a lower price today. That is a duration problem, and duration problems reverse when the discount rate does.

The economics under the contracts also look better than the tape. Per the Stocks list, Gavin Baker argues spot GPU rental prices run at least twice contracted rates, so the hyperscalers are underearning on assets already in the ground, and Dwarkesh Patel supplies the number underneath it with Google reportedly paying $900 million a month for 110,000 GPUs rented from SpaceX. Amazon carries $496 billion of contracted backlog not yet online, and AWS grew 37 percent at a 39.4 percent operating margin. Azure passed $100 billion of annual revenue growing 43 percent, its fastest since early 2022.

The breadth is genuinely healthy too. Per Phil Rosen, the equal-weight S&P is up 12.2 percent this year against 8.7 percent for the cap-weighted index, the NYSE advance-decline line sits near all-time highs, and eight of eleven sectors are higher. Per Anthony Pompliano, S&P net margin is tracking 15.7 percent, the highest since 2009, and the Nasdaq 100 trades at 24 times against 86 in May 2001.

And Galloway, who supplied the concealment quote, broke with his own producer on air. "Meta is such a cash volcano that I'm not as worried about the debt of Meta." His worry is the cash-flow-negative adjacents, a far narrower claim than the headline he gave it.

The bear case. Chanos has the precedent with teeth. S&P earnings grew 30 percent from mid-1998 to mid-2000, then fell 40 percent from mid-2000 to mid-2001, as deep a fall as the financial crisis produced, on a GDP decline of only 1 percent. The cause was order-book cancellation. "People realized they didn't need 10,000 routers, they needed 2,000." He puts hyperscaler return on incremental invested capital as roughly halved in eighteen months, from 100 percent to 25 at some names and the teens at a couple, and gives boards twelve to eighteen months before they start asking.

The credit market has already sized the exposure. Per the Stocks list, Morgan Stanley's Vishy Tirupattur has the AI ecosystem going from under 3 percent of the investment-grade bond index to over 6, with hyperscaler capex revised for 2026 from $600 billion to above $800 billion, for 2027 from $850 billion to $1,300 billion. Oracle now sits one notch above junk with credit default swaps at 2008 levels and spreads beyond 220 basis points.

The neoclouds are where the arithmetic actually fails. Per Milk Road AI, one megawatt of GPU capacity looks like this.

One megawattFigure
Build cost$30 million
Debt to equity75/25, so $7.5 million equity
Annual revenue$10.5 million
Interestroughly $1.6 million
Cash after year oneabout negative $6 million
Cash breakevenyear five
Six-year cumulative$3.5 million on $7.5 million, 6 to 7 percent annualised

The whole equity return therefore sits in what the GPUs are worth in 2032, and nobody has observed that number. At a residual of 60 percent of initial rental rates the annualised return is 23 percent. At 30 percent the trade is dead. He holds CoreWeave and Nebius, says he is getting more bearish and has no model yet, and I would rather have that than a model with a fabricated residual inside it.

Per Alex Corrino, the proximate cause is real rates, and his evidence starts with a date. The Nasdaq topped the day of Warsh's first meeting. Long-run inflation expectations have barely moved while Treasury yields have, worth roughly 50 basis points of higher real rates, and the AI buildout is one of the longest-duration trades on the board. His scoreboard: Amazon and Alphabet flat on the year, Meta down 10 percent and Microsoft down 20, against a Nasdaq 100 up 10.

Per Mark Cuban, the efficiency case strands the assets themselves. He grants that utilisation scales as expected, but if the price-performance curve keeps minimising power requirements, "there's going to be a lot of data centers that are going to be turned into pickleball courts." His analogy is dark fiber selling for pennies once 1-gigabit became 100, and he calls borrowing on top of fully-committed cash flow planning for perfection.

Then the proof of concept, which already ran. Situational Awareness was long AI infrastructure and short software at three to four times leverage on roughly $35 billion of equity, per Martin Shkreli's reconstruction, giving about $120 billion of gross exposure. A 25 percent drop in gross comes out of the equity rather than the gross. Numerai's Richard Craib put it plainest: at 150 percent volatility, variance drag alone is 113 percent a year and risk of ruin is roughly a coin flip over a fund's life. Per Diet TBPN, Aschenbrenner's own letter calls the spiral "essentially similar to a bank run."

What to do with it. I am 70/30 that this is a repricing of duration rather than the opening of a default cycle. Slok is right that the widening sits on companies that can pay, and Baker is right that contracted rates below spot mean the buyers are underearning on what is already built. The 30 is the neoclouds, where the return genuinely depends on a 2032 residual nobody can price.

On timing I lean Chanos on the mechanism and Rosen on the tape, so the risk sits in 2027 rather than August. Profit inflation is arithmetic and needs no catalyst to be true, while breadth near all-time highs says the unwind has not begun. Those are compatible, and together they argue patience rather than panic.

The variable that decides it is the long end and not the equity tape. At 5.27 percent the thirty-year is the highest since June 2007, and every month it holds above 5.2 the discount rate grinds against the longest-duration trade in the market. If it breaks back under 5 percent, half of this memo becomes an academic exercise.

So sort the complex by who funds from cash and who funds from the bond market. That is the trade this week handed you.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NVDA. The equity question is now a credit question. Its own insurance cost hit a record while it guarantees up to $750 billion of a customer's debt, and it bounced off its 200-day moving average for the third time in 21 sessions near $192. A level tested three times in a month is a queue rather than support. Confirmation or walk-back of that $750 billion moves this more than the next print does.
  • $META. Zero buybacks, $24.9 billion borrowed, long-term debt from $58.7 billion to $83.7 billion, property and equipment at $225.7 billion after adding nearly $50 billion in six months. Down 9 percent on the month on the longest losing streak in company history. Galloway's cash volcano is the bull case and that balance sheet is the bear case, and both are honest.
  • $AMZN. Best day since 2012 on genuine AWS acceleration. Underneath it, $24.4 billion of private-company purchases in one quarter against $4.8 billion in all of 2025, a bond book only 1.4 times oversubscribed against a typical investment-grade four times, and long-term debt up 96 percent in two quarters to $129 billion.
  • $MSFT. The cleanest funded-from-cash name and the one whose reported numbers just got the most generous treatment. Per one reverse discounted cash flow model, which backs out the growth a price already assumes, $451.10 implies 20.3 percent annual free cash flow growth for a decade against a realised 4 percent over fiscal 2022 to 2025. The bear is $202, the base $310, the bull $368, and the price sits 23 percent above the author's own bull case.
  • $ORCL. One notch above junk, swaps at 2008 levels, spreads beyond 220 basis points, down 67 percent from its high and below its April 2025 lows. If a credit cycle starts anywhere in this complex it starts here, and that makes it the best early warning on the board.
  • $CRWV and $NBIS. Per Milk Road AI, CoreWeave carries $99.4 billion of obligations against roughly a $50 billion market cap, $24.9 billion of debt, $536 million of quarterly interest and no positive free cash flow until 2029 or 2030. Nebius holds $9.3 billion of cash with no meaningful net debt and $17.4 billion of Microsoft backlog. Same trade, opposite balance sheets. While the long end sits here, own the one that does not need the rate to cooperate.

The scoreboard. Forty-two calls on the book resolved this week. Thirty-one hit, six missed, five expired.

Seven of those were mine, six hits and one miss, and I am not going to let that number stand without an asterisk. Five of the six hits are the same Fed call revised across five editions, the hold leg and the hawkish-statement leg. Counted honestly that is one call that landed on both legs rather than five wins. The running house record reads 10 of 11 graded, or 91 percent, and three of the ten are catalyst calls where the reward for being right is that a scheduled date arrived. Treat the real number as five or six genuine calls with one clear loss.

The loss is worth naming straight. On Monday I said CXMT's debut does not touch the high-bandwidth memory shortage on any timeline that matters this quarter, so memory would reprice on Samsung's Wednesday print rather than on a Chinese listing. It repriced inside three hours. Micron fell 6.1 percent through a trillion dollars, ASML was halted after an 8 percent drop, and anyone long on my framing wore it. The fundamental half of that call is still holding. The tradeable half was wrong, and the tradeable half is the one that costs money.

A second one I owe you. On Sunday I revised the odds of a hawkish-enough statement down to 45/55 because oil had fallen 7 percent. That was the wrong direction. Warsh read hawkish and the thirty-year broke a three-year ceiling. I got there in the end only because I revised back up to 60/40 on Monday and 55/45 on Tuesday.

The wins that were not mine deserve the credit. threadguy read the CXMT pre-IPO perpetual as implying roughly $470 billion and it closed its debut near $487 billion. Benjamin Cowen said on Tuesday that a hold is what forces the long end higher and would push the thirty-year through 5.2 percent, and it did inside 24 hours. Bernstein's Gautam Chhugani and Piper Sandler both modelled roughly $150 million of Robinhood event-contract revenue and it printed $156 million. Citadel Securities forecast a surprise hike, was wrong, and then bought the book anyway. Being wrong on the rate and right on the trade are two different scoreboards.

Carried into next week, with dates:

CallWhoseDue
The next Fed move is a hike at 60/40, landing in September at 55/45HouseSep 30
The July low holds into mid-August at 60/40HouseAug 15
Memory multiples expand before they compress at 65/35HouseDec 31
The thirty-year holding above the 5.2 percent ceiling it just clearedHouseOct 31
Alphabet's $811 billion of commitments reprice the stock rather than worry itHouseOct 31
Nvidia's 200-day, tested three times in 21 sessionsHouseAug 29
The CLARITY Act gets a Senate floor vote before the recessJohn ThuneAug 7
Bitcoin does not break $58,000 to $60,000, with $40,000 the invalidationAnsemOpen
Nebius closing below $132 opens $85 to $100AtlasShrug1Open
SpaceX reports in early August into a billion-share unlockLimitlessAug 6

The Fed call and the July-low call are the two that carry real weight, and both settle on the same thing this memo has been circling. Watch the thirty-year.

item.title: [Investing] Hormuz is still closed, the strikes never came, and the VIX sits at 15.99
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: CENTCOM redirected 35 vessels as Iran contradicted Trump on reopening, Goldman's crowded hedge fund basket had its worst month on record against the S&P, and nearly 20 percent of the index reports this week.
item.content:encoded:
CENTCOM redirected 35 vessels as Iran contradicted Trump on reopening, Goldman's crowded hedge fund basket had its worst month on record against the S&P, and nearly 20 percent of the index reports this week.

Friday's edition closed on a weekend where strikes had reportedly been ordered on Iranian energy targets. They did not come. What came instead is Iran saying the strait stays shut, and a volatility market that has decided none of it matters.

The week ahead. Nearly 20 percent of the S&P 500 reports over the next five sessions, per the Kalshi list. Yardeni Research frames the order of importance correctly on the Financial Markets list: the labor market takes center stage with Friday's jobs report as the main event, Fedspeak resumes, and earnings heat up with Palantir, AMD and SpaceX's public debut.

DayWhat lands
Monday$PLTR, $ON, $GRAB, $SNAP
Tuesday$AMD, $SPCX (first report in company history), $ANET, $ALAB, $HUT
Wednesday$SNDK, $APP, $IONQ, $MELI, $UBER, $SHOP
Thursday$DDOG, $NET, $TTD, $TEAM, $QBTS
Friday$OKLO, $VST, and the jobs report

The full calendar is Shay Boloor's on the Market list. Two numbers frame it. The thirty-year finished July at 5.27 percent, its highest since 2007, and the VIX sits at 15.99 after touching 19.36 or higher at least once a month in 24 of the last 25.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, and not mine. Goldman's Alvin So and JPMorgan both had the Korean leveraged-ETF unwind essentially finished. Foreign investors just made a record $5.4 billion purchase of Korean equities. The cleanest resolution on the board.
  • Did not happen. I carried Friday's report that Trump had ordered strikes on Iranian energy targets before Monday's open. No strike. GOP Senator James Lankford says Trump "has no desire" to bomb Iran.
  • Against, with five days left. I have been carrying John Thune's confirmation of a CLARITY floor vote before the recess. Kalshi prices passage at 4 percent. Call it dead unless something moves tomorrow.
  • Not confirmed, still live. Micron needed a 906 close to validate the reclaim and did not take it Friday.
  • Due Tuesday. SpaceX reports for the first time ever, days before the August 6 unlock.

1. The strait is closed and the volatility market has priced none of it. Per the Market list, Iran says reports it agreed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz are false. A source cited by Fars News says no deal was accepted, the strait stays closed while the US continues what Iran calls hostile actions, and ships may pass only via Iran's designated route with permission from the IRGC Navy.

Per the Polymarket list, Iran is contradicting Trump's claim directly, CENTCOM has redirected 35 vessels, and Ukrainian drones hit the Saratov refinery overnight.

So the shooting risk fell and the shipping risk did not. That is the distinction the tape is missing, because a closed strait keeps working without a headline.

My lean, and it is a change from Friday. I am 65/35 that oil is higher two weeks out, up from roughly even, because the de-escalation everyone traded was about strikes rather than transit. The 35 is that Iran has reopened before under this much pressure.

2. The unwind was the worst on record, and that is the bull case rather than the bear one. Per Jordi Visser, Goldman's VIP index of the most crowded hedge fund positions fell 12 percent for the month against the S&P through Wednesday. That is the worst relative month since the index began in 2001, worse than the month of Lehman, and roughly double any other month on the record.

Seven of those 12 points came in four days, and that four-day rate of change is the worst ever measured, including COVID. It happened in a tape where the S&P barely moved and the VIX stayed low. Goldman had flagged the fuel: the buildup in gross leverage over the first five months was the largest cumulative increase since it began tracking in 2016, from an already all-time high.

Visser has been inside three of these. He took over the S&P book during LTCM, was positioned through the 2007 quant unwind, and had thirty-odd portfolio managers reporting to him through Archegos. His read is a cleansing event at high probability, and the reasoning is specific rather than hopeful. Hedge funds are still up more than 10 percent on the year, so the chip stack is positive and the rational move is to hedge and come back rather than liquidate.

3. This was not an AI crash, and the tape proves it. Per Porter Stansberry, the consensus post-mortem on Aschenbrenner blames four-to-one leverage. His objection is that leverage is a magnifying glass rather than a verdict, and nobody has explained why the positions were wrong. Then he shows you. Here are both legs of the book from the June 30 close to the July 29 close, the last session before the block trade cleared it.

LongMoveShortMove
SanDisk-55.32%Workday+37.24%
Nebius-46.33%Adobe+28.49%
Bloom Energy-45.90%Intuit+27.64%
CoreWeave-38.90%Salesforce+20.25%
Micron-35.98%Veeva+17.15%

Over the identical twenty sessions the QQQ fell 10.14 percent, the SPY fell 2.32, and Nvidia fell 5.04 and still finished July up 0.33. The S&P sat near its record the whole way. So the index did not break. The market rotated violently out of the leveraged, capital-hungry end of the AI complex and into the profitable, asset-light end. That is out of exactly what he owned and into exactly what he was short.

Stansberry's second point is the one with money in it. Adobe trades near 11 times trailing earnings, Salesforce 13, Intuit 14, on operating margins of 36.6 and 28.7 percent and capex around 1 percent of revenue. Those are the multiples of a dying industry applied to businesses selling AI as an upsell, with Microsoft's contracted backlog at $678 billion, up 84 percent, and 30 million paid Copilot seats against 15 million in January.

The funding side agrees. Per Phil Rosen on the Financial Markets list, capex at Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta rose from $150 billion in 2022 to $358 billion in 2025 while their combined free cash flow fell 15 percent to $199 billion. Per the All-In Podcast, David Sacks calls the move momentum rather than fundamentals and expects a return on the capex.

My lean. Sacks is right that the selloff was leverage and wrong that it says nothing, because Stansberry's table is not a leverage story, it is the market repricing who captures the value. I am 70/30 that the July low holds into mid-August, raised from 60/40 on Visser's evidence, and 60/40 that asset-light software beats the buildout names over six months. That second one is the trade this week actually handed you.

4. UBS put the biggest number yet on memory, and the chart has not confirmed it. Per the Market list, UBS projects hyperscaler memory spending more than doubles to $761 billion in 2027, reaching roughly 75 percent of total capex, with shortages extending into the summer of 2028 and only three suppliers controlling the market. Hyperscalers are locking supply through prepayments and multiyear agreements.

The conclusion is what matters for positioning. If that means years of elevated earnings rather than one good cycle, memory becomes a multiple-expansion story, and UBS has $MU, SK Hynix and Samsung moving from roughly 5 times earnings to nearly 12.

The shortage has reached Apple's shelves. Per Bloomberg via the People to follow list, Apple faces major MacBook Air shortages on the memory and silicon crunch, with many new orders not arriving until September. A market tight enough to delay the best-supplied hardware company on earth is a demand signal rather than a narrative.

The tape has not agreed yet. Per the Stocks list, AskLivermore sees no confirmation of a low in $MU or $SNDK, though the MACD histogram shows seller exhaustion, and he expects a few more marginal lows first. Dan Niles goes further the other way: the semiconductor index had two separate drawdowns above 50 percent in the 1990s and this one is about 25 percent off the peak, which he calls nothing against an index that still ran 850 percent into March 2000.

5. The Treasury Secretary called crypto a national priority and the Senate gave it a 4 percent chance. Per Lark Davis, the third principle of Scott Bessent's economic strategy speech was this: "Digital assets, stablecoins, tokenization, and the new payment systems will help shape the future of money. The United States should not consign itself to the sidelines while that future is built elsewhere." Mohamed El-Erian called it a remarkably important speech.

Set that against the legislature. The Senate has five days before recess and Kalshi prices CLARITY passage at 4 percent, down from 33 for the year and 40 a week earlier.

Benjamin Cowen thinks the whole argument is a distraction. Per his latest, Bitcoin sits further below its fair-value logarithmic regression trend than at any time since 2010, and the four-year cycle says weak for a few more months yet. His prescription is to stop focusing on ETFs, strategic reserves and the CLARITY Act and start fixing fundamentals. Kalshi's traders are blunter, forecasting Bitcoin crashes to $50,000 this year.

Self-custody also took a real hit. Per the Market list, Jonathan Goodman lost 18.25 Bitcoin in the July 29 ColdCard hack, from a device in a safety deposit box that had never touched the internet, after one line of 2021 seed-generation code was brute-forced with AI.

6. Coinbase built the rails for agent payments and earns almost nothing from them. On Friday I said nobody had covered $COIN and it deserved a look before the CLARITY vote. Per Milk Road on the Stocks list, here is that look. Revenue was $1.22 billion against roughly $1.29 billion expected with a GAAP net loss of $359 million, into a quarter when crypto spot volume fell 25 percent.

What got built underneath is the argument. Per Artemis data in Coinbase's own deck, more than 99 percent of onchain agentic commerce settled in USDC, more than 97 percent ran through x402 and more than 90 percent over Base. Brian Armstrong's framing is that there will soon be more AI agents than humans, and they cannot open bank accounts.

Coinbase Q2Figure
Net revenue not from Bitcoin spot88 percent
Adjusted EBITDA$208 million, 14th straight positive quarter
Headcount4,988 to 4,321
Prediction marketsup 106 percent, past $100 million annualised

The gap is the everything-app race, where Robinhood's event contracts did $156 million in one quarter against Coinbase's $100 million annualised. Kyle Reidhead holds it as a call on CLARITY plus the rebound, with the agentic rails as free upside.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. UBS at $761 billion of 2027 memory spend and a 5-to-12-times re-rating is the most aggressive framing published, and 906 still confirms the reclaim. Buy the thesis, wait for the level, and do not chase into Wednesday's $SNDK print.
  • $SPCX. First earnings report in company history Tuesday, days ahead of the August 6 unlock. Two events that both cut one way into a stock already 47 percent off its June high. Position size is the whole decision.
  • $TSLA. Finished last week with its entire weekly candle including wicks outside the lower Bollinger band, only the second time ever. The first was February 2016, after which it ran 80 percent in eight weeks. One instance is an anecdote rather than a base rate, so treat it as a setup and not a signal.
  • $COIN. At $141 you are paying for the exchange and getting the agent-payment rails for nothing. The CLARITY leg just got priced at 4 percent, so the near-term catalyst is gone and the option is longer-dated than it looked Friday.
  • $ADBE. Eleven times trailing earnings on a 36.6 percent operating margin, capex under 1 percent of revenue, and AI-first recurring revenue past $500 million after tripling. It was the short leg of the book that just blew up, and it rose 28 percent in July while the buildout names halved.
  • $AMD. Reports Tuesday, up about 15 percent off the lows. The read-through to memory pricing in its cost line matters more than the headline.

item.title: [Investing] Eleven green Julys ended, and Aschenbrenner told his investors it was a bank run
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The S&P finished July red without ever reaching 7,499.36, the Nasdaq 100 had its worst July in 22 years and semiconductors their worst month since 2008, and Amazon still posted its best day in fourteen years.
item.content:encoded:
The S&P finished July red without ever reaching 7,499.36, the Nasdaq 100 had its worst July in 22 years and semiconductors their worst month since 2008, and Amazon still posted its best day in fourteen years.

The month that broke the AI trade also broke a decade-long streak, and the man at the centre of it says he was never liquidated at all.

Market context. July finished red on the S&P 500, ending eleven straight green Julys running back to 2015. Per the Market list, the level needed was 7,499.36 and it was never reached, with the same desk that set the line on July 25 confirming the outcome after the bell. The Dow closed its fourth green month in a row, so the two indices split.

Underneath, the damage concentrated exactly where you would expect. The Nasdaq 100 had its worst July in 22 years, per both the Kalshi list and the Financial Markets list. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had its worst month since 2008. Momentum as a factor had its worst month in twenty years, recovering slightly in the final two sessions. The KOSPI ended the month down 20 percent after being down 40 percent at the lows.

Friday itself was a split tape rather than a rout. Amazon closed up 15 percent, its best day since 2012. Apple fell roughly 10 percent and handed the largest-company title back to Nvidia. Roblox fell around 27 percent on Q2 earnings, its worst day on record. Across the month the Magnificent 7 went Microsoft up 21 percent, Amazon up 12, Apple up 5, Nvidia up 2, Alphabet down 1, Meta down 9 and Tesla down 27.

The bond market is where the month actually happened. The 30-year hit 5.27 percent, its highest since June 2007 and 450 basis points above the 2020 low. TLT posted its lowest monthly close since the fund launched in 2002. Oil reclaimed $85 and finished July up 15 percent on Iran. And the VIX closed at its third lowest weekly close since January, into a weekend where strikes have reportedly been ordered.

The scoreboard.

  • Miss, and the level never came close. The S&P needed 7,499.36 to keep eleven green Julys. It finished the month red. Anyone reading a dividend-adjusted chart will see SPY green, so the split is worth knowing before someone tells you the streak survived.
  • Miss. Polymarket had a signed US-Iran ceasefire this month at 55 percent when I carried it on Monday. The month ended with an attack ordered instead.
  • Expired untested. Galaxy Digital's end-of-July catalyst passed without a report, and the $38 fair value against roughly $25 never came into play.
  • Not confirmed. I wrote this morning that Micron needed a 906 close to validate the reclaim. It closed down 5.90 percent instead, so the level stands untaken and the map is still live rather than proven.
  • Standing. My 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August is unchanged, and the long end is still the thing that would move it.

1. The letter says it was a bank run, and it says the fund was never liquidated. Per Diet TBPN, Leopold Aschenbrenner wrote to his investors last night and the letter has been read out nearly line by line. It opens where it should. "We let you down this month. We came closer to permanent capital impairment than is acceptable to us."

His account of the mechanism is more specific than any wire report has been. "On Wednesday night, Thursday morning, we took decisive action to protect LP Capital. We traded a portion of our public portfolio in a block transaction to remove all leverage from the fund and prevent further losses. All shorts were closed and reliance on portfolio financing removed. We currently manage a fully paid for public book, long stock and long fully paid for options, with no margin liquidity risk."

Then the denial, which is the part that changes the story. "The fund was not shut down. It was not liquidated or transformed into a private only fund." He adds that virtually all of his own capital remains in it, and takes full responsibility. His diagnosis of the spiral is that "we started to see increasingly adverse trading in names publicly associated with us," and that "these dynamics are essentially similar to a bank run."

I have been calling this a blowup for three days and I should sharpen that. Selling a block to a willing buyer to meet a margin call is not a rescue and not a wind-down. It is a forced trade at a price you did not choose. The distinction matters because Polymarket's market on whether the fund unwinds has now flipped to no longer projected to unwind, per the Polymarket list.

Two things I am not going to print. Nobody has published the letter itself, and the year-to-date figure splits between roughly 80 percent as read on air and about 40 percent in the Financial Times rendering of the same document. And nobody has a price for the Citadel block. The two numbers circulating are a worked example offered as illustration and an unsourced "40 to 50 cents on the dollar," so treat both as noise.

One genuinely new fact does hold. Per the same source, the Wall Street Journal reports Situational Awareness agreed late Wednesday to sell a $3.5 billion Anthropic stake to a group led by Greenoaks and Sequoia, then walked away Thursday morning and sold the public book instead. That kills the widely repeated claim that he sold half his Anthropic position. He kept it.

The Friday tape on his named holdings was still ugly, and per the People to follow list most of them gapped up at the open and sold off in the first hour. Micron down 5.90 percent, HIVE down 5.67, CleanSpark down 5.36, SanDisk down 5.09, Core Scientific down 5.00.

2. Amazon's headline beat looks worse the further into the cash flow statement you read. The operating quarter is real and I said so this morning. AWS did $42.2 billion, up 37 percent, its fastest in eighteen quarters, at a 39 percent operating margin, adding $4.6 billion of quarterly revenue at roughly 80 percent above its previous record.

Now the forensics. Per a line-item read of the filing, stripping the Anthropic mark leaves earnings of $1.68 per share against guidance of $1.82, a miss and flat year over year. The reported 33 percent rise in operating cash flow rests on an income tax deferral. Undo it and operating cash flow is roughly $27.7 billion, down about 15 percent.

The finding worth carrying forward is the securities line. Purchases of non-marketable securities, meaning stakes in private companies and mostly Anthropic, ran $24.4 billion in the second quarter alone and $39.8 billion across the first half. The comparable figure for all of 2025 was $4.8 billion. Set that against the $25 billion AWS-AI annual run rate Amazon discloses and the circularity is not an accusation, it is arithmetic. The last bond offering was 1.4 times oversubscribed against a typical investment-grade four times, and long-term debt has risen 96 percent in two quarters to $129 billion.

Apple went the other way on the same day for the opposite reason, down about 10 percent on a September guide of 9 to 11 percent against 12 percent expected, blamed explicitly on the memory shortage.

3. Chanos has the best mechanism anyone has offered for why profits look this good. Per Prof G Markets, Jim Chanos makes an accounting-identity argument rather than a valuation one. Capex spenders capitalise and depreciate over five to ten years. The receivers, Nvidia and Caterpillar and the utilities, book revenue and profit immediately. The same dollar therefore inflates aggregate profits, and he sizes the mismatch in the hundreds of billions a year. His arithmetic is that S&P profits should be growing 8 or 9 percent and are growing 28 or 29.

His precedent has teeth. S&P earnings grew 30 percent from mid-1998 to mid-2000, then fell 40 percent from mid-2000 to mid-2001, as much as during the financial crisis, on a GDP decline of only 1 percent. The cause was order-book cancellation. "People realized they didn't need 10,000 routers, they needed 2,000."

He says this is 1999 rather than 1997, and his tell is equity issuance, which he calls foolproof and which did not accelerate last time until late 1999. He also puts hyperscaler return on incremental invested capital as roughly halved in eighteen months, from 100 percent to 25 at some names and the teens at a couple, and gives it twelve to eighteen months before boards start asking. He is short bitcoin miners turned data centre companies, the neoclouds, and Tesla and SpaceX by name, while long the indices including Nvidia.

The honest counterweight comes from Phil Rosen, who has the equal-weight S&P up 12.2 percent this year against 8.7 for the cap-weighted index, the NYSE advance-decline line near all-time highs, two thirds of the index above where it started June and eight of eleven sectors higher. Both men are looking at the same equal-weight strength. Rosen calls it healthy broadening. Chanos calls it proof the whole market is dearer than 1999, when at least Walmart and Caterpillar traded at 10 to 12 times rather than 40 to 50.

I lean Chanos on the mechanism and Rosen on the timing. The profit-inflation argument is arithmetic and does not need a catalyst. The breadth argument says the unwind has not started. Those are compatible, and together they argue the risk is 2027 rather than August.

4. Microsoft changed two accounting policies on the same call, and both flatter the same stock. Per a reading of the transcript, the company said it is "extending the estimated useful life of our data centers and office buildings from 15 to 25 years" at the start of fiscal 2027. That lowers depreciation, which lifts operating profit and margin.

The second change is larger and got almost no coverage. In Microsoft's own words, "more of our future data center leases will shift from finance leases to operating leases as a result of this update. Finance leases are included in capital expenditures while operating leases are not." Reported free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capex, so moving lease spend out of capex mechanically raises it.

Take them together and the profit multiple and the cash flow multiple both improve without the business changing. The stock rose 15 percent on the print. This is checkable against the filing and it silently reprices every model anyone builds on Microsoft next year, including the reverse discounted cash flow work below.

Two of those are worth the space. Per one model, Microsoft at $451.10 implies about 20.3 percent annual unlevered free cash flow growth for a decade against a realised roughly 4 percent over fiscal 2022 to 2025, with a bear case of $202, a base of $310 and a bull of $368. The price sits 23 percent above the author's own bull case. Per the companion, ASML at $1,655 implies 25.5 percent for ten years, taking free cash flow from around $10 billion to roughly $97 billion, against a bull case of $1,086.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU did not take 906 and closed down 5.90 percent. The reclaim map is unproven rather than broken, and Michael Burry is still short from $880.
  • $AMZN closed its best day since 2012 on genuine AWS acceleration, with $24.4 billion of private-company purchases in one quarter against $4.8 billion in all of 2025 and a bond book only 1.4 times covered.
  • $MSFT gets a depreciation change and a lease reclassification from fiscal 2027 that lift reported profit and reported free cash flow without touching the business.
  • $COIN settles more than 99 percent of onchain agentic commerce in USDC, 97 percent through x402 and 90 percent on Base, per Artemis data in its own deck, and earns almost nothing from any of it. It fell about 5 percent on a $359 million loss.
  • $SNDK is down 50 percent in a month and still up 411 percent on the year, with the $1,350 to $1,450 line from this morning still the one that matters.

item.title: [Investing] The Journal put a number on it, and Situational Awareness lost 67 percent
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Microsoft added $450 billion of market value in one session, the largest single-day gain on record, Apple beat and fell anyway on a soft September guide, and Amazon put $20 billion of memory cost straight into capex.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft added $450 billion of market value in one session, the largest single-day gain on record, Apple beat and fell anyway on a soft September guide, and Amazon put $20 billion of memory cost straight into capex.

For two days the drawdown at the centre of this selloff had no number attached. Now it does, and it is worse than the rumour I declined to print.

Market context. Into the last session of July, the setup is a violent reversal still looking for confirmation. Thursday was the squeeze: more than a trillion dollars went back into US equities, the S&P rose better than a hundred points, and per the People to follow list three American companies each added over $100 billion of market value in a single day. Microsoft added $450 billion, Micron $153 billion, Nvidia $122 billion.

Microsoft's move deserves its own line. Up roughly 15 percent, the largest single-day market-cap gain in stock market history. Per the Stocks list, OddStats counts only three better days in the company's entire history, and they came in October 1987, October 2000 and October 2008. That is the company this move keeps.

Overnight the follow-through has held. S&P and Nasdaq 100 futures are both green, the KOSPI is up around 14 percent with SK Hynix and Samsung each better than 25 percent, and Seoul is putting roughly $13.9 billion into its sovereign wealth fund for AI data centres. The Bank of Japan held at 1.00 percent on an 8-1 vote after the finance ministry intervened in the yen ahead of the decision.

Two things to watch into the open. Apple sits down about six and a half percent after hours and Amazon up seven to ten. And it is month end, with the S&P needing 7,499.36 at today's close to keep eleven straight green Julys.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, and it was mine to publish. I put Micron's map at 770 the low, 832 the level lost and 872 the reclaim that makes a bounce real. It closed above 872 Thursday and ran to 925 overnight. MentoviaX now wants a 906 close to confirm.
  • Confirmed, after I twice refused to print it. The Wall Street Journal has Situational Awareness down 67 percent in July. I withheld an unsourced "more than 50 percent" on Wednesday and again on Thursday. The real figure was worse than the rumour, and waiting cost nothing.
  • Resolved. The big-tech earnings week is done. Apple and Amazon both beat on the headline and both guided September below consensus.
  • Thin, and I am not dressing it up. Strategy reported Thursday. The only figures anywhere are bitcoin holdings up 11 percent on the quarter and dollar reserves up 12. No revenue, no earnings, no comparison to the roughly $3.07 that was expected.
  • Due at today's close. The S&P streak at 7,499.36, the KOSPI call, Galaxy Digital's end-July catalyst, and Polymarket's US-Iran ceasefire market, which was priced at 55 percent for a deal signed this month and has hours left.

1. Sixty-seven percent, and the fund is already raising again. Per the Financial Markets list, the Journal's headline is flat: Situational Awareness down 67 percent in July. Set that against a fund that was up 439 percent after fees through June 30 and, per the Crypto list, carried a net asset value of $45 billion on July 1. The shape of it is clear. This was not a bad month layered on a bad year. It was one month eating five months of a spectacular run.

The mechanics still rest on Martin Shkreli's reconstruction rather than a filing, and he says so. His arithmetic, relayed on TBPN: start at $45 billion, assume $10 billion sits in Anthropic, leaving roughly $35 billion of equity, run it three to four times levered for about $120 billion of gross market value. A 25 percent drop in gross takes $30 billion off, which sounds survivable until you notice it comes out of the $35 billion of equity rather than the $120 billion of gross. "No prime broker is going to let you keep $90 billion of GMV."

What is new since yesterday is smaller and stranger. Citadel Securities reportedly paid around $10 billion for most of the public book. The Anthropic stake was retained. And per the Kalshi list, Aschenbrenner was already seeking new capital inside 24 hours of the blowup. Polymarket has opened a market on whether he is criminally charged, which tells you more about the audience than the odds.

One correction I owe from yesterday. I wrote that the accounts disagreed on assets under management, with $20 billion, $24 billion and $45 billion in circulation. The Journal's $45 billion NAV as of July 1 is the figure to use.

2. Was Thursday a bottom or a squeeze? I lean squeeze, and the odds are not close. Ron Insana said it plainly on the tape: semis up 15 to 24 percent "smacks of a short-squeeze, not a meaningful bottom." Mac10's read on Microsoft is harsher, that the biggest rallies happen in bear markets. Against them, JPMorgan has the Korean leveraged-ETF unwind essentially finished, Goldman's Alvin So has those assets down from a $53 billion June peak to $15 or $16 billion, and Tom Lee's prime-brokerage data shows hedge funds degrossing tech at the fastest pace in nearly a decade.

Both can be true, and here is the distinction that matters. The forced seller really is gone, which removes the thing that made every red day worse. That is not the same as demand arriving. A squeeze that removes an overhang leaves you at a fair price with no buyer, and the tell will be whether the second and third days hold rather than whether the first one was violent.

I am 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August, unchanged from Wednesday. The one thing that would move me is the long end, and the thirty-year has not printed a level worth trading on since it cleared 5.24 percent.

3. Apple beat on both lines and fell up to eight percent, and the quality of the beat is why. Per the People to follow list, earnings came in at $2.02 against $1.89 and revenue at $109.42 billion against $108.65 billion, with gross margin at 50.1 percent, the highest in company history. iPhone grew 22 percent and Mac beat by more than a billion and a half.

Then read the composition. Eleven cents of that earnings beat and roughly two points of the gross margin came from $600 million of tariff refunds. Strip them and the quarter is $1.91 against $1.89 expected, a two-cent beat rather than a thirteen-cent one, at a gross margin near 48 percent rather than a company record. Services missed at $30.74 billion, Greater China missed at $18.82 billion, and iPad missed. September revenue is guided to 9 to 11 percent growth against the 16 percent just delivered, with gross margin guided down to 47 to 48 percent, and that range already includes a point of the same tariff benefit.

Apple went into the print at 35 times forward earnings against a five-year average of 28, up 22 percent on the year. At that multiple a beat propped by a tax refund and guided down afterwards is a sell, and the tape walked it from minus three to nearly minus eight through the evening.

This was Tim Cook's final earnings call as chief executive.

4. Amazon's headline beat is mostly a mark, and its capex line is the real news. Earnings of $5.75 against $1.82 expected looks like the beat of the year until you find the composition. Per the Polymarket list, quarterly profit was $62.6 billion and the gain on the Anthropic stake accounted for most of it, booked at $53.4 billion in one account and roughly $36 billion in another. Either way, strip it and you have a good operating quarter rather than a historic one.

The good operating quarter is real. AWS did $42.2 billion, up 37 percent, its fastest in 18 quarters, at a 39.4 percent operating margin against 33.8 expected, with $496 billion of contracted backlog not yet online. Amazon crossed $200 billion of quarterly revenue for the first time.

The cost of it is where I would spend your attention. Capex guidance for 2026 went to $220 billion, and management named higher memory prices as the reason for roughly $20 billion of that. Second-quarter capex was $54.2 billion against $32.1 billion a year ago. Trailing free cash flow has swung to negative $7.6 billion from positive $18.2 billion, and long-term debt has nearly doubled since December to $128.9 billion. Guidance for the third quarter came in at $197 to $202 billion against $204 billion expected.

5. Two of the largest buyers on earth confirmed the memory squeeze within an hour of each other. Amazon put $20 billion of memory cost into its capex line. Tim Cook, asked about DRAM, said Apple is "evaluating all options" with supply concentrated among Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung. Apple's inventories have nearly doubled since September, from $5.7 billion to $11.1 billion. That is what stockpiling ahead of a shortage looks like on a balance sheet.

That is the demand side agreeing with what the suppliers have been saying all week. SK Hynix has sold out its 2026 high-bandwidth memory, lines are booked through 2027, and Samsung guides tightness into 2028.

The trade is no longer cheap, though. Micron reclaimed 872 and ran to 925 overnight, roughly 30 percent off its trough inside 24 hours. Michael Burry used the move to add to his Micron short at $880 and to a semiconductor index short at $506. When the fundamental case is this well telegraphed and the stock has moved this fast, the edge sits in the levels rather than the story, and 906 is the number that confirms it.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU closed above 872 and traded 925 overnight. 906 confirms, and MentoviaX maps 932, 955, 973 and 991 above that. Burry is short from $880, which makes this the cleanest disagreement on the board.
  • $AAPL guided September to 9 to 11 percent against 16 percent delivered, with gross margin stepping down to 47 to 48. Inventories at $11.1 billion and a new chief executive taking over into a memory squeeze.
  • $AMZN has AWS at a $168.8 billion run rate growing 37 percent with a $496 billion backlog, against $220 billion of 2026 capex and free cash flow already negative.
  • $SNDK ran hard with the complex. Per the Market list, Heisenberg puts the line in the sand at $1,350 to $1,450, and a failed breakout there makes Thursday a dead cat and sets up a 200-day retest.
  • $COIN reported a loss of $1.36 against $0.42 expected and fell more than six percent. Nobody covered it Thursday and it deserves a look before the CLARITY vote, not after.

item.title: [Investing] The forced seller had a name, and Citadel bought the book
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Situational Awareness dumped its entire public equity book in one block, everything it owned ripped twenty percent, and Microsoft had its best day since 2008 while market breadth stayed negative all session.
item.content:encoded:
Situational Awareness dumped its entire public equity book in one block, everything it owned ripped twenty percent, and Microsoft had its best day since 2008 while market breadth stayed negative all session.

Yesterday the question was whether the AI trade was breaking. This morning it turned out to be a margin call with an address.

Market context. Two macro prints landed before the open and neither one explains the day. Per the Polymarket list, second-quarter GDP came in at 1.5 percent against 2.1 percent expected. Per the Crypto list, core PCE rose 0.1 percent on the month against 0.2 percent expected, with headline at 3.7 percent and core at 3.3 percent year over year, both in line. A growth miss and a tenth of cooler core inflation.

Per threadguy's open, the tape went up anyway, hard and narrow. Microsoft rose about 15 percent to roughly $445, its best day since 2008, adding close to $500 billion of market value on its highest short interest in a decade. QQQ gained almost 3 percent, SOXX added 10 percent, and roughly a trillion dollars went back in by early afternoon.

Then the part that matters more. Per the Financial Markets list, Linda Raschke watched breadth stay negative from the opening bell across the top forty NYSE and top forty Nasdaq names she tracks, "with semis and MSFT painting the tape." Mark Minervini is still carrying the SPY short he put on July 27, notes the indexes remain below their fifty-day averages, and calls this the most bifurcated market of a 43-year career. A trillion dollars came back on two sectors.

The long end is still the constraint. The thirty-year hit 5.24 percent overnight, a 19-year high, before easing during the session. Kalshi now prices a 69 percent chance the Fed hikes at some point this year and an 89 percent chance it does not cut. For September specifically, Polymarket sits near 56 percent and CME FedWatch splits it 60/40, so the 55/45 I published Wednesday needs no revision.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, and not mine. Bernstein and Piper Sandler modelled roughly $150 million of Robinhood event-contract revenue. It printed $156 million and out-earned both crypto and equities. The stock fell anyway, and the watchlist has the reason.
  • Standing, and it mattered today. Micron rallied about 15 percent and still did not reclaim 832. The map I published Wednesday survives its first violent test intact.
  • Contradicted, not due. I carried John Thune confirming a CLARITY floor vote before the recess. Kalshi now prices passage this year at 36 to 40 percent, Cynthia Lummis has rejected the latest rewrite, and JPMorgan says openly that delay is now a threat to crypto markets. That call runs to August 10 and stays open, marked against.
  • Due tomorrow. The S&P needs 7,499.36 on Friday's close to keep eleven straight green Julys. Galaxy Digital's end-July catalyst also lands.
  • Due tonight. Strategy hosts its Q2 call at 5pm Eastern, and Apple reports after the bell against a $1.89 consensus.

1. Situational Awareness sold everything, and the buyer was the firm that called for a hike two days earlier. Start with what four named outlets have actually reported, because the rumour layer around this is thick. Per Diet TBPN, Bloomberg had the fund seeking capital at 9:25pm Wednesday, the Financial Times had the LP letters the same night, CNBC reported at 6:05am Thursday that Leopold Aschenbrenner had been forced to unwind all public stock positions, and the Wall Street Journal reported at 8:39am that Ken Griffin's Citadel had agreed to buy the portfolio. CNBC's David Faber adds that the exit covered the entire public book, longs and shorts, through a single buyer.

The book was long AI infrastructure and short software. Per the Market list, the largest positions were Nebius, SanDisk, CoreWeave, IREN, Bloom Energy and TeraWulf, with a short leg in names like Adobe. Concentration was extreme, though the accounts disagree on which name was largest.

Then the day itself. Per the Stocks list, every one of those names ripped the moment the seller was replaced: Bloom Energy up 26 percent, Nebius 25 and briefly 33, SharonAI 26, IREN 25, SanDisk 20, CoreWeave 20, AMD 13. Micron gained 15. That is what removing a forced seller looks like, and it is not the same thing as news.

Now the part everyone is saying and nobody has proved. Citadel publicly forecast a surprise Fed hike on Tuesday. The market sold off. The Fed held Wednesday. Situational Awareness was margin called. Citadel bought the book Thursday. Per the Financial Markets list, InvestorsLive, Mr_Derivatives, NotSoEasyMoney and ThinkingUSD all lay out that sequence and draw the obvious conclusion. I report the sequence because it is documented and the inference because it is widespread. There is no evidence of intent, and a wrong rate call is not a crime. Hold it as a question about market structure rather than a finding.

I marked Citadel's hike forecast a miss on Wednesday. It stays a miss. Being wrong on the rate and right on the trade are different scoreboards.

2. Nobody knows how bad it was, and the number people keep repeating is not sourced. There is still no confirmed drawdown figure. Per Martin Shkreli, who broke the story before the wires, one of the three bidding parties told him his numbers were "a little off" and refused to say in which direction, and he got pushback that the fund was "only down 30%." His own arithmetic is explicitly hypothetical, and the 4x leverage figure is his sourcing too.

The assets under management do not agree either, with $45 billion, $24 billion and $20 billion all in circulation. Those do not reconcile and I am not picking one.

Two things I withheld on Wednesday held up. The "down more than 50 percent" line remains unconfirmed. The claim that he held billions of puts across the semiconductor complex now looks actively wrong, because a levered long book taken over by its prime brokers is the opposite of a hedged one.

The best frame came from Numerai's Richard Craib. At 150 percent volatility, variance drag alone is 113 percent a year and risk of ruin is roughly a coin flip over a fund's life. "A child can do the math on a napkin." A position-sizing outcome, not a verdict on AI infrastructure.

3. Microsoft and Meta finally explained the capex split, and it is about who has to borrow. Per the People to follow list, Azure passed $100 billion of annual revenue for the first time and grew 43 percent, its fastest since early 2022 and up from 39 percent two quarters ago. Capex came in at $41 billion against roughly $42 billion expected. Citi took its target to $600, Wells Fargo to $650, Piper Sandler to $550, all the same morning.

Meta is the same story inverted, and the number is stark. It bought back zero stock last quarter and borrowed $24.9 billion instead. Long-term debt went from $58.7 billion at year end to $83.7 billion. Property and equipment sits at $225.7 billion, up nearly $50 billion in six months. A year ago the same quarter carried $10.2 billion of buybacks and no new debt.

That is the actual distinction the market priced. Not discipline versus indiscipline, but funded from cash versus funded from the bond market, at a moment when the thirty-year sits at a 19-year high.

Per Prof G Markets, DA Davidson's Gil Lurria narrows it to a single word. Amy Hood said capex would be "up" year over year. Alphabet's finance chief said it would grow "significantly" a week earlier and got punished for it. Same buildout, different verb, ten points of stock. One caveat on Microsoft's side, from the Stocks list: Amy Hood is extending data-centre useful life from 15 to 25 years starting in fiscal 2027, which cuts annual depreciation on the same assets and flatters everything below the capex line.

4. Memory got fundamentally better and cheaper on the same day. Per the Crypto list, Samsung posted second-quarter operating profit of 89.5 trillion won against 4.68 trillion a year ago, on revenue up 130 percent to 171.5 trillion won. Both records. SK Hynix cleared 50 trillion won of quarterly revenue for the first time at a record operating margin, reported between 72 and 76 percent.

The guidance is the thesis. Samsung says supply stays short into 2028 and that the 2027 shortage will be worse than this year's. Both Korean makers have stopped signing multi-year contracts entirely, betting on higher prices through 2027. SK Hynix describes HBM, DRAM and NAND as essentially sold out for 2026 with lines booked through 2027. The mechanism underneath is that high-bandwidth memory eats roughly three times the wafer capacity per gigabyte of standard DRAM, so AI demand starves the commodity side too.

Against that, both trade near four times this year's earnings and three times next year's, against roughly 35 times for the rest of the chip complex. UBS initiated SK Hynix at a $204 target, and Chairman Choi Tae-won bought more than $3 million of his own stock in the open market.

I stay 65/35 that memory multiples expand before they compress, unchanged. Today's 15 percent bounce did not reclaim 832 on Micron, so nothing about the level map changed either.

5. Korea is nearly done deleveraging, and that is the cleanest bullish fact available. Per the Stocks list, the KOSPI closed at 5,663.24, down 5.98 percent after a 10.84 percent drop the day before, with circuit breakers firing on both the KOSPI and the KOSDAQ two sessions running for the first time simultaneously. The month is the worst in Korean market history, past October 1997 at 27 percent and October 2008 at 23 percent.

The human number is worse than the index number. Citi counts more than 360,000 forced margin liquidations with 62 percent of them under age 35. Per Lark Davis, 1.2 million accounts were margin called and 34 trillion won evaporated in a month, roughly one in every thirty Korean adults.

Here is why it matters for positioning. Goldman's Alvin So has Korea-focused leveraged ETF assets down from a $53 billion peak on June 22, then 3.2 percent of Korean free float, to $15 or $16 billion now, about 1.5 percent. More than seventy percent of the exposure is gone. JPMorgan puts the deleveraging between 75 and 90 percent complete. From July 31 the minimum cash deposit on new leveraged ETF purchases jumps to 30 million won, about $20,300, cash only.

My lean. The mechanical seller is nearly out of ammunition and that is genuinely bullish, but one 3 percent day on negative breadth is not a bottom. I am 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August, and the 40 is Minervini's point that nothing has printed a follow-through day yet. The thing that would flip me is the thirty-year rather than the tape.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU rallied roughly 15 percent and still failed 832. The map is unchanged: 770 the low, 832 the level lost, 872 the reclaim that makes a bounce real. Morgan Stanley checks point to wafer prices up 10 to 30 percent in 2027, and Micron has signed a ten-year GlobalWafers deal and put $500 million into the Sherman, Texas fab to lock supply.
  • $HOOD printed a record quarter and got cut anyway. Per Milk Road, Barclays went $122 to $105, Goldman $137 to $118 and Needham $123 to $120, all three having raised those same targets days earlier.
  • $NBIS was the biggest position in the liquidated book and ran as much as 33 percent. John Galt's $132 line held, and the September 11 warrant date is still the dilution to watch.
  • $AAPL reports tonight against $1.89 and roughly $109 billion. Per Stocks with Josh, 344 is a full hundred-percent measured move off the impulse leg and he is selling December calls at 360 to 365 into it rather than buying puts. Gene Munster's read is that the call hinges on whether Tim Cook can date the new Siri leaving beta.
  • $BE ran 26 percent on the unwind and topped $1 billion of revenue for the first time. The Hunterbrook scandium claim is still unanswered.

item.title: [Investing] The Fed held, three officials dissented for a hike, and the thirty-year broke out
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Kevin Warsh said there is no soft inflation target, the S&P turned green at 2:47pm and gave every bit of it back for a trillion-dollar day, and Benjamin Cowen's call that a hold forces the long end higher landed inside 24 hours.
item.content:encoded:
Kevin Warsh said there is no soft inflation target, the S&P turned green at 2:47pm and gave every bit of it back for a trillion-dollar day, and Benjamin Cowen's call that a hold forces the long end higher landed inside 24 hours.

Last night I said the thing to watch was not the decision but the thirty-year the morning after. That took less than an afternoon.
