Market context. The Fed held the target range at 3.50 to 3.75 percent, a fifth straight hold, and the vote is the story. Per the Polymarket list it went 9 to 3, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan all dissenting in favour of a hike. Per the Stocks list that is the most dissents since 2016, and every one of them wanted rates higher.

Kevin Warsh then removed any comfort the hold offered. He said the committee remains resolute on price stability and that "there is no soft inflation target because the target is 2%." On killing forward guidance he was plainer still: "Market participants are learning to play the ball, not the referee." Andreas Steno's read was blunt. "Warsh is the driver of the tech sell-off."

The tape agreed and then disagreed with itself inside forty minutes. Per the Kalshi list, almost $400 billion was added to the S&P 500 in the five minutes after 2pm, and by 2:47pm the index was green on the day. It ended with more than a trillion dollars erased. QQQ went 680 to 663 into the bell and printed $656 after hours, the Nasdaq 100 is more than ten percent off its peak, and the S&P is tracking its worst July since 2007.

The long end is where the damage actually is. The thirty-year yield had been trying to clear 5.2 percent since October 2023 and broke through today, its highest since before the 2008 crisis. Jeff Park dated it precisely, the highest since July 31, 2007.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit. My hold call at 78/22 landed, and so did the hawkish-statement leg at 55/45. Warsh gave the market the pause and none of the relief.
  • Hit inside 24 hours, and not mine. Benjamin Cowen said last night a hold is what triggers the revolt and would push the thirty-year through 5.2 percent. It did, today. The rest of his thesis, a September hike and a 10 to 20 percent drawdown, runs to end-September and stays open.
  • Miss, and not mine. Citadel Securities flipped its forecast to a hike and was wrong. Polymarket never took the hike above 26 percent.
  • Hit, and not mine. Bernstein's Gautam Chhugani and Piper Sandler both modelled roughly $150 million of Robinhood event-contract revenue. It printed $156 million.
  • Due inside two sessions. GDP and June PCE tomorrow morning, Apple and Amazon tomorrow after the close, Strategy's Q2 on Thursday.

1. The Fed got less hawkish on the front end and the bond market revolted anyway, and that contradiction is the trade. Per Cowen, market-implied odds the Fed is still at 3.75 percent in September rose from 23 percent before the release to almost 43 after, so September hike odds fell from roughly 77 to 57. That is a dovish repricing. Meanwhile Michael Bento left the press conference saying "this sounded very hawkish" and now expects a September hike, and the thirty-year broke a three-year ceiling.

Both are true once you separate the instruments. Warsh made the next meeting less certain and the inflation target less negotiable. Killing forward guidance cuts the odds on any single meeting while raising the premium demanded for thirty-year paper, because the buyer no longer gets told what comes next. Per the threadguy stream, meetings used to sit at 90 to 98 percent certainty a week out. This one sat at 75.

My lean, and it is a change. I am 60/40 the next move is a hike and 55/45 that it lands in September, revised down from the near-certainty the odds implied on Monday. Warsh has now shown he will accept three dissents rather than move early, and a chair who tolerates that much internal disagreement is not being rushed by it.

2. Good numbers kept getting sold, and tonight the market finally said what it is actually pricing. Per the Milk Road note, the pattern was already two for two. Alphabet grew revenue 24 percent with cloud up 82 against a 67 percent expectation, and fell more than 5 percent on raised capex and its first negative free cash flow ever. SK Hynix printed the biggest quarter in its history, revenue up 257 percent and profit up 557 at 76 percent margins, and fell 9 percent on a 6 percent miss caused by capacity rather than demand.

Then tonight resolved it. Per the People to follow list and the Market list:

Microsoft FQ4Meta Q2
Revenue$90.0B vs $87.6B est$60.8B vs $60.3B est
EPS$4.74 vs $4.22 est$6.18 vs $7.22 est
Capex signal2026 guidance held flatfull-year floor raised to $130B
Free cash flow$19.6B$784M, from $8.55B a year ago
After hoursup as much as 10%down as much as 10%

Microsoft also extended data-centre useful life from 15 to 25 years, which cuts annual depreciation on the same assets by roughly 40 percent and lands straight in reported earnings. Meta said a cloud business is not a priority and fell to fresh 52-week lows on its longest losing streak in company history.

Amit Kukreja put the tape in five words. "The street hates capex." That is not quite it. The street hates capex it cannot see the end of, and it paid up today for the company that drew a line.

3. The memory trade has floor prices underneath it now, and the tape does not care yet. Micron has signed 16 multi-year take-or-pay agreements. Per Rick Orford, 14 carry about $100 billion of cumulative revenue at minimum contract prices, plus $22 billion of expected deposits, and most of the largest include explicit floor prices. Per his longer piece they cover roughly 20 percent of DRAM volume and a third of NAND, against a reported quarter of $41.5 billion at an 80.4 percent operating margin and 9.2 times earnings.

Now the other side. Per Chip Stock Investor, Jason Hall's point is that memory names are price takers, so "they can look the cheapest right when they are the most expensive," and the tell that supply is coming is ASML calling memory a huge opportunity to place machines while Micron guides its own capex up.

The floor prices break the tie for me. A fifth of DRAM volume contracted at a minimum price is the first structural answer anyone has given to what happens when the cycle turns, and Hall's argument, for all its mechanical elegance, arrives with no numbers attached. I stay 65/35 that memory multiples expand before they compress, unchanged from Saturday, and the thing that flips it is ASML order detail rather than another week of red candles.

4. Korea stopped being a chart and became a retail solvency event. The KOSPI is down roughly 40 percent from its high, more than 360,000 margin accounts have been wiped out, and Korean retail has lost 56 trillion won, about $38.7 billion, on leveraged products. The finance minister apologised publicly.

Two facts sit against that. Samsung posted record Q2 operating profit of $61.7 billion, up 1,814 percent. And per Milk Road's panel, the CXMT listing that triggered the unwind may not deserve the read-through it got, because CXMT runs zero EUV layers against Samsung's seven and cannot make high-bandwidth memory at all for lack of an advanced logic die.

5. Torsten Slok has the best explanation for why the AI trade cracked now, and it is a credit story. Per Prof G Markets, Apollo's chief economist notes hyperscalers shifted financing from equity to debt and credit default swap prices hit record highs on Oracle, SpaceX, Google, Amazon and now Nvidia. These are among the most profitable companies alive, so the widening is not about default. It is the market repricing when the AI payoff arrives, and slower future cash flow means a lower equity price today.

His diversification math is the uncomfortable part. The ten largest stocks are 40 percent of the index and 87 percent of venture capital is now AI, so the same bet sits in public equity, public credit and private markets at once. Nine of the twelve biggest contributors to the S&P 500's first-half return were semiconductors.

The bull rebuttal is specific enough to weigh. Per the Stocks list, Gavin Baker argues spot GPU rental prices run at least twice contracted rates, so hyperscalers are underearning and whoever signed compute contracts in 2024 or 2025 is overearning. Dwarkesh Patel supplies the number underneath it, with Google reportedly paying $900 million a month for 110,000 GPUs rented from SpaceX at roughly twice spot.

6. Bitcoin refused to move all month, and the most bullish voice in crypto just named his floor. Per the Crypto list, BTC sat either side of $64,000 through the Fed, pinned in a $4,000 range for nineteen days, with a month low of $62,206. Long-term holders control a record 79 percent of supply and the fear gauge reads 28.

Per the Ansem interview, the man who called himself more bullish than ever gives a band rather than a slogan. The top of the range is $85,000, he was certain $60,000 would break and it did not, and his floor is explicit: "I really don't think we're going to break 58 to 60." His invalidation is clean at $40,000, which he says would mean SOL near $40 and another four to six months of waiting. He also names who defended the level. Michael Saylor sold $200 million at $60,000 after buying every top for five years, the ETFs were sellers too, and quiet institutional money took the other side.

Hold that band against the book. It contradicts Nansen's $52,000 to $58,000 retest call, answers Zach Pandl's open question about a $58,000 bottom, and sits inside Novogratz's $60,000 to $85,000 range for the year. Three independent people now bracket the same zone, and the argument is down to about two thousand dollars on the low end.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU filled 751 and closed under 800. The map from four handles is 770 as the low still standing, 832 as the level lost, and 872 as the reclaim that makes any bounce real. Floor-priced contracts on a fifth of DRAM volume is the thesis. The 100-day average is the line.
  • $HOOD is the cleanest print of the night. Event contracts did $156 million against $129 million of equities and $100 million of crypto, so prediction markets out-earned both, and 13 business lines now clear $100 million of annual recurring revenue on record $21.7 billion of net deposits.
  • $NBIS has Nvidia holding 9.3 percent after a $2 billion investment and 5 gigawatts of planned capacity by 2030. Per Rick Orford it trades near 54 times earnings. The September 11 warrant date and $4.3 billion of convertibles are the dilution to watch, and John Galt's line in the sand is $132.
  • $BE raised full-year revenue guidance to $3.9 to $4.2 billion on revenue up 166 percent, and Brookfield expanded its financing from $5 billion to $25 billion on June 30. Per Milk Road the unresolved risk is Hunterbrook's claim that five gigawatts of output needs about 220 tons of scandium oxide a year against roughly 240 tons of global supply. Bloom calls that false and has published no counter-number.
  • $QCOM beat on revenue and guided fourth-quarter earnings to $2.15 against $2.38 expected, a ten percent shortfall nobody wrote about tonight. The company blamed "unprecedented increases in memory pricing," so the memory trade is now arriving as somebody else's cost line.
  • $SPCX printed a new low of $107 against a $135 listing and reports for the first time in early August, with roughly a billion shares unlocking days later. Per the Limitless podcast the offset is about $60 billion of compute sold over nine to twelve months, Anthropic alone at $1.25 billion a month. Morningstar has it at $63 and Morgan Stanley's bull case is $600, and a ten-fold analyst spread is its own information.

item.title: [Investing] A Jerusalem wire report turned the Nasdaq 100 correction green by lunch
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: QQQ printed $673 premarket, ten percent off the June peak in 38 trading days, then the Times of Israel reported Washington and Tehran near reviving the failed memorandum and the tape reversed. Apple touched $5 trillion on the way through.
item.content:encoded:
QQQ printed $673 premarket, ten percent off the June peak in 38 trading days, then the Times of Israel reported Washington and Tehran near reviving the failed memorandum and the tape reversed. Apple touched $5 trillion on the way through.

Market context. The levels below run through midday. The Tuesday close lands in tomorrow's AM.

The session did something worth the whole edition. QQQ hit $673 premarket, which put the Nasdaq 100 down ten percent from its June peak and into a correction. Per the Stocks list, it took 38 trading days to get there against more than a hundred for the prior ten-percent drawdown, and this was the fifth consecutive down day, the worst run of 2026. By 10:39am the index was eleven percent off its all-time high. At 11:42am it was green.

The catalyst landed at 11:20am, a Times of Israel report that mediators believe the United States and Iran are close to reviving the memorandum that collapsed earlier this month. Crude fell five percent on it, Brent went below $84 and WTI below $80, and the ten-year sat at 4.5 percent. Hold the oil move against one fact from the Financial Markets list: physical transits through Hormuz today were zero tankers in either direction. Crude fell five percent on a report about a document while the actual waterway carried nothing.

SPY held $735. The Dow was up one percent, and the internals under that number cut against something I relayed yesterday. BowTied Bull's rotation call, corroborated by Yardeni Research, had money leaving megacap tech for industrials. Today XLI finished the morning lower while the index it belongs to rose one percent, and Caterpillar fell specifically on data-centre exposure while Deere rose. That is the AI trade leaking into an industrial name and dragging it, rather than a rotation into the sector. One session does not settle a call dated to December, so I am recording it as contradicted and leaving it open.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit. The Netanyahu meeting call from Saturday resolved this morning. He is at the White House today, on the eve of the decision, exactly as Polymarket priced it.
  • Contradicted, not resolved. The industrials rotation I relayed from BowTied Bull yesterday runs into CAT falling on data-centre exposure while DE rose, per the Market list. The call is dated to December and stays open, marked against.
  • Hit, and not ours. 0xResearch's CXMT pre-IPO market called the Shanghai debut to within 2.6 percent, implying roughly RMB48.20 into a RMB49.50 opening print against public forecasts spanning RMB45 to RMB75. Per 0xResearch, that is a real resolved call for a venue I have been sceptical of.
  • Due in eighteen hours. The Fed, at 2pm tomorrow, into Kevin Warsh's first press conference. Six of my own entries now point at this single decision and I am revising the standing one rather than adding a seventh.
  • Due tonight and tomorrow. SK Hynix reports around 8pm Eastern into the memory tape described below. Robinhood reports tomorrow after the close.

The memory trade has flipped east, and today it stopped being a narrative. Per the threadguy episode, ASML fell 2.5 percent on a headline that China has begun mass-producing homegrown deep-ultraviolet lithography tools for its domestic industry. Tulip King's version of the trade is four words: "long Eastern semis, short Western semis."

CXMT is the instrument. It priced its IPO at $85 billion and now trades near $500 billion. On its first day it took 1.14 percent of all Shanghai Stock Exchange volume, $234 million against an exchange total of $20.5 billion. Per Prof G Markets, that leaves it at roughly 1,600 times earnings, a payback year of 3626, and Ed Elson's summary is the one to keep: "memory investors are beginning to lose their grip on reality." It also has a five-year ByteDance supply agreement worth more than $7 billion and plans that may more than double monthly wafer output.

Two policy datapoints sit underneath, both from the threadguy digest and both single-sourced: the Trump administration is split on additional limits for CXMT and YMTC, and Apple has sought assurances that CXMT will not be added to the entity list. A customer lobbying pre-emptively against a supplier's designation tells you where that customer thinks the supply is.

The cost of the trade showed up in Seoul. Per the Market list, the KOSPI was halted after falling 10.84 percent to 6,023.66, the second-biggest single-day drop on record, and it is now down nearly 29 percent for the month. Per 0xResearch, an SK Hynix perpetual on Hyperliquid flash-crashed to $900 before the KOSPI opened at all, and the guest quoted on it drew the right lesson about thin tokenised wrappers on assets whose real market is shut.

Two things make this more than a China story. Micron broke below $800, and per Chip Stock Investor memory pricing has now appeared as a named cost line in Intuitive Surgical's results. That is the memory cycle arriving in surgical robotics. A DRAM buyer does not get much further from a hyperscaler than that. Meanwhile per AI Central, CoWoS packaging is sold out through year-end with lead times into 2027 and N3 is fully committed through 2026, and AMD signed a definitive agreement with Rackspace for phased deployment of 30 megawatts of Instinct MI355X and MI350P compute beginning late 2026. Supply is committed at the front of the queue and repricing violently at the back.

The problem with the NeoClouds finally has a date on it, and the date is 2032. Per Milk Road AI, the reason to care is not utilisation. It is that the GPUs, the customer contracts and the debt all mature at roughly the same moment, so the entire equity return sits in a residual value nobody has observed. Here is the megawatt he builds it on.

One megawatt of GPU capacityFigure
Build cost$30 million
Debt / equity75 / 25, so $7.5 million equity
Annual revenue$10.5 million
Interest~$1.6 million
Year-one cash$1.4 million, so about negative $6 million after year one
Cash breakevenYear five
Six-year cumulative$3.5 million on $7.5 million, roughly 6 to 7 percent annualised

Then the sensitivity. That is the whole argument. At a residual of 60 percent of initial rental rates the annualised return goes to 23 percent. At 30 percent the trade is over. He holds CoreWeave and Nebius, says he is getting more bearish, and has no model yet. I would rather have that than a model with a fabricated residual in it.

Put that against the other side of the trade and you get a genuine conflict. Per The Chairman's Ledger, a disclosed long in IREN, Nebius and NUAI argues the buildout cannot be stopped because two of its three buyers cannot afford to wait for obvious returns and the third has barely started. His best move is the distinction that depreciation risk sits mostly with whoever owns the chips and far less with whoever owns the site, power and lease. His most honest line is the one he refuses to beat: "It's telco in 1999... The demand did show up, just ten yrs late, and the people who bought it out of bankruptcy made the money." What is missing is every number. No megawatts, no backlog, no capex, no price target, nothing comparing his three names at these prices.

Meanwhile per Rick Orford, IREN's buildout is described as phase-funding-phase, which cannot be reconciled with negative $6 million per megawatt in year one unless someone else is funding the phase.

The credit market is already voting. Per the Stocks list, Morgan Stanley's Vishy Tirupattur has the AI ecosystem's weight in the investment-grade index going from under three percent to over six, hyperscaler capex revised for 2026 from 600 to above 800 billion, for 2027 from 850 to 1,300, and 2028 near 1,300. Oracle is now one notch above junk with credit default swaps at 2008 levels and spreads beyond 220 basis points. He rejects the CDO analogy for late-1990s telecom on issuer credit quality, and that rejection is doing a lot of load-bearing work for a comparison two independent sources reached for tonight.

The Fed, where four institutions sit on three sides and the disagreement is tradeable. Per the Financial Markets list and 0xResearch:

Venue or deskOn tomorrow
Kalshi77 percent hold, down from 96
CME FedWatchjust under 40 percent hike
Bespoke29 percent hike and falling
DeFiTracer35.8 percent hike and rising
BofAno change
Citadel Securitiesa surprise hike is live, per Bloomberg
Cowenhold tomorrow, hike in September

Cowen's is the only one with a mechanism attached, and per Benjamin Cowen it runs backwards from the usual framing. A hold is what triggers the hike. The two-year already sits at 4.1 to 4.2 percent, above the funds rate, so a hold pushes the thirty-year through 5.2 percent and the ten-year toward 5, and the bond market forces the September move the Fed declined to make. He pairs it with a ten to twenty percent equity drawdown and three precedents, August 2022, September 2018 and September 2014, all midterm years.

My lean, revised in place rather than restacked. A hold is 78/22, up from 75/25 this morning, because Kalshi's drift to 77 and Bespoke's fall to 29 outweigh Citadel's position and CME's outlier. The statement reading hawkish enough to move the tape is 55/45 and that is where the risk actually is. If Cowen is right the sequencing means tomorrow's relief is the setup rather than the resolution, and the thing to watch is not the decision but the thirty-year the morning after.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • Apple briefly touched $5 trillion today, the second company ever to do it after Nvidia, which itself peaked near $5.7 trillion. It did this on a day the index it anchors entered a correction.
  • Supermicro is the most fragile balance sheet on the tape. A second criminal probe, this one in Taiwan, a $7 billion raise whose 45 million shares at $27.50 are now underwater, seven percent mandatory convertible preferred, $6.6 billion of quarterly cash use, trailing free cash flow of negative $6.9 billion, and short interest of 103.2 million shares or twenty percent of float into August 11 earnings, per Rick Orford.
  • Nvidia bottomed near $192 and bounced off its 200-day for the third time in 21 sessions. A level tested three times in a month is not support so much as a queue.
  • SPCX fell 5.5 percent and now sits 47 percent below its June 16 high with roughly $1.2 trillion of market value gone. Per VirtualBacon it is below its $135 listing price, and the first major shareholder unlock is August 6.
  • Meta has closed lower nine sessions running and reports tomorrow.
  • Micron below $800 leaves a gap fill at 751 underneath and 872 then 891 above. Tesla held 300.

item.title: [Investing] South Korea's market halted limit-down overnight on memory, and the hyperscaler credit-default basket hit a fresh record on the same tape
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The KOSPI fell as much as 9 percent with Samsung and SK Hynix making up roughly half the index, and SK Hynix closed below its $149 IPO price for the first time. Meanwhile the 30-year Treasury printed its highest weekly close since July 2007 and Nvidia's insurance cost hit a record on reports the OpenAI financing is now above $750 billion.
item.content:encoded:
The KOSPI fell as much as 9 percent with Samsung and SK Hynix making up roughly half the index, and SK Hynix closed below its $149 IPO price for the first time. Meanwhile the 30-year Treasury printed its highest weekly close since July 2007 and Nvidia's insurance cost hit a record on reports the OpenAI financing is now above $750 billion.

Last night I said the memory shortage survives CXMT at 70/30 on units while the multiple does not. Overnight Korea took the second half and ran with it. The pre-open, the scoreboard, then five stories.

Into the open. Futures are red across the board. Per the Market list, the KOSPI opened up 1 percent, fell 7, tripped its circuit breaker below minus 8 and reached minus 9 before halting, while the Nikkei is down 3 percent and Capital Flows calls it "a warning sign. The carry trade hasn't even unwound yet." Crude settled at $82.61, down 7.50 percent, and is off another 2 percent this morning.

Where things standFigure
30-year Treasury weekly close5.17 percent, highest since July 2007
Hyperscaler CDS basket3bps wider to a fresh record
$QQQfour losing sessions, the year's longest, 8.2 percent below highs
$METAdown eight straight days, the longest run in its history
$SMHfell about 2.5 percent, on its highest volume in seven years
$AAPLmost valuable company in the world, first time since April 2025
$SKHYfirst close below its $149 IPO price

Levels, all per the Stocks list. $MU breached the 902 right shoulder and needs 955 to repair. $NVDA breached 199 with 189, 183.70 and a 177 gap fill below. $TSLA has to defend 286 to 292. $QQQ heads for 643 to 648 at the 200-day unless it reclaims 686 on a daily close. Today brings SK Hynix around 8pm ET, Bloom Energy and Corning.

The scoreboard.

  • My $MU level call is a miss. I gave the pivots as 906 and 972 with 991 as the neckline and 1155 and 1186 as targets. The breakdown invalidated that inverted head-and-shoulders setup outright at 902. The structure is gone rather than merely untriggered.
  • The fundamental half of my CXMT call is holding. Per the Crypto list, Melvin puts CXMT at 6 to 9 percent of global DRAM shipments against Samsung's 36 and SK Hynix's 29, with Counterpoint estimating it needs 15 percent to compete long term, a level it is not projected to reach even by 2028, on costs more than 30 percent higher per bit.
  • Tomorrow's Fed spread widened again. Kalshi now publishes 73 percent hold, aixbt reads 33 percent hike, one desk has 40 percent against 16 a week ago, and Citadel Securities expects a hike while Citigroup expects a hold.
  • SK Hynix reports tonight and Samsung tomorrow, into a stock that just closed below its IPO price.
  • Bloom Energy reports today, the call I relayed on the 24th when it was the desk's largest position at $222, down 30 to 35 percent from a one-month high.

1. Korea halted and the memory bull case got stronger, and that pairing is the whole story. Per the Crypto list, Melvin's supply data is the densest thing on the tape. TrendForce has DRAM contract prices up 90 to 95 percent quarter over quarter in the first quarter and NAND up 55 to 60, with another 58 to 63 percent DRAM jump in the second.

Samsung memory average selling prices are up 146 percent against the 2025 average and it hiked HBM3E another 20 percent for 2026 orders before HBM4 ramps. SK Hynix says HBM, DRAM and NAND are essentially sold out for the year, Micron has left consumer memory entirely, and new capacity does not arrive meaningfully until late 2027 because HBM eats roughly three times the wafer capacity per gigabyte of standard DRAM.

Samsung also forecast a nineteen-fold jump in quarterly operating profit while its stock was falling, and it and SK Hynix have committed $520 billion to four new plants. Korea broke anyway on index construction plus leverage: the two names are roughly half the KOSPI, and the selling concentrated in leveraged single-stock products tracking exactly those two.

So take the lean. The supply story is intact at 75/25, up from 70/25 last night, because every datapoint this morning tightened it. But John Galt's bear case deserves respect, and per the Stocks list it is specific: a decisive breakdown in Hynix pointing at 1 to 1.1 million won, another 35 to 40 percent lower, consistent with $SMH in the 335 to 400 range over several months. Note also that Jordi Visser has trimmed memory, because the DRAM ETF took six billion dollars in one of the fastest inflows in history and retail is heavily involved. A right thesis bought at a crowded entry is still a bad entry.

2. The actual break is in credit, and it set a record last night. Per the Financial Markets list, zerohedge reports "unprecedented carnage in AI IG CDS" with the hyperscaler CDS basket another 3bps wider to a record. Per the Market list, the cost of insuring Nvidia's debt "surged to a record" after reports it is discussing more than $750 billion of AI infrastructure financing tied to OpenAI. I have been carrying $250 billion for the Ohio campus, and the reported total is now triple that.

Charlie Bilello supplies the rates half: the 30-year ended last week at 5.17 percent, its highest weekly close since July 2007. The financing machine did not slow. BlackRock closed a $12.5 billion bond sale against a Meta data centre in Texas, the 2048 notes priced 287.5 basis points over ten-year Treasuries with roughly $20 billion of demand, about 1.6 times the deal, BlackRock-backed entities owning 80 percent and Meta 20, backed by lease commitments so the debt stays off Meta's balance sheet.

Jim Cramer named the precedent: "I lived through 2000. I don't want the sequel," and "What we learned in 2000 is that you don't lend to companies who buy your goods." His conditional is the honest version: if OpenAI can pay, perhaps because it comes public, Nvidia is fine, and if not, different story. He also told anyone who borrowed to buy the data-centre theme to sell at today's open, while calling the Nvidia selloff "absurd" and saying he still owns it. Same session.

Goldman's desk put numbers on the internals: momentum factor down 7 percent, software and internet up 4 against semis down 3.5, AMD down 6, SanDisk down 13, semicap down 5 to 7, on three named catalysts. The Nvidia-OpenAI deal reigniting the circular-financing debate, China starting homegrown DUV tools, and cheaper Chinese open models.

3. The best single explanation of why this is happening came from a reader's saved post rather than a bank. Per Alex Corrino, the proximate cause is real rates, and his evidence starts with a date: "the Nasdaq topped the day of Warsh's first FOMC meeting." Long-run inflation expectations have barely moved while Treasury yields have, worth roughly 50 basis points of higher real rates. Warsh drives both legs, because the committee has begun indicating hikes and he is an avowed balance-sheet hawk who plans to let mortgage-backed securities and long-duration Treasuries roll off, removing a buyer of duration.

The collision is with peak capex. The AI buildout is one of the longest-duration trades in the market, so higher real rates hit the present value of data-centre cash flows hardest, and the cushion that would have made debt unnecessary is already spent. His scoreboard: Amazon and Alphabet flat on the year, Meta down 10 percent and Microsoft down 20, against a Nasdaq 100 up 10.

His forward call is a bet against the sell side: "analysts haven't begun to move semis EPS expects down yet," and the market may be sniffing it out before they do. He then does what most macro writers will not and concedes the trade does not work, because hyperscalers treat AI as existential and semis have verifiably high backlogs while staying exposed. Read it as a frame rather than a position.

4. The money went into industrials, and two desks found it independently on the same morning. Per BowTied Bull, whose last item was a 69-word paywalled stub and who this time published in full, the Nasdaq topped around June while the Russell 2000 is up since June. He eliminates financials, because a tech seller is not buying banks, and energy, because a tech mandate cannot hold it, then lands on industrials. His named holdings there: Caterpillar, GE Vernova, GE Aerospace, RTX, Eaton and Boeing. The useful part is his framing, that "you can argue that industrials are technology in heavy machinery form," an easier story to tell a committee than oil.

Yardeni Research reached the same place hours later: "Investors can't figure out AI's future returns, but Industrials are outperforming Tech this year. The capex is real even if the payoff isn't clear yet."

Two caveats. His financials logic is contradicted by the tape, because JPMorgan hit a record high in the same session on its way to a $937 billion market cap. And there is a competing answer, because per the People to follow list capital also rotated into crypto equities, with BitMine up 13.49 percent at $17.96 after adding nearly 10,000 ETH. Both can be partly right, and neither is measured.

5. Four institutions are on three different sides of tomorrow, and the venues cannot agree either. Per the Kalshi list, its traders forecast 73 percent that the Fed holds, and separately 69 percent for a hike this year against 19 for a cut. That leaves roughly 12 percent for no change all year, which does not sit beside 73 percent hold on one meeting.

Polymarket has 73 percent no change and 26 percent for a quarter-point hike, with a full-year distribution of two hikes at 32, one at 31, none at 29. Citadel Securities expects a hike, Citigroup expects a hold, and Melvin says futures price basically zero chance of a surprise and "this is a hold meeting, not a hawkish pivot." Ben Emons of FedWatch Advisors gives the hawks their mechanism: "Within the Fed there is a big shift of tone. People are eager to start hiking again because they worry about inflation going higher."

My numbers move again. A hold goes to 75/25 from 80/20, because two named institutions now expect a hike and the front-end repricing has run one way for a week. A hawkish-enough statement stays at 60/40. If Corrino is right that Warsh wants forward guidance out of his mandate, the statement is where the damage lands.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. 902 broken and 955 needed to repair, on a fundamental picture that improved overnight. That tension is the trade: contract prices up 90 to 95 percent quarterly and capacity sold out for the year, against a retail-crowded ETF bid Visser just trimmed into. Tonight's SK Hynix print matters more than any level.
  • $NVDA. 199 breached with 189, 183.70 and a 177 gap fill beneath, at 14-month lows relative to Apple, with its own credit insurance at a record. The equity question has become a credit question, and what matters is whether the reported $750 billion of commitments is confirmed or walked back.
  • $TSLA. Must defend 286 to 292, at its most oversold since March 2025. Deutsche Bank cut its target to $420, and Cathie Wood bought roughly 27,864 shares, about $8.5 million.
  • $HOOD. Reports tomorrow after the close. Bernstein's Gautam Chhugani models roughly $150 million of event-contract revenue against about $104 million in the first quarter, enough to pass crypto as a revenue line for the first time, and Piper Sandler agrees. He sees $1.7 billion by 2028 and took his target to $160, the Street high.
  • $SPCX and $RKLB. SpaceX closed at its lowest price ever, red in 13 of its last 16 days, roughly 50 percent off June's peak, with Aug 4 earnings and an Aug 6 lockup freeing 911 million insider shares. Against that, per the People list, ARK's Brett Winton says mastering Starship reusability this year raises their 2031 revenue and EBIT expectations roughly threefold and 2036 by six to seven, because reusable versus disposable is $100 against $570 per kilogram. Rocket Lab is in its largest drawdown in four years.
  • The second-derivative infrastructure names. Per Milk Road AI, Morgan Stanley mapped the buildout across seven layers, and the useful output is the roster below the GPU line: Vertiv and CoolIT in liquid cooling, Siemens and Eaton in power electronics, ABB and Legrand in UPS, Arista and Ciena in networking, Yageo, Murata and Unimicron in components. It carries no capex figures and leaves three of its own layers unpopulated, so treat it as a name list.

item.title: [Investing] I said this morning the memory thesis would reprice on Samsung's print rather than on the Chinese listing, and by 10:38 the tape had answered me
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Micron fell 6.1 percent through a trillion dollars, ASML was halted after an 8 percent drop, and Apple took the largest-company crown back from Nvidia. The trigger was not CXMT alone. It was China mass-producing its own DUV lithography tools on the same morning Nvidia's credit spreads started widening on the OpenAI guarantee.
item.content:encoded:
Micron fell 6.1 percent through a trillion dollars, ASML was halted after an 8 percent drop, and Apple took the largest-company crown back from Nvidia. The trigger was not CXMT alone. It was China mass-producing its own DUV lithography tools on the same morning Nvidia's credit spreads started widening on the OpenAI guarantee.

This morning I said CXMT's debut does not touch the HBM shortage on any timeline that matters this quarter, so memory would reprice on Samsung's print and not on a Chinese listing. The fundamental half may still be right. The market half was wrong within three hours. The session, the scoreboard, then five stories.

The session. Stocks gapped up hard on the Iran pause and gave it all back before lunch. Per the Market list, the Dow was up 1.08 percent at the bell, the S&P 500 banks index hit a record high up 1.3 percent, and airlines ripped as crude fell over 7 percent, JetBlue up 6.5 and United up 4. Then a report that a state-backed Chinese firm had begun mass-producing domestic DUV lithography tools hit the semis, and at 10:38 the same feed printed the Nasdaq down 0.5 percent and the S&P down 0.1.

Be straight about the limits: that 10:38 print is the last index-level number in tonight's sources, so treat everything below as intraday, not a close. Per the Kalshi list, $700 billion was added at the open, the S&P later turned negative as chips led, and over $1 trillion came off US stocks in two hours. $GOOGL crossed $4 trillion on the same tape.

NameIntraday move
$MUdown 6.1 percent, below $1 trillion in market cap
$ASMLhalted after an 8 percent drop, resumed down 7.4 to 8 percent
$SNDKdown over 11 percent, roughly $17.3 billion of market cap
$NVDAbroke below $200, down 4 to 5 percent
$AMDdown about 8 percent
$SOXXdown almost 10 percent from premarket highs
$AAPLreclaimed largest company in the world from $NVDA
$JPMfresh all-time high
$SPCXnew all-time low at $110

The scoreboard.

  • My CXMT call was half wrong, and the wrong half was the tradeable one. I said the repricing would wait for Samsung. It came today, on the listing plus a DUV headline I did not have. Anyone long memory on my framing got hurt.
  • Kimi K3 shipped and David Ondrej called the date and venue exactly. Weights landed on Hugging Face today, per the Hermes list. His "three times cheaper than the US frontier" was backwards. At $3 in and $15 out per million, K3 is premium, roughly seventeen times DeepSeek V4 Pro's 87 cents.
  • I cannot grade the Tesla 300 call, and that is my sourcing failure rather than a result. Not one source tonight carries a Tesla price. It came due today and I cannot settle it.
  • Wednesday is the whole week. Fed at 2pm, Kevin Warsh's first presser at 2:30, no updated dot plot, per Arbitrage Andy. $MSFT, $META, $HOOD and Samsung all report the same day.
  • Tuesday carries SK Hynix near 8pm ET and Bloom Energy. SK Hynix pulled 65 percent of first-quarter revenue from the US, so it reads American hyperscaler capex rather than Korea.

1. China broke the memory trade, and the rebuttal is better argued than the selling. Per the Financial Markets list, CXMT closed its debut up roughly 465 to 500 percent near a $500 billion valuation, the most valuable company in mainland China, and it is also the destination for China's first domestic immersion DUV deliveries. The Market Ear: "Wall Street de-risked tech. China didn't. Instead, it launched a $500 bn DRAM champion and appears to have started producing domestic DUV lithography systems."

Melvin did the arithmetic the tape ignored. Per the Market list, Shanghai Micro Electronics ran its own 28-nanometer DUV tools above 90 percent utilisation on SMIC lines this year, and 28 nanometres is over 60 percent of the global chip market, so this is real. But ASML took twenty years and roughly $40 billion to walk from 65 nanometres to below 3, and China sits at the 65-nanometre line ASML occupied in 2003. Wayne Liang adds the volume: about five machines this year against the hundreds ASML ships, and DUV is not EUV.

Then Morgan Stanley added a separate bear catalyst, warning memory contract prices could peak in late 2026. Shay Boloor's SanDisk rebuttal is checkable: $42 billion of remaining performance obligations on multiyear deals with floors near $0.29 per gigabyte, so a pricing peak is not an earnings peak. On Micron and SK Hynix he calls the selloff overdone, because CXMT has no meaningful HBM presence and no EUV access.

My lean, with odds. The fundamental case survives at 70/30, because per the Crypto list Kimi K3's weights need roughly 1.4 terabytes of memory just to load at 4-bit and HBM is sold out through 2027, so frontier open models are a memory demand story. The multiple does not survive, and that is the half I got wrong. A trade can be right on units and wrong on price for two quarters.

2. Nvidia became a bank this weekend and the credit market noticed before the equity did. Per the Market list, it is weighing roughly $250 billion of guarantees on OpenAI's 10-gigawatt Ohio campus, a project that could top $500 billion, first phases in 2028, on land previously used for federal nuclear work. Futurum: Nvidia is "increasingly the credit backstop for its own demand."

The new fact is the pricing. Kyle Reidhead reports Nvidia's CDS spreads rising on the news, and he is a bull volunteering it. Cramer named it twice, calling it the "First National Bank of Nvidia" and adding that "if there were no financing involved Nvidia's stock would be soaring," with the market fixated on it "BECAUSE of memories of 2000." Per the Stocks list, John Galt put it in a position, "Added $NVDA short on the company becoming a bank," and Mark Minervini added an SPY short with a stop above 755, citing August to September as the weakest two-month stretch in 37 years. Nothing is signed.

3. The debt behind all of this is off balance sheet and larger than the debt they report. Per Prof G Markets, Nikkei Asia puts roughly $1.65 trillion of off-balance-sheet obligations across Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Oracle against about $1.35 trillion of reported debt, with Bloomberg nearer $1.8 trillion. Meta's is $420 billion, three times what it reports. Per the clip, Scott Galloway: "when you're hiding a bigger number than what you're reporting, that's not accounting. It's concealment."

Ed Elson supplies the mechanism and a correction to the frame I have been running. The vehicles are not hidden recourse, they are genuine risk transfer, and "the guy responsible for that isn't big tech, it isn't Nvidia. It's the private credit funds." That cuts against the supplier-underwrites-demand argument I quoted Sunday rather than confirming it. Both can hold at once, but they are different failure modes. Their precedent is First Brands, Chapter 11 in September 2025 on private credit money.

Per Mark Cuban, the efficiency case strands all of it. He grants utilisation will scale as expected, but if a price-performance curve minimises power requirements, "there's going to be a lot of data centers that are going to be turned into pickleball courts." His analogy is dark fiber at pennies once 1-gigabit became 100, and he calls borrowing on top of fully-committed cash flow "planning for perfection."

Galloway then breaks with his own producer, and that is the honest part of the episode. He argues leverage equates to growth, and on Meta: "Meta is such a cash volcano that I'm not as worried about the debt of Meta." His worry is the cash-flow-negative adjacents.

Set against it, per Anthony Pompliano, four charts say the bubble is a myth: S&P net margin on track for 15.7 percent in Q2, the highest since 2009, 86 percent of reporters beating EPS, and the Nasdaq 100 at 24 times against 86 in May 2001. Read the two side by side and notice they never touch. Pompliano answers an equity question with equity data and never mentions debt, vehicles or leverage. The bull case is measured in margins, the bear case in liabilities that never reach the multiple.

4. Alphabet is the one name everybody is buying for four incompatible reasons. Per Fin Tek, Berkshire's latest 13F shows another $10 billion of Alphabet, nearly tripling the stake on brand and engineering talent. Per Tom Nash, it is a discounted toll booth at $320, down 22 percent from its high, on a 2030 target of $560, with cloud operating income up 215 percent as margins went from 20.6 to 35.6 percent. Per the Milk Road AI email, their analyst bought the 7 percent post-earnings drop, is down about 13 percent, and rests on Gemini's 950 million monthly users.

Elson uses the identical 82 percent cloud growth to argue the opposite, estimating roughly half of it comes from OpenAI and Anthropic, both venture-funded and cash-flow negative. Same number, four verdicts, nobody citing anybody. The figure that settles it is undisclosed.

5. Wednesday's Fed is a hike-risk meeting with no dot plot and a brand-new chair at the microphone. Per Arbitrage Andy, hike odds sit near 36 percent and there is no updated dot plot, so "it is likely every word in the statement and Warsh's press conference will carry more weight than usual." Per the Financial Markets list, September hike odds are above 50 percent, up from 18 a week ago. Per the Milk Road crypto letter, the same repricing reads as 1-in-10 to 4-in-10 in a week, driven by oil through $100.

Kalshi is the outlier, still calling a fifth straight hold at 3.50 to 3.75 percent without publishing a number, which leaves this morning's 83 percent standing twenty points from everyone else two days out.

So I am moving mine. A hold goes from 85/15 to 80/20, because the oil relief that argued for patience arrived alongside a strike on Saudi processing capacity. A hawkish-enough statement goes from 45/55 to 60/40, because with no dot plot the statement and the presser are the only instruments left.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Down 6.1 percent and back below a trillion. Per Rick Orford, the cloud memory unit ran an 83 percent gross and 78 percent operating margin last quarter, HBM4 is in high-volume production for Vera Rubin above 2.8 terabytes per second, and the entire 2026 HBM book is contracted on price and volume. His second-order point is the one I want: capacity shifting to HBM starves conventional DRAM, so Micron gets paid twice. He names his own bear case, cyclicality, and rests on contract structure. Wednesday settles that better than any chart.
  • $MSTR. Up 7 percent intraday while the fundamentals went the other way. Per the Crypto list, Strategy sold 5,429,160 shares for $544.5 million last week and bought zero bitcoin, a fourth straight week, $1.27 billion sold at roughly 0.6 times the coins behind it. Holdings sit at 843,775 coins averaging $75,476, about $8.5 billion underwater near $65,400. The credit is getting safer and the equity is paying for it. Q2 lands Thursday.
  • $PLTR. Per Orford, the trailing multiple has fallen as earnings grew, but a name that has traded above 100 and sometimes 400 times trailing earnings leaves no room for a small miss. Watch net dollar retention. He independently reaches the least-margin-for-error half of last week's ranking.
  • $SPCX. An all-time low of $110 while sitting inside Morgan Stanley's five biggest AI capex spenders, and Amazon just filed for up to 5,105 direct-to-device satellites from 2028. Lieberman would get interested at $60 to $70.
  • 402340.KS, SK Square. Per Edelbridge Alpha, a holding company whose 20.1 percent SK Hynix stake is now over 98 percent of net asset value, historically at a 55 to 68 percent discount against a floor near 22 percent from Korean capital-gains tax. Interactive Brokers opened retail access in May and it roughly doubled by late June, so the easy money is gone.
  • $XRP. Per Lark Davis, Ripple president Monica Long says institutional demand for XRP and RLUSD is "nothing like we've ever seen," on no figure, no named institution and no date. Kalshi's traders forecast Ripple at $1.30 this year. Unprecedented demand does not price to $1.30.
  • Housing. Per ClearValue Tax, June prices rose 3 percent year over year, inventory is 1.56 million at 4.6 months of supply, identical to a year ago, and the 21 percent foreclosure surge is 227,548 filings against 1.65 million in the same half of 2010. The 30-year sits at 6.6 percent on a 4.63 percent ten-year, below the above-4.7 print Prof G used.

item.title: [Investing] Alphabet's future purchase commitments went from $332 billion to $811 billion in a single quarter, with about $200 billion of it due inside twelve months
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: That is what the 7 percent post-earnings drop was actually about, not the paper gains everyone spent the weekend arguing over. Meanwhile China's CXMT listed up 470 percent to roughly $487 billion, three venues publish three different odds on Wednesday's Fed decision, and Nvidia is co-signing $250 billion of OpenAI's debt.
item.content:encoded:
That is what the 7 percent post-earnings drop was actually about, not the paper gains everyone spent the weekend arguing over. Meanwhile China's CXMT listed up 470 percent to roughly $487 billion, three venues publish three different odds on Wednesday's Fed decision, and Nvidia is co-signing $250 billion of OpenAI's debt.

Sunday night I led on the $99 billion of equity-stake gains that flattered Alphabet's headline earnings. Confirmed overnight. What I did not have was the other side of the ledger, and it is bigger. The open, the scoreboard, then five stories.

Into the open. Futures reopened green on the US and Iran halting strikes, and Brent fell 7 percent at the Asian open before settling around down 4 percent, per the Financial Markets list. That relief lands into the most crowded week of the quarter. Per the Stocks list, the ten-year has passed 4.7 percent, the Nasdaq proxy is on the brink of correction territory, the S&P risks finishing July red for the first time in eleven years, and the VIX crossed 20 last week heading into its seasonally strong August-to-October window. Watch $MU at 906 and 972, with 991 the neckline to clear. $TSLA has to hold 300.

WhenWhat
TodayCME 24-hour single stock futures go live, 55 standard and 22 micro contracts
TuesdaySK Hynix earnings, roughly 8pm ET. Trump meets Netanyahu
WednesdayFed decision, Kevin Warsh's second meeting. Samsung earnings. $MSFT, $META, $HOOD, $SOFI report
Thursday$AAPL, $AMZN
FridayMonth-end. The S&P needs to close above 7,499.36 to keep eleven straight green Julys

The scoreboard.

  • CXMT listed and threadguy was nearly exact. On the 16th he read the pre-IPO perpetual as implying roughly $470 billion against an $80 billion offering. It priced at $85.5 billion and closed its debut up 470 percent near $487 billion. Called.
  • The market-implied read I relayed Sunday was wrong, and it was the only one I had. lookonchain's whale was short 2.10 million units and up about $502,000. That whale is now short 2.6 million and down $1.7 million, and a second trader was fully liquidated for $249,000. Anyone who read the short as information got run over.
  • TicTocTick's Monday launch is confirmed. Per the Financial Markets list, CME single stock futures start trading today.
  • Kimi K3 comes due today and has not shipped. Per the Hermes list, Moonshot has a live countdown on the Hugging Face repo. A countdown is not weights, and David Ondrej's July 27 date has hours left.
  • Wednesday's Fed call is mine to lose. I said Sunday a hold was 85/15. Nothing overnight moves that, but the venue spread got worse, not better.

1. Alphabet's obligation wall is the story, and it dwarfs the paper-gains argument. Per Ticker Symbol: YOU, the $99 billion of gains on the Anthropic and SpaceX stakes and the resulting $2.85 of operational earnings per share are both confirmed, so Sunday's read stands. But the same filing shows $811 billion of future purchase agreements against $332 billion three months earlier, about $200 billion of it due within a year, with some energy contracts running to 2054.

The balance sheet agrees. Free cash flow was negative $5.9 billion against positive $24.6 billion two quarters ago, long-term debt more than doubled in six months, the interest bill roughly quintupled, and buybacks have stopped for the first time since 2017.

One correction from Sunday. I gave the cloud backlog as $106 billion to $514 billion over twelve months and this source gives $462 billion to $514 billion. Both are right, because it is one sequence: $106 billion a year ago, $462 billion last quarter, $514 billion now, up more than $50 billion in a single quarter per the Crypto list. The slowing rate of increase is the part nobody is saying out loud.

Two more specifics. The SpaceX stake is marked at $94 billion as of June 30, but $80 billion unlocks in stages to December 8, $14 billion stays frozen into next year's third quarter, and SpaceX is down about 25 percent in a month. That mark is stale in the wrong direction. And for the first time cloud revenue comes primarily from selling TPU systems rather than renting them, which neither Microsoft nor Amazon does.

Alex at Ticker Symbol: YOU says Wall Street is making a big mistake and is buying. Per Stocks with Josh, Google's MACD and signal line both sit beneath the zero line and his instruction is to leave it alone until they clear it. My lean is the momentum read for two weeks and the fundamental read for two years, because a $200 billion obligation inside twelve months reprices a stock rather than merely worrying it.

2. Three venues are publishing three different numbers on the same Fed decision, and that gap is the trade. Per the Kalshi list, Kalshi has an 83 percent chance the Fed holds in July. That is notable on its own, because Kalshi published no rate market at all three days before the last decision. Per the Financial Markets list, Barchart says hike odds have climbed to 36 percent, while Evan at StockMKTNewz puts Polymarket traders at 17 percent on a hike. Those cannot all be right.

Charlie Bilello supplies the frame: the bond market priced two cuts in January and now prices one to two hikes, a full one percent swing. October hike odds have passed 75 percent per the Stocks list.

So take the lean. A hold is 85/15, unchanged from Sunday. But the sharper trade is not the decision. Per the Stocks list, MoneyPrinter0x argues the edge is that forward-looking hike sentiment has topped and mean-reverting down would lift rate-sensitive risk assets, and Citi is calling for a dovish outcome. I put a hawkish-enough statement to move the tape at 45/55, down from 50/50 on Sunday, because oil falling 7 percent overnight removes the one input that was forcing Warsh's hand.

3. CXMT is the memory trade's new variable and the loudest bull is telling you why it does not matter yet. Per the Crypto list, Melvin calls it the largest chip IPO in mainland China's history. China's biggest DRAM maker has gone from under 4 percent to roughly 7.7 percent of global DRAM in under a year, first-quarter revenue up 719 percent to 50.8 billion yuan. On the raise, he says roughly $9.8 billion while the Financial Markets list reports $8.6 billion, and that is not a rounding difference.

His bear case on his own bull day is the useful part. CXMT's monthly wafer output is capped near 290,000 to 320,000 against Samsung's roughly 630,000 and SK Hynix's near 500,000, and its yields run about 42 percent below their mature-process yields, so on HBM "it won't compete there for years." The shortage driving DRAM and NAND up 60 percent or more per quarter does not end because a new Chinese supplier showed up.

Two desks read the identical fact opposite ways. Per the Financial Markets list, KraneShares argues US export restrictions were "designed as a ceiling" and have "become a floor," while zerohedge calls the same facts China's two-front squeeze on America's AI build-out. Both describe a Chinese supplier that got stronger. Only one thinks that is America's problem.

4. Nvidia is now underwriting its own customer's debt, and the bear argument against it is specific rather than vague. Per the Market list, Nvidia is in talks to guarantee up to $250 billion of financing for a 10-gigawatt OpenAI campus in southern Ohio developed by SoftBank's energy arm, with total project cost possibly above $500 billion, power controlled by the US government and funded by Japan under a recent trade deal, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick involved in allocating it. OpenAI has no investment-grade rating, so the guarantee is what makes the debt cheap. Separately, Nvidia is discussing financing chip purchases that could total $350 billion.

Per Jose Najarro, the correction that matters is that a $250 billion guarantee is not $250 billion of funding, and Nvidia pays only if OpenAI misses. His bull read is that prior backstops ran $3 billion to $6 billion, so a number this size is existential and nobody fakes an existential commitment. His open question is whether Nvidia keeps and re-rents the campus on a default.

The bear case, from Douglas Swift on the Stocks list, is the sentence to sit with: a vendor is backstopping its customer's balance sheet to secure its own order book, the structure by which Lucent and Nortel financed the CLECs that bought their switches, and "when the supplier underwrites the demand, the demand signal stops being independent information." Wayne Liang asks why Nvidia would underwrite $250 billion of demand that supposedly is not real. Swift just answered him. And the pattern runs wide: $1 billion into Nokia, $2 billion into Marvell, $1 billion into Naver, equity in Lumentum and Coherent, $500 billion-plus with SK Group, $30 billion already in OpenAI.

5. Supply got locked up in size over the weekend, and both companies doing it report inside 48 hours. Per Najarro, SK Group and Nvidia signed above $500 billion covering next-generation AI memory including HBM, with SK Hynix also building its own AI cloud business on Nvidia's platform, first site online in 2027. Samsung and Broadcom signed roughly $200 billion across memory and foundry over five years, and the foundry leg is the interesting half, because Broadcom becomes a 2-nanometer customer as a condition of getting the memory. Locking in supply has become the moat.

Larry Fink said it plainly on the People to follow list: "We have more demand for memory than we have supply," and maybe in three or four years there is enough. Against that, Charlie Bilello has the discipline datapoint of the week on the same list. Apple generated $129 billion of free cash flow last year and Oracle burned $24 billion, and the stocks went plus 56 and minus 52 percent. Per Chip Stock Investor, the tape is wobbling because markets price capex six to twelve months ahead and the visibility window that lengthened in the first half is now contracting.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Pivot pair 906 and 972 after touching 960 overnight, neckline 991, stated targets 1155 and 1186. CXMT's debut does not touch the HBM shortage on any timeline that matters this quarter, and DRAM contract prices jumped as much as 95 percent in the first quarter alone. Long bias, but the thesis reprices on Samsung's Wednesday print, not on a chart.
  • $MRVL. Down about 37 percent from its June 18 high. Melvin has bought from $269 through $186 and sees little room below $150, expecting earnings to reprice it. Treat $150 as his conviction, not a support level. The source gave two custom-silicon targets ten times apart, $10 billion and $100 billion by fiscal 2029, and $10 billion is the plausible one.
  • $TSLA. Has to hold 300, having closed two candles entirely outside the lower Bollinger band. Per Stocks with Josh, the call is Tesla hits 300 by today, testable by the close. Heisenberg liked it at 400 and loves it at 300, and says he would marry it at 250. Nobody is buying it here for the car business.
  • $GLXY. Tapped roughly $21.60 last week and bounced double digits. Helios is 800 megawatts fully contracted to CoreWeave on a fifteen-year lease averaging over $1 billion a year, Phase I delivered on time and collecting rent. Milk Road says $38 on Helios alone against a Street average near $41. The cleanest contracted-cash-flow story in the complex, and the only one where rent is already flowing.
  • $BTC. Back above $65,000. Per Benjamin Cowen, the week ran 63.7 to 67 against a 64.7 open, and he expects a rejection at the bear-market resistance band in late July or early August, then a decline into an August-to-September window that was red in 2014, 2018 and 2022. He never puts a number on the band, so the structure is the argument and not the level. Zach Pandl's three swing factors on the People list are more usable: Strategy has stabilised, the Fed is open, the CLARITY Act is uncertain. One of three is green, and $58,000 versus new lows turns on the other two. For contrast on the altcoin side, per Lark Davis, Chainlink "remains in tatters" while its utility case has never been stronger, on no revenue figure, no valuation and no catalyst date. Cowen's prescription is the opposite, own what makes a profit, and he thinks retail is leaving precisely because utility keeps never reaching the token. One of them is wrong inside a quarter.

item.title: [Investing] The memory trade spent this week getting attacked from two directions nobody had priced, a Morgan Stanley demand note that tripped a circuit breaker in Seoul and a Chinese model architecture that quietly threatens the thing Micron actually sells
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Last Sunday the crash needed no thesis to break, just a rate hike in Korea. This week the thesis itself got tested, and it survived on price while losing ground on argument. SK Hynix trades at four times 2027 earnings while Michael Burry presses a short at $934, and China's largest memory IPO ever lists tomorrow morning.
item.content:encoded:
Last Sunday the crash needed no thesis to break, just a rate hike in Korea. This week the thesis itself got tested, and it survived on price while losing ground on argument. SK Hynix trades at four times 2027 earnings while Michael Burry presses a short at $934, and China's largest memory IPO ever lists tomorrow morning.

Last Sunday I wrote that the memory round-trip was a test of leverage rather than a test of the story. That was right, and it is no longer the interesting question. This week the story itself came under attack, twice, and from directions the bulls had not modelled. Here is the arc, the bull case, the bear case, what to do about it, and then the week's scoreboard.

The arc of the week. Monday and Tuesday were the melt-up. Per the Market list, Micron hit $945 intraday Tuesday, kissed its 50-day and closed up about 10 percent after Bank of America added it to best ideas, with the memory fund up roughly 20 percent in days to near $58 and monster bounces in SanDisk, Western Digital and Seagate. Morgan Stanley called the pullback a compelling entry and modelled DRAM contract prices up at least 25 percent from the second quarter to the third. UBS said undersupplied to at least 2028.

Wednesday the floor thinned out underneath the price. Per Trader Mayne, Goldman had hedge funds as net sellers in six of eight weeks, the largest eight-week technology outflow in over a decade, with tech exposure at a 2026 low near 15.5 percent even as semiconductors reached about 14 percent of US market capitalisation, roughly double the dot-com peak. A trade can be crowded in index weight and abandoned in active positioning at the same time, and that is what memory was.

Thursday was Alphabet, and memory passed the test. Cloud grew 82 percent to $24.8 billion on a $514 billion backlog, capex went to $195 to $205 billion, free cash flow printed negative, and the stock fell 7.6 percent into seven target cuts. Memory decoupled and held, with relative strength across Micron, SanDisk, Seagate, Western Digital and SK Hynix. The market punished the spender and left the supplier alone. That is the single most important tape fact of the week.

Friday it broke. Per the Stocks list, Morgan Stanley's Shawn Kim published a demand warning arguing demand has evaporated, with NAND module inventories near 13 weeks, price increases slowing to 5 percent a quarter into the fourth quarter, high-bandwidth memory growth capped near 40 percent, and Tencent saying it had already secured 90 percent of its requirements. The Kospi fell 6 percent intraday to around 6,500 and tripped a circuit breaker. Per the People list, Intel beat on every line at $16.13 billion and $0.42 against $14.42 billion and $0.21, then round-tripped from $113.72 to under $100 for the crime of raising capex to $20 billion.

By the weekend the price had held and the argument had not. Per threadguy, Micron printed 961 and down 3 percent, holding its 955 fifty-day, with DRAM spot at $56 off the bottom. Per Shay Boloor, Michael Burry added to his Micron short at $934 and his Nvidia short at $210.

The bull case, stated cleanly. The demand is contracted, the supply is not coming, and the multiples assume the opposite. Per Boloor, the complex trades cheap because the market has already assumed peak earnings, so the debate is duration rather than level.

2027 earnings multiple
$SKHY~4x
$MU~6x
$SNDK~7x
$NVDA~16x
$GOOGL~22x
$AMZN~23x

The contracts are the part that separates this from a normal cycle. Per the Crypto list, Micron has 16 strategic customer agreements, 14 carrying roughly $100 billion of minimum contracted revenue through 2030, against $22 billion of upfront deposits already banked. Customers are funding supplier capacity. That is not what the end of a cycle looks like.

Then this week's signatures, all inside five days. Per the People list, Nvidia and SK Group signed letters of intent on a $500 billion-plus initiative including a 2-gigawatt Vera Rubin factory online in 2027 running SK Hynix HBM4, plus a long-term partnership co-developing future memory generations, and Nvidia put $1 billion into NAVER alongside Brookfield to triple Korea's buildout from 55 megawatts to 200 by 2028. Per the Polymarket list, Broadcom and Samsung signed a five-year memorandum worth more than $200 billion through 2030. Per Boloor, Dario Amodei confirmed Anthropic has locked memory supply with SK Hynix and Samsung, who together hold about 85 percent of high-bandwidth memory. Nobody signs a decade of supply into evaporating demand.

The cleanest version of the bull case is not about memory at all, it is about where the money ends up. Per the Crypto list, Gavin Baker has Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and Applied Materials on pace for roughly $430 billion of combined free cash flow next year, triple two years ago, while the five hyperscalers' free cash flow falls from about $250 billion in 2024 toward $100 billion by the end of 2026. The capex the market is punishing is arriving on the suppliers' income statements. Per BlackRock's Tony Kim, that is why he models a trillion dollars of capex this year and $10 trillion over five, calls it the primacy of memory, and points out that only three companies control it.

The bear case, taken seriously. Kim's note is the near-term threat and it is specific rather than vibes: 13 weeks of NAND inventory, price increases decelerating to 5 percent, a major customer already 90 percent covered. Against Morgan Stanley's own equity desk telling clients to buy memory the same morning, and against the same bank calling the dip a compelling entry three days earlier. That contradiction inside one firm went unreconciled all week and it should make you humble about the confidence on either side.

The more interesting attack is structural, and it arrived from a model release rather than a sell-side note. Per Bubble Boi on threadguy, Kimi K3 uses linear attention, which makes the key-value cache a fixed size instead of one that grows with context length. Less offloading means less commodity DRAM per user, existing racks serve far more users, and his question is the one that matters: how do you justify spending $500,000 on a new server rack.

He exempts high-bandwidth memory explicitly. He also walked it back on air, conceding only about 75 percent of the model is fixed, saying after more research that he does not think it is as clear-cut, and dating the impact roughly two years out. And he insists it is net bullish Nvidia, because linear attention keeps the GPU busy instead of idle waiting on memory.

Where that lands on Micron specifically is the part worth internalising. High-bandwidth memory is sliced and stacked out of commodity DRAM wafers, so HBM consumes DRAM as an input. HBM pricing has been steady to flat because all three makers have capacity, while commodity DRAM has gone vertical, and commodity DRAM is where Micron's money is. Per the same interview, Micron's HBM has always been the lowest quality of Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, so it earns a higher margin than Nvidia on a far less differentiated product. He is not short it. He is long the substitute, flash broadly and Phison specifically, because they are getting rid of DRAM, and his trigger is stated plainly: when you start seeing flash take DRAM's job, sell DRAM.

The third threat lists in a few hours. CXMT comes to Shanghai's STAR Market tomorrow at 8.66 yuan, raising roughly $8.5 billion at about $85 billion, the largest Chinese semiconductor listing on record, on first-quarter revenue up 719 percent, already the fourth-largest DRAM maker by capacity.

Per Chip Stock Investor, no American hyperscaler will touch Chinese memory and they put the odds of the ban lifting as very low, but memory is one global supply pool, so the ramp reprices every buyer regardless of who is legally allowed to buy. Their threshold is the useful number: at single-digit share of world bits the barrier holds, and in the teens spot pricing gets set in Hefei rather than Seoul. The lobbying confirms the stakes, with Apple pressing Commerce to allow Chinese memory in non-US products and calling Micron's 80 percent margins gouging.

And the demand-side worry has a name now too. Per the Market list, Jim Cramer's reading is that the market is saying it has seen the last of the capital-expenditure increases, and after Google the buyers leave traditional tech because the suppliers will not get the orders. If he is right, the contracted backlog is the last good backlog.

What to do with it. Own the cycle, but the vehicle matters more than the direction, and this week made that concrete. SK Hynix at four times 2027 earnings holds 56 percent of high-bandwidth memory share to Micron's 23, makes about 70 percent of Vera Rubin's HBM on parts co-designed with Nvidia, and now has a $500 billion letter of intent behind it.

Micron at six times carries the commodity-DRAM exposure that both the Kimi mechanism and the Chinese ramp attack, plus the quality knock. If you want the trade with the least argument against it, it is the Korean one. Per the Stocks list, John Tinsman's caution is the practical catch: the SK Hynix American receipt trades at a 33 percent premium to the Korean shares, so the obvious vehicle is the wrong one.

The level is the referee and it is unusually clean. Micron held 955 at 961. Above it the next move is 972. Losing 921 opens 891 to 906. Josh's 996 breakout trigger from Friday never armed and is dead.

The calendar does the rest of the work, and this week is dense. CXMT lists tomorrow. Per the Financial Markets list, the Fed decides Wednesday with CME futures at a 38 percent chance of a quarter-point hike against 13 percent a week earlier, and Polymarket at 25 percent, with a cut at zero in both. Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Amazon report from Wednesday. Per Joseph Hogue and Bridget of MarketBeat, hyperscaler earnings are the moment memory capex either shows up or does not, and her line is the honest frame for the whole position: this low probably only lasts until we see those hyperscaler reports.

My lean, with odds and a horizon, because a lean without both is just a mood. I am 65/35 that memory multiples expand before they compress, and that is a statement about the next quarter rather than the next three years. The duration argument wins the near term because CXMT and the Fed and four hyperscaler prints all land inside five days while linear attention is dated 2028.

Two things would flip me, and both are checkable. If fourth-quarter DRAM contract prices come in at Kim's 5 percent rather than the 20 to 30 percent the bulls model, the duration case is gone. If CXMT takes teens of world bits rather than single digits, pricing power moves to China and the multiple never re-rates. Hold the position with an exit trigger rather than a conviction, and the trigger is flash visibly taking DRAM's job, with Phison as the tell.

The scoreboard. Fourteen calls on the book resolved this week. Nine hit, four missed, one expired.

The wins, with the receipts. Michael Burry's Micron short, logged on the 12th betting on roughly a 30 percent drop, delivered about 36 percent as Micron fell from $1,255 to $804. Stocks with Josh's 861 reclaim held the 804 area, recaptured 861 on the 20th and ran to 945 by the 21st. Heisenberg's Nvidia target of 208.65 to 210 cleared 208 as Nvidia pushed back over $5 trillion. threadguy's long Brent from around 82 went above 100 by Thursday. Mentovia's 955 reclaim on Friday printed 961 and held.

The misses, said as plainly. Milk Road Macro rotated into Tesla ahead of the July 22 print and Tesla earned $0.33 against roughly $0.50 expected on a 16.8 percent gross margin and fell about 14 percent. Mike McGlone's Brent resistance near 83 with a base case rotating toward 40 was wrong in the most expensive direction, because Brent blew through 83 and traded above 110 by Friday. The Stocks list's Meta setup with a close stop at 615 broke that stop and traded near 600. Sykodelic needed Bitcoin to hold $66,000 on the weekly and it was near $64,100 by the weekend. One expired: Josh's Micron 996 trigger never armed, sitting about 4 percent above where Micron actually trades, so no position ever existed.

The house record needs a caveat more than it needs a victory lap. Four house calls have settled and all four hit, so the raw number is 4 for 4. Every one of them was a dated-catalyst call, that CPI would decide the tape on the 14th, that Tesla reports on the 22nd, that Alphabet is the referee on the 22nd, that Intel reports on the 23rd. Calling a scheduled event is the easy kind. The house has not yet settled a single directional call, so read 100 percent as unproven rather than good, and the 65/35 memory lean above is the first one that will actually cost something if it is wrong.

Nineteen open calls carry into next week, and they are front-loaded. CXMT and the Kimi weights land tomorrow, Bloom Energy reports Tuesday alongside the Trump and Netanyahu meeting, the Fed and Robinhood land Wednesday, Galaxy Digital's $38 fair-value call runs out Friday, and the prediction market on an Iran strike expires the same day. AppLovin follows on August 5, the SpaceX unlock on August 6, and the CLARITY floor vote by August 7. Micron's 12-times-trailing dip-buy thesis from Hogue is dated August 7 too, which means the entire memory argument gets marked to market inside two weeks.

item.title: [Investing] Alphabet's headline earnings of $9.11 a share were flattered by roughly $99 billion of gains on equity stakes, and the operational number was about $2.85, a slight miss rather than a blowout
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The backlog nobody priced went from $106 billion to $514 billion in twelve months with about $260 billion recognisable in the next twelve. Meanwhile Polymarket says 83 percent that the Fed holds Wednesday while CME futures put a hike at 35 percent, and that gap is the widest dislocation on the board.
item.content:encoded:
The backlog nobody priced went from $106 billion to $514 billion in twelve months with about $260 billion recognisable in the next twelve. Meanwhile Polymarket says 83 percent that the Fed holds Wednesday while CME futures put a hike at 35 percent, and that gap is the widest dislocation on the board.

This morning I led on Micron's take-or-pay contracts. Tonight the more important number is Alphabet's, and it cuts both ways at once. Here is the week ahead, the scoreboard, then five stories.

The week ahead. Market closed. Wednesday carries a rate decision and a third of the Nasdaq 100 in one session.

WhenWhat
Mon Jul 27CXMT lists in Shanghai. Kimi K3's weights. 24-hour single stock futures on the CME
Tue Jul 28Bloom Energy. Trump meets Netanyahu
Wed Jul 29The Fed, then Microsoft, Meta, Robinhood, SoFi, Arm, Qualcomm and Fortinet. Four names making up 29 percent of the Nasdaq 100 report right after the decision
Thu Jul 30Apple, Amazon, Coinbase. Q2 GDP and inflation
Fri Jul 31The S&P needs 7,499.36 to keep eleven straight green Julys
Wed Aug 5AppLovin
Thu Aug 6The SpaceX insider unlock

The scoreboard.

  • The Fed hold got more crowded and the venues disagree badly. Per the People list, Polymarket has 83 percent unchanged, up from 75 this morning. Per Joseph Hogue, CME futures put a hike at 35 percent against 12 a week ago, and September at 80. Kalshi again published no rate market, so there is no third read.
  • CXMT lists tomorrow and the silence is total. Nothing across roughly 26,000 words of weekend lists mentions it, and the whale short from this morning has no follow-up.
  • Kimi K3's weights are due tomorrow on David Ondrej's call from the 24th, with no confirmation for a fourth straight list. Per Jordi Visser, the model needs so much compute he cannot run it at home and Moonshot has paused subscriptions on capacity. That is the opposite of a smooth release.
  • Bloom Energy reports Tuesday. No source this weekend previews it.
  • The Iran strike call resolved as a miss this morning and the de-escalation held for a second night, though a tanker hit a mine in the strait anyway. Story five.

1. Alphabet's print was worse than the headline and better than the reaction. Both halves matter. Per Jordi Visser, the reported $9.11 a share included roughly $99 billion of gains on equity stakes, so operational earnings were about $2.85, a slight miss rather than a blowout. Operating cash flow was $39 billion against $45 billion of capex, and that is how the first negative free cash flow quarter happened, and Google is renting Nvidia chips from SpaceX for about $920 million a month.

That connects to this morning's asterisk. Per Ed Yardeni, three companies contributed $9 per share of the S&P's 37.9 percent blended growth through accounting gains on venture investments, and stripping them leaves 22 percent. Alphabet looks like one of the three, and the two findings are the same finding from different ends.

Now the half the selloff ignored. The backlog went from $106 billion to $514 billion in twelve months, up $50 billion in the quarter, with roughly $260 billion recognisable over the next twelve against about $200 billion of capex. On his framing the backlog is the whole ball game and the negative cash flow is a timing artifact.

One source called this failure mode before the print. Per Rick Orford, on Alphabet's custom silicon and the stack around it, the cash goes out first while the benefits arrive later, so Alphabet could be successful while the stock underperforms. His numbers never get a line item: Gemini serving costs down 78 percent last year, core AI response costs down more than 30 percent after Gemini 3. Alphabet does not need to replace Nvidia, only to keep reducing the tax.

He is honest about the odds, and that is what makes the number usable. He puts it at 70 to 75 percent that the capex programme is value-accretive over three to five years, and names the three risks: chip lives closer to four years than six, more than a trillion dollars of off-balance-sheet commitments, and backlog concentration.
