If that $514 billion is mostly OpenAI and Anthropic and OpenAI busts, it evaporates.

2. The Fed is the sharpest dislocation on the board, and Warsh has no comfortable move. Per BlackPantherCap, June payrolls came in at 57,000 against 115,000 expected with the prior two months revised down 74,000, and unemployment held at 4.2 percent only because 720,000 people left the labour force. June CPI printed minus 0.4 percent month over month, the biggest drop since April 2020, with core flat at 2.6 percent. Then the war restarted on July 8, Brent hit $100 on the 23rd, and September hike odds went from below 53 percent to around 82 in a week.

His conclusion is the one to carry into Wednesday: Warsh cannot cut into an oil shock and cannot hike hard into a weakening jobs market, so he holds and lets oil decide. As that desk puts it, the number that matters is not the CPI print, it is the count of ships.

Per Visser, the reason not to panic is that inflation swaps and two-year breakevens have not budged despite the oil move and the first non-zero CPI read does not arrive until mid-September. His line: they may raise rates and it is not going to kill the market. Per Hogue, PCE Thursday is expected to fall to 3.7 percent from about 4.

My lean, and I am moving it. This morning I said 70/30 for a hold. The venue spread argues for more confidence on the decision and less on the tone, so call it 85/15 hold and 50/50 that the statement reads hawkish enough to move the tape. The reason to trust the hold over the CME 35 percent: both macro sources quoting that hike probability still predict a hold themselves, so the 35 is a hedge rather than a forecast.

3. Memory got louder on both sides, and one of the loudest bulls just admitted the sentiment turned. The fundamental case is now enormous. Per Melvin, Meta and Micron published an LPDDR5X paper showing one third the power of DDR5 at under 7 percent of system draw and two to three times the throughput in Spark SQL. DRAM contract prices jumped as much as 95 percent in the first quarter, Micron's data-centre revenue runs above a $100 billion annualised rate and up sevenfold year over year, and Goldman sees undersupply through 2027. Per Milk Road AI, DRAM prices are up 171 percent year over year and Micron is sold out through the end of 2026.

Hold that against how the year actually looks, per Shay Boloor.

2026 performance
$SNDK+505%
$AEHR+278%
$DELL+247%
$MU+223%
$WDC+202%
$INTC+150%
$AMD+144%

Micron is up 223 percent this year and 27 percent off its high at once, and both facts are doing work.

The disagreement is not about the contracts. Per Visser, who is long, sentiment finally turned against him and Korea broke down, and he names Intel and Micron as beaters that will find a bottom. Against him, per Hogue, the instruction is one line: avoid most of these tech names like Micron. That comes from a value-rotation frame rather than any analysis of the take-or-pay structure, so weigh it accordingly. On levels, per Mentovia, Micron is bouncing out of a falling wedge and must hold the right shoulder and break the 991 neckline, with 1,155 and 1,186 above.

4. The neocloud trade is a balance-sheet argument, and two desks reach opposite conclusions on the same stock. Per Milk Road AI, the two names are CoreWeave and Nebius. CoreWeave has signed $63.9 billion this year alone, including more than $21 billion from OpenAI to 2031, $14.2 billion plus a further $21 billion from Meta, $6.3 billion from Nvidia and $6 billion from Jane Street, for $99.4 billion of obligations against roughly a $50 billion market cap. It also carries $24.9 billion of debt, $536 million of quarterly interest and a $740 million net loss, with free cash flow not positive until 2029 or 2030.

Nebius is preferred for that asymmetry: $9.3 billion of cash and no meaningful net debt, AI cloud revenue up 841 percent to $389.7 million, a guide of $3 to $4 billion toward a $7 to $9 billion run rate, and $17.4 billion of Microsoft backlog. In a week when the Fed decides, owning the one that does not need the rate to cooperate is cleaner.

Then the opposite view, from someone putting money on it. Per Invest with Henry, CoreWeave is his favourite AI name to sell puts against at $80 with an RSI of 35, below its 50-day, selling the August 21 $75 put for $7.50 against 102 percent implied volatility, with the $65 strike at 21 delta as the safer version. Same stock, and the leverage is either the reason to avoid it or the reason the options are paid.

One note strengthens both sides. Asked how guaranteed those commitments are, Melvin says they have to pay up and there is no way around it. Same take-or-pay structure as Micron's memory agreements, different corner of the supply chain.

5. Iran de-escalated for a second night and a tanker hit a mine anyway. Per the Market list, Iran has tied its military pause to the American suspension after 13 consecutive nights, and an Iranian source reports more scepticism than optimism. Per the Financial Markets list, an oil tanker struck a naval mine in the strait and exploded, and oil spiked above $100 into a week carrying a rate decision and four megacap reports.

The price read is the tradeable part. Per Heisenberg, the oil fund hit $142.50 Thursday on its most overbought reading in three and a half months and he expects roughly $130. Against that, per the Polymarket list, a wallet created yesterday put its entire $18,000 on Hormuz traffic normalising by August 31, roughly 15 cents on yes. Tonight's News edition has the reason the shooting stopped, and it is not diplomacy.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Operational earnings near $2.85 against a $9.11 headline flattered by about $99 billion of equity gains, with a $514 billion backlog up from $106 billion and the capex 70 to 75 percent likely to pay off, per Visser. Per Chamath, the bull case in one number is a 32 percent average return on invested capital since the IPO, and his argument is that model fragmentation helps Google because it monetises at the silicon and cloud layers whichever model wins.
  • $MU (Micron). Must hold the right shoulder and break 991 for 1,155 and 1,186, on DRAM contract prices up 95 percent in the first quarter and a data-centre run rate above $100 billion, per Mentovia and Melvin.
  • $NBIS and $CRWV (Nebius, CoreWeave). $9.3 billion of net cash against $24.9 billion of debt and $536 million of quarterly interest, with $99.4 billion of CoreWeave obligations against a $50 billion cap, per Milk Road AI.
  • $MRVL (Marvell). Visser's largest position on an expected step-up in optical and photonics, and he bought Applied Optoelectronics this week. Per Milk Road, Goldman sees co-packaged optics going from roughly $1 billion to tens of billions, though their own analyst calls that timeline hot.
  • $NOW, $PLTR and $TEM (ServiceNow, Palantir, Tempus). The owners-over-builders rotation: ServiceNow at 22 percent growth on a $28 billion order book, Palantir at 85 percent total and 133 percent US commercial, Tempus at 36 percent. Favourite, highest upside and most speculative in that order, per Rick Orford.
  • $GLXY (Galaxy Digital). The desk's target moved from $38 on Friday to about $57 tonight against roughly $24, on Helios at 800 megawatts contracted to CoreWeave. A target moving 50 percent in two days deserves scepticism on its own.
  • $ADA against $SOL (Cardano, Solana). Cardano is the named overvalued one: 15,000 to 17,000 daily transactions, app fees of two to three thousand dollars a day and $59 million of stablecoins against a $6 billion cap, versus Solana at over 100 million daily transactions, $16 billion of stablecoins and fees in the millions, per Lark Davis.
  • A caution on the framework itself. Per Chip Stock Investor, who helped popularise bottleneck analysis, timing which layer rises next is a fool's errand because a hundred-trillion-dollar economy does not decompose into layers.
  • BTC (Bitcoin). Per Sykodelic, it is not safe under $66,000, with a clear path to the realised cap near $54,000 and $58,000 the level that gets it there fast. Per Milk Road, a Bitcoin Magazine Pro analyst argues the opposite from lower prices, that $57,000 to $58,000 put Bitcoin in the bottom fifth percentile of its valuation history and at total production cost. That video was filmed July 14, twelve days stale, and the two sources disagree on where the 200-week average sits, roughly $63,000 against Lark Davis's 68,500 on Friday.

item.title: [Investing] Micron's contracts turn out to be take-or-pay with floor prices underneath them, and that is the fact that would have moved my memory odds if it had landed three hours earlier
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The only market-implied read on tomorrow's Chinese memory listing is a whale short of $13 million already up half a million into it. The S&P sits 3 percent from a record while Oracle is down 67 percent, and Yardeni found the accounting gain propping up the best earnings quarter since 2021.
item.content:encoded:
The only market-implied read on tomorrow's Chinese memory listing is a whale short of $13 million already up half a million into it. The S&P sits 3 percent from a record while Oracle is down 67 percent, and Yardeni found the accounting gain propping up the best earnings quarter since 2021.

The Sunday memo went out three hours ago at 65/35 that memory multiples expand before they compress. Two facts arrived after it, one on each side of the ledger, and both are more specific than anything in the memo. Here is the week ahead, the scoreboard, then five stories.

The week ahead. Market closed. Wednesday is a collision rather than a day.

WhenWhat
Mon Jul 27CXMT lists in Shanghai. Kimi K3's weights drop. 24-hour single stock futures go live on the CME. $APLD, $AMKR, $CDNS, $NVTS report
Tue Jul 28Bloom Energy, $KLAC, $PYPL, $V, $TER, $ENPH. Trump meets Netanyahu
Wed Jul 29The Fed, and in the same session $MSFT, $META, $HOOD, $SOFI, $ARM, $QCOM, $VRT and $LRCX
Thu Jul 30$AAPL, $AMZN, $COIN, $MSTR, $RDDT
Fri Jul 31$CVX, $XOM, $CCJ. The S&P needs 7,499.36 to keep eleven straight green Julys
Wed Aug 5AppLovin's second quarter
Thu Aug 6The SpaceX insider unlock

The scoreboard.

  • The Iran call flipped direction overnight. Yesterday's memo carried Polymarket at 55 percent for a US or Israeli strike by July 31. Per the Market list, Trump halted planned strikes on Friday despite having approved the attack plans, hours after Oman-mediated talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz resumed and reportedly made progress. Per the Polymarket list, the live market is now 54 percent that the two sides extend their 60-day negotiation window. The call stays open, but it is pointing the other way.
  • CXMT lists tomorrow and the only price signal is a short. Per the Financial Markets list, whale 0xf292 holds a 2.10 million CXMT short worth $13.04 million, up about $502,000, with a further $4.32 million of limit shorts queued and liquidation at $13.45.
  • Kimi K3's weights are due tomorrow on David Ondrej's call from the 24th. Nothing in roughly 37,000 words of weekend lists mentions the release, so treat the date as unconfirmed rather than done.
  • Bloom Energy reports Tuesday, still Milk Road's largest position at $222.
  • The Fed has not moved in a week. Per the People list, Polymarket has a 75 percent chance rates are unchanged Wednesday, the same 25 percent implied move as Friday's read. No venue in today's sources prices a cut.

1. The contracts are take-or-pay with floor prices, and that is the strongest single fact for the bull case. Per Rick Orford, Micron's 16 strategic agreements include 14 carrying roughly $100 billion of cumulative revenue at minimum contract prices, plus $22 billion of cash deposits and related commitments. The part nobody had put on the page until now is the structure: they are take-or-pay, so the customer either lifts the volume or still owes the money, and most of the largest agreements carry explicit floor prices. High-bandwidth memory is sold out through the end of the year.

That is the mechanism by which $100 billion survives a spot-price collapse, and it is exactly what the bear case needs to break. His own framing of the risk is sharper than most bears manage: memory stocks look most expensive at the bottom of the cycle and cheapest near the top, so 13 times forward earnings is precisely what a peak prints.

He also hands over two falsification triggers with a date attached, and that is rare in this format. A miss on the roughly $50 billion guidance in late September guts it. So does any whisper that floor prices are bending, and he concedes those floors are untested by a real downturn and that a customer facing slashed budgets would plausibly renegotiate or pay damages and walk.

One correction to carry forward. Burry initiated the Micron short near $1,051 in early July and added at $934, so with Micron at 961 he is roughly flat on the add rather than comfortably ahead. Per the Stocks list, Mentovia's response to the panic is worth the space: one investor's position is not an investment thesis and a 13F is not a crystal ball. Note also that CNBC's scorecard of Burry's July has his Tesla and Caterpillar legs paying off and does not mention Micron at all.

2. Tomorrow's Chinese memory IPO has one market-implied opinion and it is bearish. Nobody on the X lists is talking about the listing itself, and that silence says something about how narrowly this is being watched. What exists instead is a live position, and it is large, in profit and still being added to. That whale is short into a listing rather than positioned for a pop, with liquidation at $13.45 giving a clean level to watch.

Set that against what the sell side thinks the real supply threat is. Per Orford, his supply worry is not CXMT at all, which he never mentions. It is SK Hynix, whose July 10 Nasdaq listing raised about $26.5 billion and whose mid-to-long-term Korean fab plan runs to roughly $800 billion, with the pricing pressure landing in 2027 and beyond. Two credible bears, two completely different threats, on two different clocks.

3. The index is three percent from a record and its leadership is in a bear market. This is the gap that explains why portfolios feel worse than the tape looks. Per Mentovia:

Drawdown from the high
$NVDA-13%
$AMZN-17%
$GOOG-22%
$META-25%
$MU-27%
$MSFT-31%
$INTC-35%
$TSLA-37%
$MRVL-41%
$PLTR-42%
$SPCX-49%
$ORCL-67%

Per the Market list, Oracle is down 28 of its last 37 sessions and now sits below its April 2025 lows. Memory at minus 27 percent is one of the better performers in that table, so the bull case and the crowding risk sit in the same number.

The flows say the rotation is real. Per the People list, last week saw $9.21 billion leave the largest S&P tracker, $5.03 billion leave the Nasdaq proxy, $1.42 billion leave semis and $1.16 billion leave software, while $3.53 billion went into Vanguard's S&P fund and $1.72 billion into financials. Per Charlie Bilello, 17 of the 30 worst S&P performers this year are software and related services, and the top nine are all AI-infrastructure beneficiaries.

One desk is positioned for it rather than commenting on it. Per Stocks with Josh, his hourly momentum screen has sell signals on the majority of the Magnificent Seven and he is making money short, with a stated rule of no longs next week unless a name is back above the zero line.

4. Earnings are the best since 2021 and Yardeni found the asterisk. The headline is genuinely strong. Per the People list, 27 percent of the S&P has reported with 86 percent beating on earnings and 80 percent on revenue, and blended growth is running 37.9 percent against 23.2 percent expected at the end of June.

Then the footnote that should change how you read it. Per Ed Yardeni, three companies added $9 per share of that growth through accounting gains on venture investments, and stripping those out leaves 22 percent. The AI capital cycle is now showing up inside reported earnings per share rather than only in capex lines, which makes the quality of this quarter harder to trust than the number suggests.

Buffett's posture is the one to hold against it. Per the People list, he calls the market a church with a casino attached, says we have never had people in a more gambling mood, sits on roughly $380 billion of cash and says plainly that we do not do anything.

5. Wednesday puts the Fed and four of the six biggest reports in one session, and the hike has been quietly de-priced into worsening data. The setup is asymmetric and nobody seems bothered. Polymarket has 75 percent unchanged with no cut priced anywhere, while per the Financial Markets list import prices ran 7.1 percent higher year over year in June and 4.2 percent excluding fuel, global bond yields sit at their highest since the financial crisis, and per the Market list US crude has gone from $68 on July 1 to $90.

Per the Kalshi list, the bond market is signalling that investors should start worrying about the war again even as equities shrugged, with weekend pricing marking the Nasdaq proxy only 0.53 percent higher on the strike-halt news. Bonds and stocks are reading the same weekend differently.

My lean, with odds. I am 70/30 that Wednesday delivers a hold rather than a hike, in line with the market, but I am closer to 50/50 that the statement reads hawkish enough to matter, because oil up a third since the war began and import prices at 7.1 percent give Warsh no room to sound relaxed. The trade that expresses it is not a rate bet, it is respecting that Microsoft, Meta, Robinhood and SoFi all report into that decision, so position sizes should assume one session can reprice both the discount rate and the earnings.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU (Micron). Held the 955 fifty-day at 961, roughly 13 times forward, with 16 agreements carrying take-or-pay floor prices on about $100 billion, against Burry short from an average between $1,051 and $934 and a late-September guidance print near $50 billion as the falsification date, per Rick Orford.
  • $ORCL (Oracle). Down 67 percent from its high, down 28 of the last 37 sessions and below its April 2025 lows, which makes it the single most damaged large-cap in the AI complex, per the Market list.
  • $AMD (Advanced Micro Devices). Baird's Tristan Gerra doubled his target to $1,250 from $625 on a model of $147 billion of AI GPU revenue by 2030 at 15 percent share against a $1.4 trillion accelerator market, per the Stocks list.
  • $HOOD (Robinhood). Reports Wednesday with Goldman at $137 and Morgan Stanley at $124 against an old high of $153. Its chain passed 2 million monthly users and 150 million lifetime transactions, though per the Crypto list only about $55 million of stock tokens traded in 24 hours and tokenized GameStop alone was $26.6 million of that, so the equity-token thesis is thinner than the chain growth.
  • $CEG (Constellation Energy). The unnamed nuclear pick, on being the largest US nuclear provider, the Calpine acquisition adding gas, and Microsoft's Three Mile Island restart, with Meta's Prometheus supercluster deal as confirmation of the demand, per Fin Tek.
  • $CRWV (CoreWeave). Has disclosed more than $63 billion of customer commitments this year, including over $21 billion from OpenAI through 2031, more than $35 billion from Meta, $6.3 billion from Nvidia as a paying customer and a multi-billion-dollar Anthropic deal, per the Stocks list.
  • ETH (Ethereum). Near $1,880 on Arthur Hayes buying another 645 coins, taking him to 3,915 since July 15 at an average $1,909 and down about $113,000, per the Financial Markets list. Per Lark Davis, the cleaner crypto relative-value trade is Lighter against Hyperliquid, on $700 million of daily volume versus $2 billion at a fraction of the market cap.

item.title: [Investing] The Fed number I could not find this morning showed up tonight, and it is a 38 percent chance of a rate hike on Wednesday against 13 percent a week ago
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Brent has gone from $71 on the first of July to $98.30, and that is the entire story behind the repricing. Memory is priced for collapse at four to six times 2027 earnings while every supplier on earth signs decade-long deals, and Bubble Boi finally put a specific mechanism under the memory bear case.
item.content:encoded:
Brent has gone from $71 on the first of July to $98.30, and that is the entire story behind the repricing. Memory is priced for collapse at four to six times 2027 earnings while every supplier on earth signs decade-long deals, and Bubble Boi finally put a specific mechanism under the memory bear case.

This morning no source carried an actual Fed probability, only a strategist's read. Tonight there are two numbers, they disagree, and neither contains a cut. Here is the week ahead, the scoreboard, then five stories.

The week ahead. Market closed. Everything lands in four sessions.

WhenWhat
Mon Jul 27CXMT lists in China at roughly $85 billion on Q1 revenue up 719 percent. 24-hour single stock futures go live on the CME. Kimi K3's open weights drop
Wed Jul 29The Fed decides. CME puts a quarter-point hike at 38 percent, Polymarket at 25 percent, and a cut at zero in both
Wed Jul 29 onMicrosoft, Meta, Apple, Amazon, Robinhood and SoFi report
Mon Aug 3Palantir's second quarter
Wed Aug 5AppLovin's second quarter
Thu Aug 6The SpaceX insider unlock

The scoreboard.

  • The Fed gap from this morning is closed, and the answer is worse than the framing. Per Anas Alhajji quoting the Financial Times, CME futures price a 38 percent chance of a quarter-point hike Wednesday, up from 13 percent a week ago, with BofA's Mark Cabana calling the meeting "definitely live." Per StockMKTNewz, Polymarket has it at 25 percent. Take the 13-point spread seriously.
  • Micron held 955 and Friday's 996 long is dead. Per threadguy, Micron printed 961 and down 3 percent, so this morning's reclaim call was right and 972 never came. The separate 996 breakout trigger from Friday is now formally expired, about 4 percent above where Micron actually trades, so no entry ever existed.
  • Monday settles two calls at once. CXMT lists, threadguy's call from the 16th, and Kimi K3's weights, David Ondrej's from the 24th. Both are now confirmed by tonight's sources rather than assumed.
  • Bloom Energy reports Tuesday, still Milk Road's largest position at $222.
  • Robinhood reports Wednesday alongside the Fed, Goldman at $137 and Morgan Stanley at $124 against a stock near $95.

1. The hike is live, and oil is the reason. Per the Market list, Brent has gone from $71 on July 1 to $98.30. Cabana's sentence pairs the two: policy may not be restrictive, "and oil is now rising again."

Here is what the war has done to the things that feed into a consumer price index, per Charlie Bilello.

Since the Iran war began
Sulfur+146%
European natural gas+98%
Heating oil+63%
Diesel+40%
Gasoline+38%
Brent and WTI+35%
Rice+35%
Wheat+15%

The market has been trading this without naming it. Per Bilello, value, small caps and international are all outperforming while the Magnificent Seven are down on the year. Per LuxAlgo, the curve now prices two hikes by year end and the 30-year is the most above 5 percent since the financial crisis.

The person to watch is not the chair. Per Milk Road, Kevin Warsh's hawkish debut was credibility theatre from a chair seven weeks in who declined to submit a dot, and the real risk is Christopher Waller, now hinting the funds rate may be too low. Their threshold is usable: one hike and done is fine, a signalled series is not.

2. Memory is priced for collapse while every supplier on earth signs a decade-long deal. Per Shay Boloor, the memory complex trades cheap because the market has already assumed peak earnings, so "the debate is really about duration," with SK Hynix guiding shortage severity through the end of the decade and Samsung through at least 2027.

2027 earnings multiple
$SKHY~4x
$MU~6x
$SNDK~7x
$ORCL~11x
$NVDA~16x
$META~16x
$MSFT~20x
$GOOGL~22x

Now the deal flow against those multiples. Per StockMKTNewz, Nvidia and SK Group signed letters of intent on a $500 billion-plus initiative including a 2-gigawatt Vera Rubin factory coming online in 2027 on SK Hynix HBM4. Per the Polymarket list, Broadcom and Samsung signed a $200 billion memorandum through 2030. And per Shay Boloor, Dario Amodei confirmed Anthropic has locked supply with SK Hynix and Samsung, who together control about 85 percent of high-bandwidth memory.

Burry is short into all of it at $934 on Micron and $210 on Nvidia, per Shay Boloor. File the lobbying tell: Apple wants Washington to clear CXMT and calls Micron's 80 percent margins gouging, the same weekend CXMT lists.

3. The Kimi shock is the first specific mechanism anyone has offered for how the memory trade actually breaks. Every bear case until now has been about demand. This one is about architecture. Per Bubble Boi on threadguy, Kimi uses linear attention, which makes the key-value cache (the working memory a model keeps per user) a fixed size instead of one that grows with context length, and unlike earlier attempts it delivers frontier-quality results.

The consequence is narrow. Less offloading means less commodity DRAM per user and existing racks serve far more users, so "how can you justify spending 500k for a new server rack?" He exempts high-bandwidth memory, walks it back partway himself (only about 75 percent of the model is fixed), and puts the impact two years out. He also insists Kimi is net bullish Nvidia, because it keeps the GPU busy during inference instead of idle.

His Micron case follows from that rather than from the chart. Micron out-earns Nvidia on margin with a less differentiated product, and per the same desk it is the most overrated name in memory, with "always the lowest quality" high-bandwidth memory of the big three and profits riding commodity DRAM pricing. He is not short it, he is long the substitute: flash broadly and Phison specifically, "because they're getting rid of DRAM," with the trigger stated plainly as "when you start seeing flash take DRAM's job, sell DRAM."

A second mechanism arrives independently. Per Chip Stock Investor, no US hyperscaler will touch Chinese memory, but memory is one global supply pool, so CXMT and YMTC ramping moves world prices regardless. Two unrelated arguments, same conclusion, and a Chinese memory IPO on Monday.

The maximal other side, per Milk Road AI, is Kyle seeing no capex slowdown until 2030, with analysts having called the tip-over "6 to 9 months away" every quarter for two years. My lean is a two-year view rather than a two-week one: duration wins into next week, architecture wins by 2028. Call it 65/35 that memory multiples expand before they compress, because CXMT and the Fed are catalysts this week and linear attention is not.

4. Alphabet's negative free cash flow is the entire capex-punishment story in one line. The numbers are better than the reaction. Per Kyle Reidhead, Alphabet's first-ever negative quarterly free cash flow came in at minus $5.9 billion on capex of $44.9 billion, up 100 percent year over year, with 2026 capex guided to $195 to $205 billion. Revenue grew 24 percent to $119.8 billion, cloud 82 percent to $24.8 billion at a 35.6 percent operating margin, backlog rose $50 billion in one quarter to $514 billion, and Gemini reached 950 million monthly users. The stock fell more than 6 percent.

Jim Cramer named the regime change in one sentence. Per the Market list, "today the market is saying we have seen the last of the cap ex increases," and after Google the buyers leave traditional tech. Per WhiteCollarExit, the trailing multiple compressed from about 21 times to under 16 in a year while cloud operating income tripled to $8.8 billion.

Somebody is acting on it. Per Milk Road PRO, the desk bought Alphabet at $319.34 as the cheapest in years, plus Intel at $93.70, ServiceNow at $97.09 on cRPO growing 21.5 percent against a 19.5 percent guide, and Nokia at $10.40.

5. The plumbing is flashing while the index looks fine. Per the Kalshi list, corporate bond funds recorded their largest weekly outflows since 2020 and retail is buying at its slowest pace in over six years. Per Bilello, 17 of the 30 worst S&P 500 stocks this year are software companies.

The internals are worse than the headline. Per Heisenberg, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Tesla and Meta all sit below both their 50-day and 200-day averages, Nvidia below the 50-day, and Apple "extremely above" both, which prompts his question about why everyone is selling every Magnificent Seven name except the most expensive one. Meta has fallen seven sessions running and has never fallen eight in fourteen years.

Per the Stocks list, NoLimitGains puts it best: "The S&P is 2% off all time highs and somehow people are down 30% in a month." And per Mandelbrot, do not read Apple's strength as safety: momentum rolls, then the Nasdaq, then the S&P, and "Apple typically stays relatively strong through all this and is the last to fall."

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU (Micron). Printed 961 and held the 955 fifty-day, 972 above and 921 the break that opens 891 to 906. Near 6 times 2027 earnings, Burry short from $934, CXMT listing Monday, per threadguy and Shay Boloor.
  • $INTC (Intel). Back under $100 after touching $113.72 on the beat and round-tripping 20 percent, down five straight weeks. Bubble Boi is "super bullish" on a $20 billion capex cap, customer prepayments and 14A with a guaranteed customer, math he takes to 100 percent revenue growth in a year, per threadguy.
  • $AMD (Advanced Micro Devices). At $521, up 133 percent this year. Anthropic committed to up to 2 gigawatts of Instinct MI250 and is buying about $5 billion of AMD equity, with most of the first gigawatt guided into 2027, near $20 to $30 billion from one customer. The 2030 server CPU forecast went $60 billion to $120 billion to $220 billion inside a year, per Jose Najarro.
  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Minus $5.9 billion of free cash flow against a $514 billion backlog and 82 percent cloud growth, multiple down from 21 times to under 16, per Kyle Reidhead.
  • $SPCX (SpaceX). Closed $118.24, down 47 percent from above $225, record short interest, and the August 6 unlock that can double the float, per the Stocks list.
  • Nuclear, ranked. NuScale has the lowest execution risk as the only certified path on sub-5 percent fuel, Oklo the greatest upside at roughly $9 billion with zero revenue and no plant until late 2027, NANO the riskiest. High-assay uranium is the constraint and Centrus does not supply until 2029, per Rick Orford and the short version.
  • BTC (Bitcoin). Near $64,000, futures open interest down 48 percent from its $95 billion peak. Lark Davis wants 67,000 and calls 63,000 the invalidation, against 270,000 coins bought by whales last month, per Lark Davis and OnChainMind.
  • Medical devices, the anti-AI trade. The sector fund is down over 20 percent this year and device makers on 5 to 6 percent cash-flow yields trade 20 to 30 percent under the S&P. Barron's names five buys and one wait: $ABT at 16 times, $DHR (beat and raised, then fell 14 percent), $ISRG (down 17 percent for delivering 18 percent growth against a 14 guide), $BSX (down 50 percent on an 8-versus-10 trim), $EW at $84 targeting $100, and $MDT a wait, per Bill Alpert.
  • Tokenized equities are a real number now. Market cap went from $329 million a year ago to about $1.7 billion, monthly transfer volume from $53 million to $9.22 billion, and the mix rotated out of crypto-linked products (79 percent to 21) into AI and chips (0.3 to 15.5). DTCC's full launch is October, per a16z crypto. Robinhood's chain is the fastest ever to 100 million transactions and the degens got there first, per Lark Davis.
  • $UNI (Uniswap). The $2.90 breakout ran to $3.90 and partly stopped out. Entry is the $3.20 to $3.30 trendline, or a reclaim of $3.90 targeting $4.50 to $4.70, per Lark Davis.

item.title: [Investing] The S&P gave back every gain and closed red on Friday as Iran escalated, the Nasdaq 100 is heading for its worst July in twenty-two years, and Apple printed a record $333 in the middle of it
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Momentum just had its worst single month in the history of both the Morgan Stanley and Goldman indexes while institutions put $680 billion back into stocks in two hours and retail bought at the slowest pace in six years. Michael Burry pressed his Micron and Nvidia shorts, and the 30-year yield has not been this far above 5 percent since the financial crisis.
item.content:encoded:
Momentum just had its worst single month in the history of both the Morgan Stanley and Goldman indexes while institutions put $680 billion back into stocks in two hours and retail bought at the slowest pace in six years. Michael Burry pressed his Micron and Nvidia shorts, and the 30-year yield has not been this far above 5 percent since the financial crisis.

Two different markets traded on Friday. One of them set an all-time high and the other had the worst month it has ever recorded. Here is the week ahead, the scoreboard, then five stories.

The week ahead. The market is closed, and what is coming is the heaviest week of the quarter.

WhenWhat
Mon Jul 2724-hour single stock futures go live on the CME, 55 standard and 22 micro contracts, cash settled with no borrow fee to short
Mon Jul 27Kimi K3 releases its open weights, the call this desk logged on the 24th
Tue Jul 28Bloom Energy reports, and Trump meets Netanyahu
Wed Jul 29The Fed decides
Wed Jul 29 onMicrosoft, Meta, Apple, Amazon, Robinhood and SoFi all report
Wed Aug 5AppLovin's second quarter, the first real scorecard on its open platform
Thu Aug 6The SpaceX insider unlock that can double the public float

Per Heisenberg, that earnings list is the whole Magnificent Seven complex reporting into a Fed decision in the same 72 hours. Per the Stocks list, the futures launch matters more than it sounds: shorting 1,000 shares of Tesla at $330 will need about $50,000 of overnight margin, roughly 15 percent of what it took before, though section 1256 tax treatment does not apply so gains are fully short term.

The scoreboard.

  • The Bitcoin call I ran on Friday missed. Sykodelic needed $66,000 held on the weekly and it was gone before the weekend, with Bitcoin near $64,100. The line that matters now is lower, the moving averages around $63,000.
  • Friday's Micron long never armed. The 996 trigger sat about 5 percent above where Micron actually traded. Per Mentovia, the fight was at the 955 50-day line all session, with 921 the break that opens 891 to 906, and his verdict into the weekend was that the bounce was "not strong enough" and needs more consolidation. No entry ever existed, and the setup only comes back if 955 does.
  • Monday brings two of the calls on this book. Kimi K3's open weights land, the release David Ondrej flagged on the 24th with twenty-plus inference providers expected within days. CXMT's listing at roughly $85 billion is also dated Monday from threadguy on the 16th, though nothing this weekend mentions it, so treat that one as unconfirmed.
  • Bloom Energy reports Tuesday, the Milk Road desk's largest position at $222 and down 30 to 35 percent from a high a month old.
  • Wednesday's Fed has repriced hardest of anything on the book. Per Tom Lee via WOLF, "monetary policy is not dovish, market was looking for two cuts, now it's two hikes." No list this weekend carries an actual hold-versus-hike probability, so that is a strategist's read on the curve and not a Fed-day number.

1. Friday's tape split clean in two, and the gap between the halves is the story. The index number hid two opposite markets.

Friday and the week
S&P 500erased all gains, closed red as Iran escalated
Nasdaq 100on track for its worst July in 22 years
$QQQdown 1.6 percent on the week, below its 50-day
$IWMdown four straight weeks, sitting on its 50-day
$AAPLrecord high $333, past a $4.9 trillion market cap
$METAlower seven sessions in a row
$GOOGLdown almost 8 percent on the week
$TSLAdown 24 percent since June 30

Per the Polymarket list, the S&P turning red was explicitly an Iran headline. Per the Kalshi list, the Nasdaq 100 is heading for its worst July since 2004 while Apple sets records inside the same index.

The dispersion underneath is historic. Per stocktalkweekly, this is the biggest one-month drawdown for momentum stocks on record according to both the Morgan Stanley and Goldman momentum indexes, from a trader who is still up 160 percent this year and was up 584 percent over twelve months. Owning the index cost you very little in July. Owning what worked in June cost you everything.

2. Institutions bought the dip on Friday afternoon and retail has stopped buying entirely. The flow data contradicts itself in a way that resolves once you split it by who. Per the Kalshi list, $680 billion was added back to US stocks in the last two hours of Friday and investors are "flooding into US equities at a record pace." The same feed, nine hours earlier, said retail investors are buying at the slowest pace in more than six years, which per Barchart is a six-year low.

Both are true and they describe different people. A late-Friday two-hour institutional bid into a tape where households have gone quiet is the definition of a market held up by professionals, and per asklivermore the average retail portfolio is down 12.7 percent this year. That is why they are quiet.

3. Rates are the transmission channel, and the 30-year above 5 percent is doing all the damage. Every bearish chain this weekend runs through the bond market rather than through AI demand. Per LuxAlgo, the 30-year yield has spent more time above 5 percent than at any point since the financial crisis. Per Lisa Abramowicz, real yields on the 10-year are the highest since 2023, and Milk Road Macro reads a 2.3 percent real yield as monetary strangulation arriving without another hike.

Per Melvin, the chain is mechanical: Iran escalation lifts oil, oil keeps inflation sticky, sticky inflation keeps yields high, and high yields compress the multiple on every long-duration name. That is why Nvidia, Micron, Nebius, SanDisk, Broadcom and Applied Optoelectronics all sold as one basket. He does not think there is a hike this year. Note the oil number is genuinely in dispute, with Chamath saying crude costs $81 and having fallen from $100, against desks the same evening describing oil as pushing $100. I am not building anything on a level two credible sources put $20 apart.

The important part is that nobody is calling the fundamentals broken. Per Melvin, the AI infrastructure thesis has not suddenly broken and what changed is the multiple investors will pay. Per Milk Road, Robinhood at the same $100 stock grew revenue 53 percent to $4.5 billion and platform assets 48 percent to $377 billion, so prices fell and the business did not.

4. Memory is the most crowded fight in the market, and Burry pressed his shorts into it. The longest-term conviction in the market sits directly opposite the worst near-term chart. Per Shay Boloor, Michael Burry added to his Micron short at $934 and his Nvidia short at $210, and per the Kalshi list his Tesla short is up 24 percent since June 30.

The other side is institutional and enormous. Per BlackRock's Tony Kim speaking to Molly O'Shea, the firm is modelling a trillion dollars of capex this year and $10 trillion over five, the "primacy of memory" becomes more important from here, and only three companies control it. Per The Tech Investor, Nvidia and SK hynix announced a $500 billion initiative including a 2-gigawatt data center running Vera Rubin chips on HBM4 memory (the stacked high-bandwidth memory that every AI accelerator needs), and IREN sits on $7.6 billion of cash against a market cap barely twice that.

My lean, and it is a lean rather than a conviction: Burry has the next month and Kim has the next three years. The specific line that settles it is Micron reclaiming 955, and until that happens the structural bulls are early and saying so out loud.

5. Five independent desks arrived at the same posture, and that agreement is the loudest thing in the data. Nobody is selling and nobody is buying. Per the Stocks list, Chairman's Ledger is "a little less long and finger off the trigger on dips, no selling but not adding," PD Philly is risk-off with 10 to 20 percent cash, Ariel calls it chop, and Jim Cramer says he is struggling to find reasons to buy, four days after saying "Intel's the one."

The disagreement is about depth and it is genuinely tradeable. Per that same list, vnkumarvnk points out the S&P is barely 3 percent off its all-time high and warns a 20 percent drawdown is still ahead, TicTocTick says the bear market is already here, and Ariel names the actual arbiter: the Nasdaq proxy reclaiming its 50-day, or a 10 percent-plus correction followed by a real follow-through day. Anything in between is chop.

I lean chop over bear market at roughly 60/40, because the equal-weight tape and the S&P are both within a few percent of highs while only the momentum cohort has broken. That view dies the moment the Russell loses its 50-day after four red weeks. That is precisely where it sat on Friday.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU (Micron). The battleground is 955, with 972 above it and an implosion to 891 to 906 if 921 goes. Burry added short at $934 while BlackRock calls memory the structural winner, per Mentovia and Shay Boloor.
  • $NVDA (Nvidia). The inverted head and shoulders is intact with 206 supporting, the 50-day near 209 as resistance, and a move over 212 opening 216 then 221, per Mentovia.
  • $MRVL (Marvell). Down about 37 percent from its June 18 high, with FY27 revenue guided to $11.5 billion and a path to $23.3 billion by FY29, Amazon at 30 to 40 percent of revenue, and Milk Road's Melvin buying from $269 down through $186 and seeing little room below $150, per Milk Road Macro.
  • $GLXY (Galaxy Digital). At $25 against fair value near $38 on the Helios contract alone, having tapped $21.60 last week, with CoreWeave signed for the full 800 megawatts on a 15-year lease averaging over $1 billion a year, and a 9.1 percent construction loan whose refinancing toward 7 percent nearly doubles free cash flow to equity. It priced $3.5 billion of senior secured notes on Friday, per Milk Road and the Financial Markets list.
  • $HOOD (Robinhood). Reports this week with Goldman at $137 and Morgan Stanley at $124 against a $100 stock and an old high of $153, per Milk Road.
  • $UNI (Uniswap). The unification proposal passed with 99.9 percent support, the fee switch is live, a portion of every swap now buys back and burns the token, 100 million came out of the treasury in one transaction, and daily gross fees have been running over $5 million, per Lark Davis. His channel is promotional, so weigh the call accordingly, but the mechanism is on chain and checkable.
  • BTC (Bitcoin). Around $64,100 on Friday's whale transfers. The fork is mechanical: per Tradermayne hold here and $70,000-plus is next with $59,000 to $60,000 the place he would add, against CryptoKaleo wanting one last leg lower, no new highs until 2027, and 45 percent odds Bitcoin sees $50,000 before $100,000. Per SuperBitcoinBro, the moving averages near $63,000 are the line his bullish case depends on, which makes 63 the number rather than the 66 weekly close this desk was watching on Friday.

item.title: [Investing] Intel beat on every single line and handed the entire rally back by two in the afternoon, because it also raised capex to $20 billion and this market has started billing anyone who spends
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Alphabet got the same treatment a day earlier and printed its first negative free cash flow in twenty years. The average stock sits a percent and a half from a record high while the index clings to support, some crude grades pushed above $110, and two desks called opposite bottoms in Tesla within an hour of each other.
item.content:encoded:
Alphabet got the same treatment a day earlier and printed its first negative free cash flow in twenty years. The average stock sits a percent and a half from a record high while the index clings to support, some crude grades pushed above $110, and two desks called opposite bottoms in Tesla within an hour of each other.

This morning the question was whether Intel's blowout could carry the tape. By two o'clock the tape had answered, and the answer had nothing to do with Intel's quarter. Here is the session, then seven stories.

The close. A day of holding the line rather than repairing anything. Per Reddog, the S&P held $735, yesterday's low, and stalled under $744 as resistance, while the Nasdaq proxy lost and then reclaimed $686, the level Heisenberg had called extremely important support before the open.

The internals were the interesting part. Per Heisenberg, the volatility index actually fell 1.6 percent through the tech damage, and the equal-weight version of the index (the same 500 companies with each one counted the same, so the mega-caps cannot carry it) sits 1.5 percent from an all-time high. Alphabet rose 2 percent on a red day. Intel fell more than 10 percent from its premarket highs to close down over 4 percent, per the Kalshi list, and Tesla printed a new low at $315.

Underneath, the commodity tape kept tightening. Per Anas Alhajji, some crude grades traded above $110, and per the Kalshi list, wheat hit a three-year high. The one clean pop came at 3:16pm on a headline about a possible Pakistan-brokered channel to Iran, where InvestorsLive booked index calls up 1,200 percent. Crypto miners were the only green sector on the board, up 1.4 percent today and 27 percent on the week, per Blockworks.

The momentum screens are uniformly bad. Per Stocks with Josh, his hourly momentum crossover shows sell signals across almost the entire Magnificent Seven with $NFLX the lone buy, $MSFT and $GOOGL both below the zero line, and a diamond-pattern breakdown on the index itself. Per threadguy, the read is simply that stocks are "really toppy," with Tesla missing earnings, Alphabet's capex up sharply on negative free cash flow, and war risk back on the board.

1. Intel delivered the quarter and lost the day anyway, and the $20 billion capex line is why. The print was not the problem. Per the People list, $INTC earned $0.42 against $0.21 expected on revenue of $16.13 billion against $14.42 billion, and then raised full-year capital spending to $20 billion after signing three-to-five-year supply agreements. Hours later the same account posted the epitaph, "Aaaand, it's gone."

The mechanism was named out loud while it happened. Per the Market list, Hulk Capital wrote that Intel was up $12 after crushing earnings "but they are ramping capex and the market is punishing big capex spenders," and Jim Cramer spent the session on the other side, asking sellers to "come back and knock these two down for us" on Intel and $AMD.

So a company that spent two years being told to invest in its foundry got sold for saying yes. That is a regime, and Intel is now the cleanest example of it.

2. The market has flipped from paying for AI spending to charging for it, and Alphabet is the bigger tell. Look at what happened to the best cloud number of the quarter. Per the Market list, $GOOGL grew Cloud 82 percent with 36 percent operating margins and passed a billion monthly users on AI Mode, and a further $15 billion capex increase in three months pushed quarterly free cash flow negative for the first time in more than twenty years. Per Heisenberg, the stock is now under both its 50-day and 200-day averages for the first time since May 2025 and has fallen in 9 of the last 11 weeks. Per this note, that cloud line was $24.8 billion in absolute terms.

The rotation is explicit. Per threadguy, Alphabet is spending north of $200 billion "at a time where their AI sucks," and his division of the market is receivers good, spenders bad, with $MU, $MRVL, $BE, $SNDK, $INTC, $AMD, $ASML and $AVGO on one side and $GOOGL, $AMZN, $META, $TSLA, $MSFT and $ORCL on the other. $ORCL is down more than 53 percent in under two months, per Heisenberg.

Then there is the part of the bill nobody has to show you. Per Prof G Markets, roughly $1.7 trillion of data-center debt sits in special purpose vehicles (separate companies that hold the debt and the chips, which the hyperscaler only partly owns so it stays off the parent's balance sheet). Their named example is Hyperion, where PIMCO and Blue Owl hold about 80 percent and Meta about 20 percent while being the only client. Asked what happens to those investors if the data-center revenue never arrives, the answer was that they do not get made whole. Their line is the honest one, "the only reason this is not considered a problem is it hasn't actually happened."

3. Micron is the consensus dip-buy of the day, and for once the bulls brought levels and a date. Two unrelated desks landed on the same name. Per Joseph Hogue and Bridget of MarketBeat, $MU is the pick over $PLTR and $ORCL on 12 times trailing and roughly 6 times forward earnings with a 75 percent EBITDA margin (cash profit before interest, tax and writedowns) against a 45 percent five-year average, and 181 percent expected earnings growth. Bridget's version is blunter, "a 75 percent profit margin can't be faked."

The catalyst is dated. Both name hyperscaler earnings in the next one to two weeks as the moment memory capex either shows up or does not. Per Stocks with Josh, millions of dollars of next-week calls printed and Micron closed green on a red tape, with his trigger at 996, targets at 1,035 then 1,089, and a stop at 983.

The bear case has a name too. Per Hogue, Louis Navellier gives memory 12 to 18 more months of explosive growth before a rethink, and per the Stocks list, John Galt spent the day taking memory profits in $SNDK, $ALAB and $EWY after calling the face-plant. Kyle Reidhead is on the other side calling the 35 percent drawdown a gift, with semis at 19.5 times forward earnings, below their ten-year average.

4. Two credible desks called opposite bottoms in Tesla within an hour, and both showed their work. This is the cleanest disagreement on the board. Per Mentovia, $TSLA breaking 321 "was no good signal, and the crash is now accelerating," with 286 to 292 as the technical destination and 321 and 332 flipping to resistance overhead. Per TicTocTick in the same digest, "I am calling a low in Tesla stock here now 300," on the argument that Tesla at roughly 12 times sales is cheaper than Apple at the same multiple.

The fundamental read is worse than either chart. Per Prof G Markets, Optimus asks Tesla to ramp a brand new product on a brand new supply chain with a brand new design, and Tesla has no track record doing that at this complexity and cost. Per Stocks with Josh, who is short into $300, the last 14 percent single-day drop took 60 days to find its bottom before doubling, and he is hedging his own long-term position through the end of August rather than picking the low.

5. The macro data quietly turned stagflationary today and nobody connected it. Read these prints together instead of one at a time. Per Fast Stock News, the July flash composite came in at 53.6 with services beating at 53.6 against 51.5 expected while manufacturing missed at 53.8, and June new home sales beat at 628,000 but the median price fell 2.7 percent year over year to $398,300 against 9.3 months of supply, with the West down 22.4 percent.

Now the other side of the same economy. Per LuxAlgo, S&P Global reports US businesses charging their highest selling prices in four years. Per the Polymarket list, a Glassdoor survey of more than 1,700 professionals found 57 percent felt pressured to accept lower pay after losing a job. Per the Crypto list, Indeed job postings are down 3.5 percent year over year and 37.2 percent since April 2022, back to February 2021 levels.

Firm prices, soft labor, cracking housing, $110 crude and three-year-high wheat. Per Noah Smith on Prof G, the AI bubble does not need a demand collapse to break, it needs "token maxing" to meet a profit-and-loss statement, the same way factories in 1900 ripped out steam boilers for electric motors, saw no gain, and reverted before reorganized workflows finally delivered three to five times the productivity twenty years later.

6. The cash-flow lens explains this whole tape better than any AI narrative does. One retail investor did the most useful work of the day. Per this post-mortem, he sold his index fund over the inelastic market hypothesis, admits it cost him ("being wrong and being early look identical for a while"), then screened about thirty names on true free cash flow yield, subtracting stock compensation as well as capital spending. The results run $ADBE at 8.59 percent, $CRM at 7.76 percent, $FDS at 6.10 percent and $NVDA at 1.82 percent. His summary is the line of the day, "the cash machines got sold and the dream got bought."

Run today's wreckage through that lens and it holds up. Per this teardown, $ORCL sits near $125.84 against a 52-week high around $345, with record operating cash flow of $32 billion and a $638 billion order book on one side, and $40 billion of data-center capex plus $85 billion of debt on the other. Per this model, $META at $600.91 needs only 16 percent annual free cash flow growth to justify its price against 33.7 percent delivered, with the honest caveat that its fair-value range of $383 to $1,026 is nearly three times wide.

The bubble argument got a scoreboard too. Per Goldman's Top of Mind roundtable, Acadian's Owen Lamont names four horsemen (overvaluation, bubble beliefs, equity issuance, surging inflows) while conceding that IPO waves can run for years and that the absence of big first-day pops argues euphoria has not arrived. Apollo's Torsten Slok adds that IPOs since 2019 underperformed over the following three years. Goldman's own Ben Snider takes the other side, putting roughly $700 billion of 2026 issuance against a $75 trillion market.

Then compare the quality of argument on the bull side. Per this conviction post, the case is that world compute goes from about 132 gigawatts to a terawatt in a decade and "anybody talking about an AI bubble is an idiot" because the hyperscalers "have smarter people than you and I," expressed as 20 percent $SNDK and 15 percent $MU. Per Anthony Pompliano, the old hedge is broken anyway, with long Treasuries down almost 50 percent over five years so bonds now amplify equity moves instead of cushioning them, though his proposed answer routes into a paid placement and should be read on those terms.

7. Bitcoin is holding the mid-60s and the leverage behind it is dangerously lopsided. The level everyone trades around is explicit. Per Sykodelic, "we want to see $66k held on the weekly," or the $60,500 test he has watched for weeks comes into play, while aixbt already sees Bitcoin below $64,000. Per Scott Melker, the fact that it held the mid-60s while $800 billion came off AI stocks and oil ran at $100 is itself the argument.

The positioning is the risk. Per Stocks with Josh, there is roughly $1.5 billion of short leverage against $10 billion of longs, and he expects a grind up toward $69,000 to be where that long stack gets flushed rather than where it gets paid. Per Jaime Coutts of Real Vision, the high $70,000s is the weekly inflection and Bitcoin does not get there without exchange-traded fund flows turning positive, though Ethereum already shows a positive divergence with each price low pairing with less selling.

Per Benjamin Cowen, the base case is a stock-market top in August or September, a 10 to 20 percent drop, and the cycle low after that. He raises his own counterpoint honestly, that this cycle topped on apathy, so the sellers a capitulation requires may never have bought in the first place.

The policy and plumbing side is moving faster than the price. Per Brian Armstrong on Market Bubble, hundreds of large US companies integrated stablecoins within three months of the Genius Act, he spent two days in Washington whipping votes for the Clarity Act against opposition from banks, law enforcement and tribes, and tokenized equities including Nvidia, Tesla and SpaceX are coming to Base. The trader alongside him says the crypto bottom is already in with a bull market in three to six months, running 60 to 70 percent majors against 30 to 40 percent speculation.

Real onchain activity is inflecting even in a dead tape, and the venue has moved. Per threadguy, Pump.fun revenue hit its best day since June 30 with most volume on Robinhood's chain rather than Solana, driven by memecoins paired against tokenized equities, where a $GME coin squeezed the thin tokenized supply until Europeans minted fresh shares to arbitrage it back. Per ETH Labs, whose executive director openly concedes that ETH "had that incredible success 5 years ago and ever since it's sideways," the fast confirmation rule now near production in every major client cuts deposits and withdrawals from minutes to seconds. Per Lark Davis, XRP funds took in $1 billion with the price going nowhere, which he reads as early holders distributing into institutional demand as it arrives.

Single names to track.

  • $INTC (Intel). Beat at $0.42 against $0.21 on $16.13 billion of revenue, raised capex to $20 billion, and gave back the whole move to close down over 4 percent, per the People list.
  • $MU (Micron). Two desks converge on it at 12 times trailing earnings with a 75 percent EBITDA margin, trigger 996 and stop 983, catalyst is hyperscaler earnings inside two weeks, per Hogue and Stocks with Josh.
  • $BE (Bloom Energy). Milk Road's largest position at $222, down 30 to 35 percent from a one-month-old high, on 2.8 gigawatts framework with Oracle, 1 gigawatt with American Electric Power, and 60-to-90-day onsite power against a seven-year grid queue. Earnings Tuesday July 28, and a short report questions scandium supply past 2027, per Milk Road AI.
  • $HOOD (Robinhood). Revenue up 53 percent to $4.5 billion and platform assets up 48 percent to $377 billion at the same $100 stock, with Goldman at $137 and Morgan Stanley at $124. Earnings July 29, per Milk Road.
  • $SPCX (SpaceX). Closed $118.24, down 47 percent from above $225, with an August 6 insider unlock that could double the public float. Cathie Wood has bought over $475 million and sits underwater, while Novogratz and Scaramucci say it trades to $100, per the Stocks list.
  • $AMD (Advanced Micro Devices). Baird doubled its target to a street-high $1,250 from $625 and Venice EPYC launched claiming 20 percent better performance than competing Nvidia CPUs, and it held up through the index break, per the People list.
  • $MCO (Moody's). Rated more than $2 trillion of debt for a second straight quarter with transaction revenue up 34 percent, and still did not raise guidance, because the incremental issuance is large data-center deals and repeat bank issuers that monetize at lower yields, per this teardown.
  • $JTO (Jito). At roughly $0.75 with a blended target of $2.75 on JTX taking 15 percent of Solana exchange volume by mid-2027, and 80 percent of JTX revenue going to buybacks, per Blockworks.
  • $MSFT (Microsoft). Two reads from the same desk put any candle under $375 in the next 30 days as a long entry, on bullish divergence plus the 50-day and 100-day averages touching without crossing, the same setup as late 2022, per Stocks with Josh and his longer-term version.
  • $MRVL (Marvell). Four green days into a back test of the 9-day average after the double-top measured move already reached 178, with 225.06 the swing target and a rejection there keeping the downtrend intact, per Stocks with Josh.
  • $IREN and $NBIS (IREN, Nebius). IREN carries about 5 gigawatts of secured power and a five-year $3.4 billion managed AI cloud deal at 16 times sales, against Nebius guiding $3.0 to $3.4 billion of 2026 revenue toward a $7 to $9 billion year-end run rate with up to $27 billion from Meta over five years, per Rick Orford.
  • $CNM (Core & Main). Municipal water distribution at $42.93 against a stated $57.72 fair value and a $46.18 buy limit, on 20 percent return on equity with depreciation running four times capital spending, per the best-argued teardown of the day.
  • $FER (Ferrovial). The non-obvious idea of the day, toll roads and airports as effective monopolies with pricing power above inflation, naming the I-24 and I-285 concessions and JFK Terminal One, per this portfolio review.
  • $FSLR (First Solar). Roughly 13 to 14.5 times earnings with about $1.9 billion of net cash and a non-China supply chain, though the accounting profit leans on $2.1 billion of projected 2026 manufacturing credits, per this case.
  • $CMCSA (Comcast). Fell 7 percent to $21.98 at 4.2 times earnings with a 6 percent dividend yield on a 26 percent payout ratio, and the catch is that the yield stops beating money market funds if the Fed turns, per this post.

item.title: [Investing] Intel just posted its strongest growth in fifteen years and jumped double digits after hours, the one green light in a market that erased a trillion dollars and watched Korea trip a circuit breaker on memory
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The chip everyone left for dead beat on every line while the dip-buyers stepped into Tesla and the bears called it phase two of a bear market. Oil is holding above $100, the 30-year yield has now sat above 5 percent for 27 days, and the tariff wall went back up at midnight.
item.content:encoded:
The chip everyone left for dead beat on every line while the dip-buyers stepped into Tesla and the bears called it phase two of a bear market. Oil is holding above $100, the 30-year yield has now sat above 5 percent for 27 days, and the tariff wall went back up at midnight.

A Friday that opens on a split screen. Intel delivered the best print of the week into the worst tape of the week, and the crowd is already fighting over whether yesterday was the bottom or the beginning. Here is the pre-open preview, then five stories.

Pre-open preview. The bounce has one clear leader and a lot of doubt behind it. Per the People list, Intel reported second-quarter revenue of $16.13 billion against $14.42 billion expected, up 25 percent for its best growth since 2022, with adjusted earnings of $0.42 against estimates near $0.21, data-center revenue up 59 percent, and the stock up 12 to 13 percent after hours, though a $12.5 billion non-cash charge on its CHIPS Act escrow shares produced a headline GAAP loss that the operating numbers sit underneath.

The rest of the setup is heavier. Per the Market list, Korea's Kospi fell 6 percent intraday and tripped a circuit breaker after Morgan Stanley's Shawn Kim warned that memory demand has evaporated, with NAND inventory near 13 weeks, even as futures at home pointed to a mixed-to-slightly-green open after yesterday's rout wiped roughly $800 billion off the Magnificent Seven. Per the Stocks list, crude is holding above $100, the 10-year yield crossed 4.70 percent, and jobless claims came in at 187,000, a labor market too strong to rescue the tape. A blowout from the market's turnaround story against a memory scare and $100 oil is the exact tension the open has to resolve.

1. Intel is the one that delivered, and the government is sitting on a $38 billion gain. The turnaround got real numbers behind it. Per the People list, Intel's foundry revenue rose 31 percent to $5.8 billion and its AI and data-center segment rose 59 percent to $6.3 billion, gross margin expanded to 41.8 percent from 38.8, and the third-quarter guide of $15.8 to $16.8 billion cleared the $15.1 billion the Street expected. Strip out the one-time CHIPS charge and the company earned $2.2 billion, and the US government's stake bought at $20.47 last year is now worth about $45.8 billion, a roughly $38 billion paper gain.

The debate is whether it is cheap or just early. Per the Market list, Gene Munster notes Intel trades at 61 times 2027 earnings against Nvidia at 17 and calls it the third inning, while Jim Cramer flatly said Intel is the one. Per Trader Mayne, the print beat earnings by about 90 percent and revenue by 11 percent, and CEO Lip-Bu Tan says 14A customers are showing up for a 2027 ship. The caution is that a CFO musing about needing to tap capital markets on the call is not what a fragile tape wants to hear, but the operating turn is the realest bull story in the group.

2. The memory scare is the thing that could break the AI trade, and Korea felt it first. The bear case found a fresh target. Per the Stocks list, Morgan Stanley's Shawn Kim published a bearish memory note arguing demand has evaporated, with NAND inventory around 13 weeks, price hikes slowing to 5 percent a quarter into the fourth quarter, and high-bandwidth memory growth capped near 40 percent, and the Kospi fell 6 percent to around 6,500 on it because Samsung and SK Hynix dominate that index.

The other side is not backing down. Per the Market list, one desk is openly calling a bottom in AI semis across Intel, Micron, and the leveraged chip fund, with named support at Micron around $850 and Taiwan Semi near $388, and Morgan Stanley's own equity desk is telling clients to buy memory even as its analyst cuts demand. That contradiction inside one bank is the whole market in miniature, a supply story that has been the cleanest bull trade of the year running straight into the first real demand warning, and the memory names are where the next move gets decided.

3. The dip-buyers are already calling the bottom, and the bears say it is far too early. The rush to buy the wreck started immediately. Per the Stocks list, Cathie Wood bought 160,151 shares of Tesla worth about $52 million into the 14 percent drop, one desk pegged the Tesla bottom at $286 to $292, and the memory-bottom callers piled in, all on day two of a selloff.

The bearish read has history on its side. Per Trader Mayne, the market is in phase two of a three-phase bear, where the indices chop sideways while individual leaders like Arm, SanDisk, and Bloom Energy take 30 to 50 percent corrections before the mega-caps finally snap, and he sees Tesla trading to $200 before it sees $400 again. Per the Stocks list, one voice drew the dot-com parallel that Cisco took 12 to 13 months to bottom in 2000 and the market is only one month in, while Chamath Palihapitiya warned the wheels are coming off AI spending. Buying the first dip in a rout that just started is how the crowd gets caught, and the tape has not earned the all-clear yet.

4. The SaaS names left for dead are quietly the AI winners, starting with ServiceNow. The most contrarian bull thesis of the morning is in software. Per Milk Road, the SaaS apocalypse narrative has it backwards, because cheaper intelligence rewards the incumbents already wired into the enterprise rather than the startups trying to replace them, and ServiceNow is the flagship, an AI control tower whose Now Assist product has already generated $1 billion in revenue with contracted obligations still growing 20 percent.

The proof is that it is replacing labor, not just selling seats. Per that show, ServiceNow runs 20 internal AI agents doing work people used to do and its CEO said on the call that AI is already arbitraging away headcount, yet the stock fell on the day inside the broad tape, which the analyst calls nonsense and used to add 16 percent to his position. His second pick is AppLovin at about $400 with 85 percent margins and a mobile-ad exchange spanning 140,000 games, a data flywheel he would add to near $380. The point is that the boring back-end names with real switching costs may be the safest way to own AI.

5. The cost of money is the vise underneath all of it, and housing is frozen. The macro that decides everything is the bond market. Per Arbitrage Andy, the 30-year Treasury yield has now traded above 5 percent for 27 days this year, the most since 2007, the 10-year pushed above 4.70 percent for the first time since January 2025, and the national debt sits near $40 trillion so every refinancing at these rates balloons the interest bill. Per the Crypto list, Jim Bianco notes the 10-year real yield now runs above 3 percent against a 0.23 percent average from 2009 to 2022, a completely different regime for every asset priced off it.

Housing is where the higher-for-longer rate shows up as a frozen market. Per Arbitrage Andy, home prices have risen 36 straight months to a record median near $440,000 even as the 30-year mortgage sits around 6.55 to 6.77 percent, with 46 percent of sellers now offering concessions at an all-time high and foreclosure filings up 21 percent on the year. The problem is not collapsing prices, it is collapsing volume, owners locked into 2 to 4 percent mortgages who will not sell into buyers who cannot afford a doubled payment. That same rate regime is why gold overtook Treasuries as the largest reserve asset and why Bitcoin near $64,500 keeps stalling, per Trader Mayne, who is waiting to buy below $60,000 rather than chasing here.

Single names to track.

  • $INTC (Intel). Beat with revenue of $16.1 billion and earnings of $0.42, foundry up 31 percent and data-center up 59 percent, and jumped 12 to 13 percent after hours despite a one-time CHIPS charge, per the People list.
  • $MU (Micron). Sits at the center of the memory scare that tripped Korea's circuit breaker, with named support near $850 and a desk calling a bottom in AI semis, per the Market list.
  • $NOW (ServiceNow). Beat and kept contracted obligations growing 20 percent with Now Assist past $1 billion in revenue, yet fell on the day, per Milk Road.
  • $TSLA (Tesla). Drew a $52 million buy from Cathie Wood into its 14 percent drop, with one desk pegging a bottom near $286 and another seeing $200 first, per the Stocks list.
  • BTC (Bitcoin). Trades near $64,500 and keeps stalling, with Trader Mayne waiting to buy below $60,000 rather than chase, per Trader Mayne.

Psychology. Watch how fast the crowd moved to call the bottom. One day after a trillion dollars vanished and Tesla fell 14 percent, Cathie Wood was buying the dip, desks were pegging exact bottoms in Tesla and memory, and Intel's blowout gave everyone the excuse to say the worst is over. That reflex, the need to be early to the turn, is the most human thing on a screen full of red, and it is exactly what a phase-two bear feeds on.

The honest read is that both sides have a real case and the tape has not settled it. Intel genuinely delivered and the government is up $38 billion on it, but Morgan Stanley's memory downgrade just tripped a circuit breaker in Korea, and Trader Mayne's framework says the leaders can still lose 30 to 50 percent before the mega-caps break. When a bank tells its clients to buy memory on the same morning its own analyst says demand has evaporated, the market is not confused, it is genuinely undecided, and undecided is not the same as safe.

So let the weekend and next week's Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon capex guides do the talking before you plant a flag. Own the turn that has numbers behind it like Intel rather than the ones that only have hope, respect that oil above $100 and a 30-year yield above 5 percent are constraints no dip-buyer can wish away, and keep enough cash that if this really is only month one of a Cisco-style grind, you are buying the third dip and not averaging down into the first.

item.title: [Investing] The market punished the best earnings it got, sending Tesla down 14 percent in its worst reaction in years and Alphabet down 7 percent in its biggest drop since 2008, and erasing $900 billion on a day the news was arguably fine
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Google grew cloud 82 percent and still took seven analyst price-target cuts, because the spend keeps rising and the cash keeps leaving. Oil broke back above $100 on Houthi tanker strikes, jobless claims hit their lowest since 1969, and the fear gauge fell to 9, lower than it read during the FTX collapse.
item.content:encoded:
Google grew cloud 82 percent and still took seven analyst price-target cuts, because the spend keeps rising and the cash keeps leaving. Oil broke back above $100 on Houthi tanker strikes, jobless claims hit their lowest since 1969, and the fear gauge fell to 9, lower than it read during the FTX collapse.

A Thursday that turned a decent set of prints into a rout. The tape sold the winners hardest, the fear gauge cratered, and the bears found their proof in the debt underneath the whole build. Here is the session recap, then five stories.

Session recap. The reaction to last night's earnings was violent. Per the Financial Markets list, Tesla fell about 14 percent in its second-largest earnings reaction ever and Alphabet dropped 7.6 percent in its worst earnings response since July 2008, even though Google grew cloud 82 percent, because the same list notes that Alphabet's record $112 billion in net income was 87 percent unrealized markups on its SpaceX and Anthropic stakes, leaving only about $33 billion from the actual business. Per the Stocks list, the stock still drew seven analyst price-target cuts on the day, from firms including Piper, UBS, and Raymond James, on the first negative free cash flow in more than 20 years and a raised capex guide.

The macro turned against risk at the same time. Per the Kalshi list, the S&P erased more than $900 billion in value, the Nasdaq 100 fell more than 2 percent, weekly jobless claims came in at 187,000, the lowest since 1969, and gold overtook US Treasuries as the world's largest reserve asset. Per the Polymarket list, Brent crude surged back above $100 for the first time since May as the fear over the Strait of Hormuz deepened. A strong labor market that keeps a Fed hike live, oil breaking $100, and the market selling its best names is the exact cocktail that ends a bounce.

1. The tell of the day is that the strongest print took the hardest hit. The verdict was not about the numbers, it was about the price. Per the Stocks list, Alphabet fell more than 5 percent even after cloud grew 81.8 percent with operating income tripling to about $9 billion and a $514 billion backlog, and it caught an EU antitrust fine of $1.02 billion on top of the print. Tesla was worse, per the same list, down about 13.5 percent to near $323 in its worst single day in over a year, with Samsung briefly worth more than the whole company after a quarter that missed on margins at $0.33 a share.

The pattern is what matters. Per the Market list, the memory and semiconductor names actually held up while the broad Nasdaq fell 2 percent, with Micron carrying price targets from $1,550 to $1,750 and the whole memory complex bid, so this was not a sector-wide flush. It was a rotation out of the crowded mega-caps that everyone owns and into the shortage names, the same divergence that has run for weeks, and a market that sells an 82 percent cloud number is telling you the good news was already in the price.

2. The bear case got its hard number, and it is $1.65 trillion of hidden debt. The most substantive bear thesis of the day is about the balance sheet. Per Prof G Markets, a Nikkei investigation found that Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle now carry roughly $1.65 trillion in off-balance-sheet debt against $1.35 trillion reported, with Meta's hidden debt about three times its visible debt and Oracle's up roughly thirtyfold in four years. Ed Zitron walks the mechanism, that the data centers are financed through special-purpose vehicles where outside investors like Pimco and Blue Owl own 80 percent so the debt never hits the parent's books, and he calls them the AI bubble's version of the CDOs with an Enron parallel.

The scary part is the math on whether it ever pays back. Per that show, Zitron estimates real AI compute demand at about $120 billion a year, while building out the roughly 130 gigawatts of planned capacity would require $1.68 trillion in annual compute revenue to service, against a global software industry under $800 billion. Per the Stocks morning list, Michael Burry is making the same point, that the off-balance-sheet obligations of the five giants grew eightfold in four years to $1.65 trillion with Oracle hiding $273 billion tied to Stargate and OpenAI. Last night Alphabet's cash actually went negative, and that is the first time the thesis showed up in the numbers of the best name.

3. Oil above $100 is the macro story now, and it is why the Fed is stuck. The commodity is back in the driver's seat. Per the Polymarket list, Brent surged above $100 from $71 at the start of the month as the Houthis struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and Trump signaled he is close to a large strike on Iran, and per the Stocks list prediction markets now show a three-way split on Fed policy this year between two hikes, one hike, and none.

That is the vise the market is caught in. Per the Financial Markets list, jobless claims at a 1969 low mean the labor market is too strong to force a cut, so an oil shock that reignites inflation leaves the Fed leaning toward hiking into a slowing tape. Gold overtaking Treasuries as the largest reserve asset, per the Kalshi list, is the quiet vote of no confidence underneath it all, the world reaching for the asset that has no counterparty while the bond market prices tighter money and the war keeps bidding crude.

4. Where the value is now is the beaten-down names, and the list starts with Netflix. The flip side of a rout is that things get cheap. Per Chip Stock Investor, Netflix trades below $70 at under 20 times forward earnings, the cheapest of the entire bull market, on 325 million subscribers and a 33 percent operating margin, and the case is a reprice from growth stock to value stock rather than a broken business. Per Invest with Henry, the same logic runs through a basket of ad-driven names, with Meta at $640 growing revenue 33 percent, Palantir up 85 percent with US commercial up 133 percent, and Amazon's AWS reaccelerating to 28 percent growth.

The infrastructure side has its own value pitch. Per Rick Orford, Nebius is building specialized AI factories that earn off the same GPUs for years at high utilization rather than selling them once, with named agreements from Meta and Microsoft and backing from Nvidia, and per the Crypto list it just installed the first Vera Rubin rack in Finland while trading near $220 against a $300 target. The through-line is that a day like today hands you the names you wanted at prices you did not expect, and Netflix at a value multiple is the cleanest of them.

5. Crypto sentiment just hit levels last seen at the bottom, and the signals agree. The fear in crypto is now extreme. Per Lark Davis, Bitcoin sits at $65,500 against its 200-week average near $68,500 with the fear-and-greed index at 9, lower than the 12 it printed during the FTX collapse, and he argues this bear market is nothing like 2022 because there is no Terra, no 3AC, no FTX, just a drawdown with rates set to fall under a Warsh Fed. Ethereum inflows are the tell he watches, with $72 million into ETH funds equal to a $400 million Bitcoin day on a market-cap basis.

The high-timeframe work says the low is close in both price and time.
