Per the Bottom Signals report, Bitcoin's realized price sits at $53,000 and only 12 percent of its history has traded below that cost basis, its relative strength versus the Nasdaq is the most oversold on record, and the cycle clock points to a low by late November 2026 with a new high before February 2028. The catalyst that could turn it is legislative, and per Blockworks the CLARITY Act now has a Senate floor vote committed before the recess around August 7, though the deepest prediction markets still price passage below 50 percent.

Single names to track.

  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Fell 7.6 percent in its worst earnings reaction since 2008 despite 82 percent cloud growth, drew seven price-target cuts, and took a $1.02 billion EU fine, per the Stocks list.
  • $TSLA (Tesla). Dropped about 14 percent to near $323 in its worst earnings reaction in years on a margin miss at $0.33 a share, per the Financial Markets list.
  • $NFLX (Netflix). Trades below $70 at under 20 times forward earnings, the cheapest of the bull market, on 325 million subscribers, per Chip Stock Investor.
  • $MU (Micron). Held up while the Nasdaq fell 2 percent, carrying price targets from $1,550 to $1,750 as the memory complex stayed bid, per the Market list.
  • BTC (Bitcoin). Sits at $65,500 with fear-and-greed at 9, below its FTX-collapse reading, and a realized price of $53,000, per Lark Davis and the Bottom Signals report.

Psychology. Read today for what it actually was. Alphabet delivered the strongest cloud number in the market and fell 7 percent, Tesla had its worst earnings day in years, and the tape erased $900 billion on news that, taken plainly, was not a disaster. When the crowd sells the best print this hard, the problem is not the companies, it is that everyone already owned them and everyone had already priced the good news, so there was nobody left to buy it.

The mood underneath has tipped into something close to capitulation. The fear-and-greed gauge fell to 9, lower than it read the week FTX imploded, Michael Burry is short and quoting the fiber bubble, and Ed Zitron is walking through $1.65 trillion of hidden debt while the bond market prices a Fed that may hike into the slowdown. That is a crowd that has stopped believing, and the signals from the Bottom Signals work say Bitcoin is the most oversold it has ever been against the Nasdaq, the kind of reading that historically sits near a low and not a top.

So hold the tension honestly. Extreme fear is usually closer to a bottom than a top, and the memory names holding while the mega-caps bled tells you the rotation is orderly rather than a panic, but oil above $100 and a Fed leaning toward a hike are real risks that a sentiment reading cannot wish away. Buy the beaten value where the cash flow is real, like Netflix at a value multiple, keep the size small into an oil shock you do not control, and remember that the day the crowd gives up on the best names is the day you want to be adding, not the day you want to be the last one selling.

item.title: [Investing] Google delivered the best cloud number the market has ever seen and the stock fell anyway, because it raised its spending again to $200 billion and posted its first negative free cash flow in a decade
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Cloud grew 82 percent with a $514 billion backlog, and Alphabet still dropped after hours because the capex guide went up and the cash went out. Tesla beat on revenue and missed badly on margins, the 30-year yield sits above 5 percent, and the bond market is bracing while stocks sit 1 percent below their high.
item.content:encoded:
Cloud grew 82 percent with a $514 billion backlog, and Alphabet still dropped after hours because the capex guide went up and the cash went out. Tesla beat on revenue and missed badly on margins, the 30-year yield sits above 5 percent, and the bond market is bracing while stocks sit 1 percent below their high.

A Thursday that arrives with the verdict already in and the verdict is unsettling. The single best set of AI numbers a company has printed was not enough to lift the stock, and that gap is the whole story. Here is the pre-open preview, then five stories.

Pre-open preview. The earnings landed after yesterday's close and the read is a market that has stopped rewarding the spend. Per the Market list, Alphabet grew Google Cloud 82 percent to $24.8 billion against a Street looking for the mid-60s, carried a $514 billion cloud backlog, and still fell 3 to 4 percent after hours because it raised its full-year capital-spending guide to $195 to $205 billion and its free cash flow turned negative by $5.8 billion. Tesla told the same split story, beating on revenue at $28.2 billion but missing badly on profit with adjusted earnings of $0.33 against roughly $0.50 expected, and it slid about 3 percent.

The macro underneath is heavy and getting heavier. Per the Financial Markets list, the 2-year Treasury yield hit 4.31 percent, the highest since February 2025, the 30-year holds above 5 percent, and the Nasdaq 100 has now closed below its 50-day average for six straight sessions. Per the Polymarket list, the S&P sits 1 percent below its all-time high while the fear-and-greed gauge reads Fear, and oil stayed bid over $95 on the Strait of Hormuz. The setup into the open is a tape that got exactly the demand it wanted and did not like the bill.

1. Google's cloud was a monster, and the market still balked at the spending. The number itself was spectacular. Per Jose Najarro, Google Cloud grew 82 percent to $24.8 billion, accelerating from 63 percent last quarter, with a $514 billion backlog the company expects to convert more than half of into revenue within 24 months, and the Gemini app now has 950 million monthly users processing 22 billion tokens a minute. The reported earnings looked enormous at over $9 a share, but per the Financial Markets list roughly $98 billion of that was unrealized gains on Alphabet's stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic, so the operating story is the cloud line and the spending, not the headline profit.

The spending is what spooked the tape. Per Najarro, Alphabet raised its capex guide by about $15 billion on each end to $195 to $205 billion, the second hike this year, and attributed it to accelerating capacity rather than to memory prices, which reads as buying more chips faster. That is why free cash flow went negative for the first time in years, and it is the exact moment a growth story becomes a spending story. The one investor voting the other way is the loudest one, with Warren Buffett's Berkshire increasing its Alphabet position 202 percent to $31 billion per the Financial Markets list.

2. The tell inside the print is that the neoclouds went up while Google went down. The most actionable read-through is a rotation. Per Najarro, Google said it would lean on third-party capacity in the third quarter to meet demand it cannot build fast enough, and the names that rent out that capacity rallied on the news, with CoreWeave up about 2.9 percent, Nebius up 3.9 percent, and IREN up 2 percent even as the hyperscaler itself fell.

The mechanism is the important part. When the largest builder of its own data centers admits it has to rent, the shortage of compute is real enough that the landlords get paid first. Per the Market list, Baird kept Nebius at Outperform with a $250 target, and the candidates for Google's overflow include SpaceX, Oracle, and CoreWeave. The trade this print rewards is not the mega-cap doing the spending, it is the second-tier names that sell the capacity the spending cannot keep up with.

3. Tesla beat on trucks and missed on money, and the robotaxi is the only story that matters now. The quarter was a tale of two lines. Per the Kalshi list, Tesla delivered $28.2 billion in revenue against $27.6 billion expected but earned only $0.33 a share versus $0.55, with gross margin at 16.8 percent against a 19.4 percent estimate, and the stock fell about 3 percent after hours. Deliveries rose 25 percent to 480,000, so the volume is there, but the profit on each car keeps shrinking.

The bull case has fully migrated to autonomy. Per the Polymarket list, the robotaxi fleet has now run more than 380,000 miles across seven metros with zero notable incidents, full self-driving subscriptions rose 56 percent to 1.48 million, and the CFO guided 2026 capital spending above $25 billion and rising for another two to three years. Per the People list, the order backlog is the largest since 2023 and Optimus production starts in Fremont later this year. The read is that the market is done paying for the car company and is waiting to see if the robot company is real.

4. The bubble question is no longer theoretical, because the negative cash flow just showed up at the best name. The bear case got a data point from the bull. Per Prof G Markets, the state of Wisconsin is demanding $7 billion in collateral from Oracle before it will let construction on a data center begin, because S&P cut Oracle to BBB-minus one rung above junk after it borrowed $43 billion against $67 billion of revenue while burning about $24 billion of cash. His line is that bubbles are built with debt, not equity, and Oracle is the most obvious name in the danger zone but not the only one.

What makes today different is that the same signature appeared at Alphabet. Per Najarro, the company with the strongest cloud business on earth just posted negative free cash flow to fund the buildout, and per the Financial Markets list SpaceX's stock is down about 48 percent and trading below its IPO price. The four largest hyperscalers are on track for more than $725 billion of combined capex this year, and the market just told you it will no longer clap for that number on its own. The demand is real and the financing is the risk, and last night was the first time both showed up in the same release.

5. Gold is down a quarter from its high and crypto stalled, and both are waiting on the same yields. The haven trade took its pain. Per ClearValue Tax, gold has fallen about 26 percent from its early-2026 peak near $5,500 to around $4,000 as the 30-year yield climbed past 5 percent and the dollar firmed, but the structural buyers have not blinked, with central banks buying roughly 1,000 tons a year for four years and China adding 15 tons in June alone against $39.6 trillion of federal debt. The case is to dollar-cost-average the correction rather than call the bottom.

Crypto is stuck at the same wall. Per VirtualBacon, Bitcoin has stalled dead at $66,000, the resistance that has capped every bounce of this correction, with confirmation only above 82,000 and a bear-case retest into the low $50,000s, while oil at $100 is the line that locks in another Fed hike. His named catalysts are Aave moving to Avalanche with tokenized index collateral and Chainlink as the oracle for a new stablecoin, but the honest frame is that gold, Bitcoin, and the whole risk complex are all hostage to a bond market that keeps pricing tighter money.

Single names to track.

  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Grew cloud 82 percent with a $514 billion backlog yet fell 3 to 4 percent on a capex guide raised to $195 to $205 billion and negative free cash flow, per Jose Najarro.
  • $NBIS (Nebius). Rose 3.9 percent as Google said it would rent third-party capacity, with Baird at Outperform and a $250 target, per the Market list.
  • $TSLA (Tesla). Missed on margins at $0.33 a share but ran the robotaxi fleet 380,000 miles across seven metros with zero notable incidents, per the Polymarket list.
  • $ORCL (Oracle). Cut to BBB-minus and asked for $7 billion of collateral by Wisconsin after borrowing $43 billion against $67 billion of revenue, per Prof G Markets.
  • Gold. Down about 26 percent from its $5,500 peak to near $4,000 while central banks buy roughly 1,000 tons a year, a dip to average into, per ClearValue Tax.

Psychology. Sit with what actually happened last night. Alphabet printed an 82 percent cloud number with a half-trillion-dollar backlog, the kind of result the whole AI trade was praying for, and the stock went down. That is not a company problem, it is a positioning problem, and the message is that the market has quietly switched from rewarding capital spending to fearing it, all while the fear-and-greed gauge reads Fear with the index a single percent off its record.

The discipline is to notice which way the money moved when the news was good. It did not chase the mega-cap that delivered, it rotated into the neoclouds that rent the shortage and into Buffett quietly tripling a stake while everyone else sold the print. Meanwhile the bond market keeps pricing the 2-year at cycle highs and the bears keep pointing at Oracle's junk-adjacent debt and the negative cash flow now bleeding through even the best names. When good news cannot lift a stock, the tape is telling you the price already holds the good news and then some.

So carry two facts into the open at once. The demand is real, the cloud backlog is real, and the robotaxi miles are real, and that is why the wreckage keeps finding buyers, but the financing is real too, and a market that fears a raised capex guide is a market running low on the thing that lifts prices from here. Own the shortage through the names that get paid first, let the spending stories prove they convert to cash before you add, and keep enough dry powder that if the bond market is right and the debt is the thing that cracks, you are the one buying it.

item.title: [Investing] Alphabet and Tesla report into tonight's close as the whole market holds one number in its head, and the day that led up to it was a memory-and-chip melt-up with Nvidia back over $5 trillion and Intel popping 9 percent
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The tape flipped from deep red overnight to green, AMD agreed to put $5 billion into Anthropic and sell it two gigawatts of chips, and OpenAI lifted its compute budget to $750 billion. Oil broke $95, the 30-year Treasury yield held above 5 percent for the longest since 2007, and the bears are all pointing at the same thing, the debt underneath the build.
item.content:encoded:
The tape flipped from deep red overnight to green, AMD agreed to put $5 billion into Anthropic and sell it two gigawatts of chips, and OpenAI lifted its compute budget to $750 billion. Oil broke $95, the 30-year Treasury yield held above 5 percent for the longest since 2007, and the bears are all pointing at the same thing, the debt underneath the build.

A Wednesday built entirely around the closing bell. The market spent the session buying the AI-infrastructure trade with both hands while a quieter group kept pointing at the leverage financing it. Here is the session recap, then five stories.

Session recap. The prints that define the quarter land as this publishes. Per the Stocks list, Alphabet was expected to report revenue near $117 billion and earnings around $3 a share with Google Cloud growth near 67 percent, and the line the market actually cares about is the capital-spending guide. Per the People list, Tesla was set to follow minutes later with consensus near $0.54 a share on $26 billion of revenue, a print the desk agrees is really about robotaxi guidance rather than the quarter itself.

The day into those prints was a melt-up in the exact names that got crushed. Per the Market list, the S&P and Nasdaq flipped from deep red overnight to green, Nvidia pushed back over $5 trillion and cleared $208 on the most bullish options flow of the day, and the memory and semiconductor complex ripped with Micron, SK Hynix, and Marvell all up sharply while Meta fell 9 percent over five days below its 200-day average. Per the Financial Markets list, Intel popped about 9 percent on a headcount-reduction announcement, gold broke $4,100, and the Atlanta Fed's year-ahead business inflation eased to 2.2 percent.

The macro backdrop stayed heavy. Per the Polymarket list, oil surged above $95 for the first time in six weeks and the 30-year Treasury yield held above 5 percent for the longest stretch since 2007. Per the Kalshi list, more than $300 billion was added to US market value in the last 50 minutes of a session that could not sit still ahead of the news.

1. Everything hinged on Alphabet's capex line, and the smart read was to fade the pop. The two prints carry the whole AI trade. Per the People list, the desk framed Alphabet at $347 and up 10 percent on the year with an implied move around 5 percent, and noted the big banks just showed what this market does to a good-but-not-perfect number, with Citi down 5 percent on a 45 percent profit jump. Per Milk Road, the bull case is simply that Google guides capital spending higher again and reignites the whole complex, and Gene Munster now expects hyperscaler capex growth near 37 percent starting with tonight.

The technicians were more skeptical of the first move. Per Stocks with Josh, Alphabet has been in a downtrend since losing $400 and needs to reclaim and hold $360, and while the stock will probably run up on the print, the higher-odds trade is to fade that pop into the seasonal weakness between August and October. His Tesla read is cleaner, that the stock needs to hold above $410 after earnings to start any real reversal, so the honest posture into the close is to let both numbers and both guides print before deciding the trade is fixed.

2. AMD put $5 billion into its own customer, and the bears say the whole build runs on debt. The deal of the day was a chipmaker financing its buyer. Per the People list, AMD agreed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic while selling it two gigawatts of MI450 chips from the first half of 2027, days after a similar Microsoft deal, and Lisa Su signaled AMD may even backstop Anthropic's data-center leases. Per the Kalshi list, OpenAI on the same day raised its projected cloud spending through 2030 to $750 billion.

That circularity is exactly what the skeptics are circling. Per Prof G Markets, Oracle is down 35 percent on the year with its credit cut to one rung above junk, it borrowed $43 billion for data centers against $67 billion of revenue while burning cash, Wisconsin just handed it a $7 billion collateral bill on a single gigawatt project, and $489 billion of AI-related debt has been issued this year with hyperscalers only 40 percent of it. Per the Stocks list, Bill Ackman put a number on the other side of it, estimating OpenAI loses about $14 billion this year on roughly $13 billion of revenue. When a chipmaker has to fund the customer who buys the chips, the demand is real but the financing is the fragile part.

3. The memory shortage is still the cleanest bull story, and photonics is the next chapter. The supply data keeps getting more extreme. Per Milk Road, SK Hynix DRAM export prices are up 527 percent year over year and roughly 20 percent month over month even as the stocks fell, 13 to 15 customers have locked in about 40 percent of SK Hynix's projected 2027 profit with next-year supply already sold out, and UBS models Micron generating more than $400 billion of cumulative free cash flow by 2028 at 85 percent gross margins and seven times forward earnings.

The trade after memory is light. Per Milk Road AI, the next leg is photonics as copper hits its limits, with Applied Optoelectronics growing its own lasers into a shortage and booking a $124 million single-month 800G order while demand runs past capacity into mid-2027, and Marvell as the connectivity layer that Wall Street sees nearly tripling revenue by 2029. Per the Stocks list, Applied Optoelectronics jumped 15 percent to around $119 on the day. These are the highest-beta way to own the buildout, so size them small, but the pricing power in memory is the part of this market with actual scarcity behind it.

4. The real bottleneck is power, and even Elon Musk is buying it with his own money. The constraint that everything else runs into is electricity. Per Limitless, Elon Musk personally spent about $1 billion to buy APR Energy for roughly a gigawatt of mobile gas-turbine power to feed Grok, surfaced only when an investor disclosed a $50 million return, and the reason is stark, that data-center demand has climbed toward 46 gigawatts while only about 5 gigawatts will actually come online this year against grid connections that take five to seven years.

The public ways to own the shortage are the power names. Per that same show, GE Vernova is the pick as the TSMC of power with orders booked through 2031 and a $7 billion Microsoft deal, alongside Bloom Energy and modular nuclear, while Oklo carries a 14-gigawatt pipeline against no operating reactor and no revenue until late 2027, per Rick Orford. And the way to own the machines that make the chips is ASML, per that channel, which controls all of EUV lithography with its high-NA tools at $400 million each and guides 2026 revenue toward $40 billion, a monopoly protected by physics that you wait to buy on the dip.

5. Crypto is arguing that the cycle low is already in, and the CLARITY Act just cleared committee. The corner that already took its pain is making a timing call. Per Crypto Currently, Bitcoin crossing 50 percent of supply in loss on June 5 is the same signal that fired at every prior major bottom, and 47 days later the low may already be behind it, though a break of the $50,000 realized price would break the thesis. Per CryptoQuant, Ethereum near $1,900 sits about 17 percent below its cost basis with two of five bottoming signals now bullish, and the desk reads Bitcoin's break above $66,000 as a bear-market rally on July seasonality rather than the all-clear.

The catalyst underneath it is legislative. Per the Stocks list, the CLARITY Act cleared the Senate Banking Committee 15 to 9 with Treasury Secretary Bessent calling it on the one-yard line, and Coinbase jumped 10 percent. Per Milk Road, the caution is that the market is buying Coinbase for the wrong reason, because clear rules also invite the banks in, and with 2026 passage still priced near 41 percent the pop gives itself back fast if the vote slips to next year.

Single names to track.

  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Reports into tonight's close as the first hyperscaler tell, with the capex guide the number that matters and technicians set to fade the first pop, per Stocks with Josh.
  • $AMD (Advanced Micro Devices). Agreed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic and sell it two gigawatts of MI450 chips from 2027, per the People list.
  • $AAOI (Applied Optoelectronics). Jumped 15 percent to about $119 on a $124 million single-month 800G order with demand past capacity into mid-2027, per the Stocks list.
  • $GEV (GE Vernova). Orders booked through 2031 and a $7 billion Microsoft deal as the cleanest way to own the power bottleneck, per Limitless.
  • $COIN (Coinbase). Up 10 percent on the CLARITY Act clearing committee, though 2026 passage is still priced near 41 percent, per Milk Road.

Psychology. Watch what the crowd did today before a single number printed. It bid Nvidia back over $5 trillion, ripped the memory names it had dumped a week ago, and pushed more than $300 billion into the tape in the final hour, all while retail kept adding and the bulls lined up behind one hope, that Alphabet guides capex higher and sends the whole complex flying. That is a market that has already decided the answer and is buying ahead of the proof.

The tell is who is standing on the other side and what they are looking at. Michael Burry is short Micron and Nvidia, Jeremy Grantham is calling for a 50 to 70 percent drawdown, and Prof G is walking through Oracle's junk-adjacent credit and the $489 billion of AI debt issued this year, and none of them are arguing the demand is fake. They are arguing the financing is, that AMD now has to fund the customer buying its chips and OpenAI loses $14 billion to earn $13 billion, a very different worry than a valuation being rich.

So hold the discipline the setup demands. The scarcity in memory and power is real and that is why the dip was bought, but a market this convinced of tonight's outcome is exactly the one that gaps the wrong way on a soft capex line or a hedged robotaxi answer. Let the guides print before you chase, own the shortage through the toolmakers and the power names the math supports, and keep enough dry powder that if the debt is the thing that breaks, you are the buyer and not the one being financed.

item.title: [Investing] The whole market is holding its breath for tonight, because Alphabet and Tesla both report after the close and Alphabet's capital-spending line is the first real read on whether the trillion-dollar AI build is still working
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Hedge funds have quietly sold tech in six of the last eight weeks while retail levers up and the beaten-down memory names rip, and the Kimi K3 shock from Friday has the market rethinking who actually wins the AI trade. IREN signed $2.8 billion of new cloud contracts, oil is back near $89, and gold has bled 30 percent from its high.
item.content:encoded:
Hedge funds have quietly sold tech in six of the last eight weeks while retail levers up and the beaten-down memory names rip, and the Kimi K3 shock from Friday has the market rethinking who actually wins the AI trade. IREN signed $2.8 billion of new cloud contracts, oil is back near $89, and gold has bled 30 percent from its high.

A Wednesday that hinges on one number after the bell. The tape has already sold the leaders and bought the wreckage, and now it waits for Alphabet to say whether the spending is paying off. Here is the pre-open preview, then five stories.

Pre-open preview. Everything about today points at the closing bell. Alphabet reports after the close tonight as the first major hyperscaler out, and the line the market actually cares about is the capital-spending guide, the read on whether the AI trade is still justified. Tesla reports the same evening as the other side of the barbell, a robotaxi story running maybe ten cars a city against a stock priced for far more.

Coming in, the tape is still digesting Friday's Kimi K3 shock that took the Nasdaq down about 1.5 percent, and the memory names that got crushed for three weeks have kept ripping, with Micron near $945 after Bank of America added it to its best ideas. Under that bounce the positioning is thinning fast. Per Trader Mayne, Goldman has hedge funds as net sellers in six of the last eight weeks through mid-July, the biggest eight-week outflow from tech in more than a decade, with fund tech exposure down to a 2026 low near 15.5 percent even as retail adds leverage.

The rest of the board is heavy. Gold sits near $4,000 and down about 30 percent from its high, oil is back near $89 with US gasoline over $4, and the odds of a Fed rate hike this year are still around 62 percent. The setup into tonight is a market that has pre-positioned for the print and now needs the capex number to tell it which side was right.

1. The AI cloud contract boom is real and it is landing in the second-tier names first. The cleanest growth story of the morning is a neocloud. Per Jose Najarro, IREN signed roughly $2.8 billion of new customer contracts and lifted its 2026 AI cloud run-rate revenue floor from $3.7 billion to more than $4 billion, with 85 percent of that already under contract and named customers including Microsoft, Nvidia, Perplexity, Figure AI, and Together AI. The company is moving from bare-metal rental into higher-margin managed cloud, funding it partly with customer prepayments that cover about 45 percent of the associated GPU capex, and targeting 480 megawatts of AI cloud by the end of this year and 1.2 gigawatts by the end of next.

The chip side of the same trade has a catalyst on the calendar. Per that video, Microsoft will deploy AMD's rack-scale Helios systems for frontier-model inference on Azure in the second half of this year, joining OpenAI and Meta, and AMD holds its own AI event Thursday. Najarro flags that the Nebius pop on Nvidia's disclosed 9 percent stake is stale news tied to a March warrant deal rather than a fresh bid, so the honest read is that the contracted revenue at IREN and the Azure win at AMD are the parts of this move with actual signatures behind them.

2. Kimi K3 broke the price of intelligence, and the trade it points to is compute, not the labs. The most important repricing of the week is not a stock, it is a cost curve. Per Prof G Markets, Charlie O'Neill of Baseten calls Moonshot's Kimi K3 a second DeepSeek moment, a roughly 3-trillion-parameter open model that beats some US flagships on benchmarks while costing about a third of Anthropic's top model, and Chinese open-weight models now hold the top five spots by weekly token usage on OpenRouter. His framing is that this is open source versus closed source rather than China versus America, and that lab margins rumored north of 80 percent compress toward 40 as the surplus flows to consumers and to whoever serves the inference.

That is why the Limitless read lands on the same place. Per Limitless, Kimi K3 runs about $0.50 to $1 per million input tokens against roughly $50 for a US frontier model, and Moonshot just paused new signups because it ran out of GPUs, the clearest sign that the constraint is compute rather than cleverness. Both takes reach the trade the same way, that infrastructure is the moat and the capital keeps flowing to the bottom of the stack, the same logic pushing inference toward simpler packaging where Intel's EMIB approach finally has a lane, per Chip Stock Investor.

3. The next bottleneck to trade is light, and the names are AAOI and Marvell. The most specific new thesis of the morning is optical. Per Milk Road, the big four hyperscalers are guiding to more than $700 billion of combined capex this year and Morgan Stanley now models $1.44 trillion by 2028, with networking running 15 to 18 percent of cluster cost and Goldman projecting co-packaged optics revenue climbing from about $1 billion this year toward $71 billion by 2028 as clusters move from copper to fiber.

The two named plays sit at opposite ends of the risk scale. Per that breakdown, Applied Optoelectronics grows its own lasers in-house against an industry laser shortage and has booked $124 million of cumulative 800G orders from one hyperscaler, but its top two customers are 82 percent of revenue, which makes it the high-beta way to own the theme. Marvell is the steadier version, a near-monopoly in 1.6-terabit optical DSPs that just bought the photonic-fabric startup Celestial AI and took a roughly $2 billion Nvidia investment, trading down about 45 percent from its June high with the analyst pegging a floor near $150. These are a promoter's picks, so size them as ideas rather than gospel, but the capex math underneath the theme is the same number Alphabet reports tonight.

4. Positioning is the fragile part, and the global unwind is already showing up in Korea and China. The risk under the bounce is that the people who have to sell are still selling. Per Trader Mayne, semis are now about 14 percent of US market cap, roughly double the dot-com peak, while hedge funds cut tech to a 2026-low exposure and retail adds leverage into the gap, the kind of split that snaps hard when it snaps.

The forced-selling is visible abroad. Per that stream, the 60-day correlation between Korea's Kospi and the Nasdaq has jumped to 0.46, the highest in years, roughly one in thirty working-age Koreans has been liquidated as margin balances hit a record 38 trillion won, and Chinese margin debt just posted its largest daily drop in about a decade with memory-chip names at the center of the liquidation. Per Capital Flows, the same fragility shows in a US market where the most-shorted stocks have squeezed for months on expanded liquidity, the sort of positioning that unwinds violently once the flow reverses. The lesson is that the AI trade has never been more global, so a margin call in Seoul now prints in Santa Clara.

5. Crypto is where the leverage already flushed, and the cash flow stories are getting sharper. The corner of the market that already took its pain is the miners. Per On-Chain Mind, Bitcoin near $66,000 sits below an estimated $76,000 cost of production, so the average miner is running a roughly 13 percent loss, hash rate is down about 18 percent in the worst drawdown since last November, and the Puell Multiple and back-to-back Hash Ribbon capitulation signals are printing in the zone that has marked past bottoms.

Two builders are turning that bear tape into revenue. Per Milk Road, Sid Powell's Maple Finance has pushed loans outstanding near an all-time high around $2 billion in the downturn and just wired its SYRUP token to rules-based buybacks that scale from 10 to 30 percent of revenue, while powering the new Robinhood Chain earn product for a platform with 30 million accounts. Per 0xSammy, the further-out bet is that AI agents become crypto's largest investor class and will only allocate into tokens with machine-readable ownership rights, and that is why projects like MetaDAO and Umia are racing to make what a token actually owns legible before the agents show up with capital.

Single names to track.

  • $IREN (Iren). Signed about $2.8 billion of new cloud contracts and raised its 2026 run-rate floor above $4 billion with 85 percent contracted, per Jose Najarro.
  • $AMD (Advanced Micro Devices). Microsoft will run its Helios rack-scale systems for inference on Azure in the second half, with AMD's own AI event Thursday, per Jose Najarro.
  • $AAOI (Applied Optoelectronics). Booked $124 million of cumulative 800G orders from one hyperscaler and grows its own lasers into a shortage, though two customers are 82 percent of revenue, per Milk Road.
  • $MRVL (Marvell). Near-monopoly in 1.6-terabit optical DSPs, down about 45 percent from its June high with a floor pegged near $150, per Milk Road.
  • Gold. Near $4,000 and down about 30 percent, with the bull-market support band near $3,800 and Benjamin Cowen looking for a low in the July-to-October window, per Benjamin Cowen.

Psychology. Notice what the tape has already done before the news arrives. Hedge funds have sold tech in six of the last eight weeks and cut exposure to a yearly low, retail has levered into the space they left, and the memory names that fell hardest have ripped back the fastest. That is a market that has pre-traded its own catalyst, and the danger in a setup like that is that the print becomes an excuse for whatever the positioning already wanted to do.

The Kimi K3 shock is the deeper unsettling thing, because it says the price of intelligence is falling faster than almost anyone modeled, and a falling price for the output is not automatically good for the companies that spent the most to build it. That is the question buried inside Alphabet's capex line tonight, whether the trillion dollars of planned spending compounds into a moat or into stranded capacity as the cost of a token collapses. The market that bought the memory dip and sold the mega-caps has already placed a quiet bet on that answer.

So hold both truths into the close. The contracted revenue at IREN and the physical bottleneck in optics and memory are real, and that is why the wreckage found buyers, but the forced liquidation running through Seoul and Shanghai is the reminder that leverage decides the tape when positioning is this stretched. Let the capex guide print before you decide the trade is fixed, keep the size small enough that a gap either way does not force your hand, and remember that the night the whole market agrees on what matters is exactly the night it tends to be wrong about which way it breaks.

item.title: [Investing] The memory names that got crushed for three weeks ripped 10 to 20 percent today while Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet all closed red, and that split is the whole market telling you what it fears
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Micron jumped to $945 and the DRAM fund is up 20 percent in days while the mega-caps that lead the index faded. A draft US Treasury report just compared the AI boom to the dot-com bubble, Mark Cuban named who actually gets wiped out, and Alphabet and Tesla both report tomorrow.
item.content:encoded:
Micron jumped to $945 and the DRAM fund is up 20 percent in days while the mega-caps that lead the index faded. A draft US Treasury report just compared the AI boom to the dot-com bubble, Mark Cuban named who actually gets wiped out, and Alphabet and Tesla both report tomorrow.

A Tuesday that rewarded the wreckage and punished the leaders. The beaten-down chips melted up while the trillion-dollar names slipped, and that is not how a healthy rally usually looks. Here is the session recap, then five stories.

Session recap. The bounce was violent and narrow. Per the Market list, Micron hit $945 intraday and kissed its 50-day average after Bank of America added it to its best ideas, the DRAM fund tracking Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron is up 20 percent in days to around $58, and Nebius jumped more than 10 percent after Nvidia disclosed a roughly 9 percent passive stake. The tell was underneath, with the Nasdaq 100 up 2 percent while Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet all closed red, per the Financial Markets list. Oil hit a five-week high with Brent back over $91, the Fed hike odds for the year jumped to 62 percent, and Alphabet and Tesla both report after tomorrow's close.

1. The memory melt-up is real, and the supply chain says the dip was overdone. The trade of the day was buying back the exact names that led the selloff. Per the Stocks list, SanDisk, Western Digital, and Seagate printed monster bounces alongside Micron, with Morgan Stanley calling the memory pullback a compelling entry and forecasting DRAM prices up 25 percent into the third quarter while UBS sees the market undersupplied until at least 2028.

The structural case is that the bottlenecks are physical rather than financial. Per Ticker Symbol YOU, TSMC's advanced packaging is sold out into 2027 with some customers waiting more than a year, ASML will build only about 65 of its most advanced machines this year, and a reported delay to Nvidia's next rack could push its top chip to 2028, and the preferred way to own the shortage is the toolmakers, ASML, Lam Research, KLA, and the power name Vertiv. Those are a promoter's picks, so weigh the specifics, but the point that the constraint is capacity rather than demand is the reason the dip found buyers this fast.

2. The bubble question just went mainstream, and the answer is that the pros get wiped out, not you. The bear case got a government stamp. Per Lark Davis, a draft internal US Treasury report obtained by NOTUS warns that the AI boom is so interconnected across stocks, banks, chipmakers, cloud providers, data centers, and private credit that a sharp downturn could hit all of them at once, making an AI bust potentially far broader than the dot-com crash that stayed mostly contained.

Mark Cuban drew the sharper distinction. Per the All-In Podcast, this is not the dot-com bubble because there is no wave of no-revenue companies IPO-ing to retail, so the damage lands on the venture funds and private equity that went all in at $40 to $60 million valuations before products even launched, and on the mega-caps borrowing billions against cash flow to fund capex while priced to perfection. His analogy is the one to keep, that just as the fiber buildout left dark fiber selling for pennies, a breakthrough in AI power efficiency could turn a lot of data centers into pickleball courts.

3. Alphabet and Tesla report tomorrow, and Google fired first. The two prints the week hinges on are 24 hours out. Per the People list, Alphabet reports after tomorrow's close as the first major hyperscaler and the first real test of whether the AI trade is still justified, with the market watching cloud growth, AI monetization, and above all the capital-spending guide, and Google pre-empted the report today by launching its Gemini 3.6 Flash models and confirming that Gemini 4 is already in pre-training.

Tesla is the other side of the barbell. Per the same list, Tesla reports the same evening having just expanded its robotaxi service to Tampa and Orlando, though skeptics note the expansion dropped one day before earnings, each city runs only about ten vehicles, and Tesla has missed its short-term robotaxi guidance three reports in a row. The bull case that a strong Alphabet cloud and capex guide reignites the whole trade, per Milk Road, is real, and so is the risk that any equivocation on AI spending deepens the correction.

4. The AI power crunch has a date now, and it is 2028. The most substantive new thesis of the day is about natural gas. Per Matt Smith on Invest Like the Best, after 18 months of well-level modeling he projects US gas storage drawing down below all prior history by 2028 as LNG exports climb from 15 to 35 billion cubic feet a day and AI compute adds another 5 to 15, against a production ceiling that cannot keep up, which takes a complacent $3.50 gas price toward $8 to $10 and pushes energy from about 10 percent of a hyperscaler's cost to 20 or even 40 percent by 2029.

His named plays are the ones with the gas and the power. Per that interview, the winners are Expand Energy, which controls roughly 70 percent of the remaining core Haynesville at about four times cash flow, plus Range Resources, Cameco for its Westinghouse nuclear stake, and BWXT, while the losers are Caterpillar and Bloom Energy building gas generation into the shortage, and the American consumer who pays the power bill. The same physical reality is why Kevin O'Leary is fighting to build the largest data center in US history in Utah against local opposition, per Anthony Pompliano, because whoever locks in power now wins the next phase.

5. Crypto went up while stocks softened, and the CLARITY Act is finally moving. The divergence flipped in crypto's favor. Per the Crypto list, Bitcoin broke $66,000 and rose about 4 percent as capital rotated out of crowded AI positions into crypto treasury names, Bitcoin ETFs took in $229 million on the day, and the prediction markets now price better than 70 percent odds that Ether holds above $2,000 into month-end, with Tom Lee targeting $2,200 by August.

The catalyst underneath it is legislative. Per Lark Davis, the White House agreed to an ethics package that could unstick the CLARITY Act, with a floor vote possible before the August recess and passage odds recovering to around 42 percent, and per Blockworks, Senate leader John Thune targeted this week for action. That same Blockworks note makes the case that PumpFun's token, up 35 percent, is throwing off a 12.7 percent buyback yield after rallying through its own unlock, the kind of durable cash flow that could re-rate it if the memecoin volume holds.

Single names to track.

  • $MU (Micron). Jumped to $945 and kissed its 50-day average on a Bank of America upgrade, with Morgan Stanley calling the pullback a compelling entry, per the Market list.
  • $NBIS (Nebius). Rose more than 10 percent after Nvidia disclosed a roughly 9 percent passive stake, per the Market list.
  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Reports after tomorrow's close as the first real test of the AI trade, having launched its Gemini 3.6 Flash models today, per the People list.
  • $EXE (Expand Energy). The top pick for the coming gas shortage, controlling roughly 70 percent of the core Haynesville at about four times cash flow, per Invest Like the Best.
  • BTC (Bitcoin). Broke $66,000 on rotation out of AI, with the 200-week average near $68,500 the line that flips the structure, per the Crypto list.

Psychology. Read the divergence honestly. The names that fell the hardest ripped 10 to 20 percent today, and the mega-caps that everyone owns quietly gave ground, the market rotating rather than rallying, buying the capitulation in memory while trimming the leaders that carry the index. That is the kind of day that feels like an all-clear and is actually a rebalancing, and the tell is that the biggest bounce came in the most beaten-down names rather than the strongest ones.

The mood underneath it is a bubble debate breaking into the open. The US Treasury is drafting warnings about AI contagion, Mark Cuban is telling Anthropic and OpenAI employees to hedge their stock, and Jamie Dimon said flat out he would not buy stocks right now, all while the Fed hike odds jumped to 62 percent and the beaten chips melted up anyway. When the smart money is quoting the dot-com comparison and the crowd is buying the dip with both hands, the two are describing the same tape and betting opposite outcomes.

So the discipline into Alphabet and Tesla tomorrow is to respect both truths. The memory shortage is physical and the demand is real, and that is why the dip was bought, but the leverage and the off-balance-sheet spending are exactly what a Treasury report and a billionaire investor are pointing at. Let the capex guides print before you decide the AI trade is fixed, own the shortage through the toolmakers and the power names that the math actually supports, and keep enough cash that if Cuban is right and some of these data centers become pickleball courts, you are the buyer and not the bag.

item.title: [Investing] The AI trade is going into Alphabet and Tesla this week carrying $662 billion of data-center leases that are not on anyone's balance sheet yet, and that off-balance-sheet pile is the bear case nobody is pricing
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: A careful accounting read says the five hyperscalers have signed lease commitments worth more than their entire adjusted debt, none of it recognized until the buildings switch on. Micron reclaimed its line, Hasbro reports this morning, and Tesla and Alphabet both print tomorrow into a market that looks priced for perfection.
item.content:encoded:
A careful accounting read says the five hyperscalers have signed lease commitments worth more than their entire adjusted debt, none of it recognized until the buildings switch on. Micron reclaimed its line, Hasbro reports this morning, and Tesla and Alphabet both print tomorrow into a market that looks priced for perfection.

A Tuesday of quiet accumulation before a loud two days. The tape recovered its footing, but the most important thing written this weekend was not a price target, it was a footnote. Here is the pre-open picture, then five stories.

Pre-open preview. The setup is calm on the surface and stretched underneath. The S&P sits just 2.18 percent off its record, per Capital Flows, while the memory names keep bouncing and Micron reclaimed the level the chartists were watching. The earnings calendar is the whole story, with Hasbro reporting before the open this morning, then Alphabet and Tesla both after tomorrow's close and Intel on Thursday. Oil is softer after Iran floated a ceasefire, and the market is treating this week's prints as the referee for whether the AI selloff was a scare or a top.

1. The $662 billion nobody has to report yet is the real risk under the AI trade. The most important analysis of the weekend is an accounting one. Per a detailed ValueInvesting writeup, the five largest hyperscalers had $662 billion of signed data-center leases sitting off their balance sheets at the end of 2025, more than two-thirds of their $969 billion of total future lease commitments and roughly 113 percent of their adjusted debt, none of it recognized because the accounting rule defers a lease until the building commences.

The obligation is real, it is just disclosed in three places at once. Per the same writeup, Moody's flags potentially hundreds of billions more in unquantified residual-value guarantees, and more than $120 billion of spending has been moved into off-balance-sheet vehicles funded by Pimco, Apollo, and Blue Owl, including Meta's roughly $30 billion Hyperion structure and $69 billion of Oracle sale-leasebacks.

Michael Burry's work projects Oracle overstating its 2028 earnings by about 27 percent and Meta by about 21 percent. The author's conclusion is the disciplined one, that he will not pay above roughly 20 times corrected earnings for any of these names until the leases commence and the guarantees get a number, which lands the group at 14 to 16 times reported. That is the bear case going into Alphabet, and it is invisible on every screen.

2. Micron reclaimed its line and the memory bounce has a target now. The technical story stayed constructive. Per Stocks with Josh, Micron fell all the way from $1,255, dropped to $804 in the morning, then recaptured the $861 level that the same trader had flagged on the way down, and if it holds $861 into a close the next target sits near $1,089.

The read across the group is that the pullback may be exhausting. The broader risk-off caution is still there, with the same trader warning that midterm-election years tend to see weakness from August into October before a rally, per that breakdown. These are chart calls from a promotional channel, so treat the exact levels as one technician's map, but the message that the memory names found support while the accounting question hangs over them is the tension the whole week has to resolve.

3. Tesla reports tomorrow and Hasbro reports this morning, and the options market is braced. The single-name catalysts bracket the week. Per Stocks with Josh, Tesla reports after tomorrow's close with the options market pricing a 7.1 percent move against a 4.3 percent recent average, its key support levels stacked at 350, 322, and 300, and one desk flagging heavy buying of the $150 puts expiring this Friday.

The sleeper same-day print is Hasbro. Per a Wall Street Bets writeup, Hasbro reports before the open this morning with the whole growth story riding on Wizards of the Coast and Magic the Gathering, where the Marvel Superheroes set is outselling expectations, a Nintendo signing for 2027 is teased as bigger than Final Fantasy, and direct-selling on Amazon captures margin that used to leak to distributors. The toy business only has to stop shrinking for the market to look past it, so a Magic beat this morning is the quiet setup nobody outside the hobby is watching.

4. The valuation reckoning is not just the hyperscalers, it is Apple too. The theme underneath the week is that the whole large-cap complex is priced for a world that may not arrive. Per a reverse-DCF writeup, Apple at around $334 implies free-cash-flow growth of 14.1 percent a year for a decade, taking cash flow from $129 billion to nearly $484 billion, while its actual three-year cash-flow growth has been negative 3.9 percent and its earnings growth has come mostly from buybacks rather than the business.

The scenarios put the stock above even the bull case. The same analysis lands Apple at roughly $120 in a bear case, $143 in a base, and $162 if everything goes right, which means the price sits above the optimistic outcome at 26 times trailing earnings. And while the crowd chases the leaders, the one name with the cleanest moat gets ignored, with a ValueInvesting post noting that Taiwan Semiconductor trades neglected on its Taiwan risk even as Intel's 18A process reportedly reaches 85 percent yield and becomes the geopolitically safe alternative.

5. The crypto crowd is compressing into October and eyeing a forced seller. The trading collectives are converging on the same clock. Per the Price optimist newsletter, the summer thesis is playing out with strong assets going sideways and weak ones drifting down, the S&P's 7,100 to 7,300 range flagged as value, and Bitcoin expected to compress into October before a fourth-quarter rally, with a loss of $57,000 the level that breaks the case. The specific risk they name is a forced seller, a digital-asset treasury company under credit stress with Michael Saylor behind it, where a reversing premium could bring fast selling toward the $40,000s.

The AI angle is the one that ties back to the stock market. Per threadguy, Kimi is raising money at roughly $30 billion while shipping a model that beats Claude Fable at a third of the cost, against OpenAI and Anthropic both valued near a trillion, which he frames as the emperor-has-no-clothes moment for the model makers, where the capex names stay bid but the model providers are squeezed. The bull counter is the one Avichal Garg lays out, per Milk Road, that real-world assets moving on-chain against $5 trillion of stablecoins hunting yield is the ETH-ICO moment for the whole category, the multi-trillion case that only pays off in 2027 and beyond.

Single names to track.

  • $HAS (Hasbro). Reports before the open this morning with Magic the Gathering carrying the growth, the Marvel Superheroes set outselling expectations and a 2027 Nintendo signing teased, per this writeup.
  • $TSLA (Tesla). Reports after tomorrow's close with the options market pricing a 7.1 percent move and support stacked at 350, 322, and 300, per Stocks with Josh.
  • $MU (Micron). Reclaimed the $861 level after touching $804, with the next target near $1,089 if it holds, per Stocks with Josh.
  • $AAPL (Apple). Trades above its own bull case at $334 on a reverse DCF that needs 14.1 percent cash-flow growth against a delivered negative 3.9, per this analysis.
  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Reports after tomorrow's close as the referee for the AI-capex debate that the $662 billion of hidden leases quietly hangs over, per the lease writeup.

Psychology. Hold two facts side by side this morning. The neocloud names ripped higher yesterday on signed contracts, and the most careful analyst of the week just showed that $662 billion of the leases underpinning those contracts is not on anyone's balance sheet, with Michael Burry's math implying Oracle and Meta may be overstating their future earnings by a fifth or more. The crowd is buying the demand and ignoring the disclosure, and both of those cannot keep being true forever.

The tell of a market priced for perfection is that even the safe names fail the arithmetic. Apple trades above its own best-case valuation, the hyperscalers only look reasonable if you ignore the leases they have not booked, and the trading desks are quietly naming a forced seller with Saylor's name attached as the thing that cracks crypto toward the $40,000s. When the bull case for the index requires lower rates and higher growth than the economy is actually delivering, single-stock analysis becomes a macro bet whether you meant it to or not.

So the discipline into Alphabet and Tesla tomorrow is to separate the demand from the accounting. The AI buildout is real and the memory names found their footing, but a trade whose leverage lives in footnotes and off-balance-sheet vehicles is one where the risk shows up all at once when the leases commence. Let the prints land, hold enough cash that a soft capex guide or a Saylor-driven crypto flush is your entry, and remember that the $662 billion does not disappear because it is hard to see. It just waits for the building to switch on.

item.title: [Investing] The broad tape was weak and Alphabet is carving a bear flag into Wednesday, but the neocloud names exploded higher on a wall of new contracts, and oil round-tripped from over $90 to under $80 in a single session
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: IREN jumped 16 percent on $2.8 billion of fresh AI-cloud deals while the sector printed one signing after another. Oil crashed below $80 on a reported Iran ceasefire proposal, gold is stuck in a two-sided fight, and the whole market is holding its breath for one earnings print in 48 hours.
item.content:encoded:
IREN jumped 16 percent on $2.8 billion of fresh AI-cloud deals while the sector printed one signing after another. Oil crashed below $80 on a reported Iran ceasefire proposal, gold is stuck in a two-sided fight, and the whole market is holding its breath for one earnings print in 48 hours.

A Monday of crosscurrents. The index went nowhere, the compute-infrastructure names went vertical, and the war that pushed oil over $90 this morning pushed it back under $80 by the afternoon. Here is the session recap, then five stories.

Session recap. The broad tape was heavy but the AI-infrastructure trade was on fire underneath it. Per the Market list, the neoclouds bounced hard on a run of new deals while Alphabet carved a weekly bear flag into Wednesday's earnings and Oracle sat in its largest drawdown in more than 25 years. The war whipsawed the whole session, with oil crashing below $80 on a reported Iranian ceasefire proposal after trading over $90 in the morning, gasoline back over $4 at the pump, and SpaceX printing a new all-time low, per the Polymarket list. Volatility sat calm near 17.65, Jim Cramer declared tech simply too hard, and everything is now queued behind the Alphabet print.

1. The neocloud names exploded on a wall of new contracts. The trade of the day was compute infrastructure. Per the Market list, IREN jumped as much as 16 percent after signing $2.8 billion of new multi-year AI-cloud contracts and raising its year-end run-rate target above $4 billion, with 85 percent of that already under contract, customers prepaying roughly 45 percent of the GPU cost, and $7.6 billion of cash worth about 60 percent of its market value.

It was not one name, it was the whole sector. Per the same tape, Hut 8 landed a fifteen-year $9.8 billion deal, CleanSpark signed its first high-performance-computing deal at $6.6 billion, Nebius booked $1 billion with Reflection AI on top of 684 percent revenue growth, and TeraWulf inked a roughly $19 billion agreement with Anthropic, while BlackRock led $12 billion of financing for Meta's Texas data centers. The read-through, per the Stocks list, is that the capex-collapse fear that drove last week's selloff keeps running into signed contracts, and the customers are paying up front.

2. Oil round-tripped in a day and gold is fighting itself. The macro whipsaw was in commodities. Per the Polymarket list, oil crashed below $80 after Iran reportedly proposed a ten-day ceasefire to revive an interim deal, a violent reversal from the morning's move above $90, even as CENTCOM completed its ninth straight night of strikes and the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia. A war being fought and de-escalated in the same day is producing a fuel price that cannot decide what it is.

Gold is running its own split-screen. Per VirtualBacon, gold has broken its 40-week average at 4,500 and entered a technical bear market with downside eventually below 3,000, pressured by the same commodity margin-call selling. Yet per Lark Davis, China's central bank bought 480,000 ounces in June, its biggest purchase since 2023 and its twentieth straight month of buying, stepping into an 11.6 percent price drop. The chartists see a breakdown and the largest strategic buyer sees a discount, and only one of them is trading for the next quarter.

3. Alphabet on Wednesday is still the referee, and it just showed its hand on chips. The print the whole week hinges on is 48 hours out. Per the Market list, Alphabet is developing a new in-house chip called Frozen V2 that reportedly runs its Gemini models up to ten times more efficiently than its latest processors, a bullish signal for its own compute even as the stock carves a bear flag into the report.

The number hanging over it is the bill. Per the Polymarket list, Goldman Sachs warned that the $5.3 trillion of AI spending planned by Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet through 2030 could start to pressure the bond market, the macro version of the same question the neocloud deals keep answering with a yes. Alphabet's capital-spending guide on Wednesday is where the market finds out whether that $5.3 trillion is a promise or a warning.

4. The memory bull got a huge buyback number, and the bottleneck may be power. The single-name memory story got sharper. Per the Polymarket list, UBS expects Micron to generate more than $400 billion of free cash flow through 2028 and to repurchase over 40 percent of its shares once its buyback restriction expires in December 2026, though the desks still flag SK Hynix as the cleaner way to own the same cycle, per the People list.

The constraint underneath the chips is electricity. Per this breakdown, Navitas makes the gallium-nitride and silicon-carbide power chips that feed Nvidia's move to 800-volt, one-megawatt racks, with about $450 million of design wins as data-center power demand heads past 1,000 terawatt-hours by the end of the decade. It is unprofitable and a design win is not an order, but the theme is real, that the AI trade is running into a physical wall of power and heat, and the same New Mexico permit fight that just hit Bloom Energy is the proof.

5. Crypto is stuck in a box while the contrarians circle Ethereum. The majors are going nowhere. Per the Crypto list, Mike Novogratz says Bitcoin is stuck between $65,000 and $85,000 and needs both the CLARITY Act to pass and the Fed to start cutting to break higher, with one of those two legs currently broken, while stablecoin supply fell another $1.24 billion and public companies added just 101.5 Bitcoin last week.

The bolder call is on the most hated major. Per Lark Davis, Ethereum is down about 65 percent with its weekly momentum reading at the third-lowest level ever recorded, a setup he compares to the June 2022 low rather than the final bottom, and the Ether-to-Bitcoin ratio just printed a bullish crossover that last preceded a 132 percent stretch of outperformance. The catalyst he points to is Robinhood Chain, where bridged Ether jumped seventyfold in a week, so the thesis is that the rotation into Ethereum simply has not happened yet. Those are one promoter's indicators, so weigh them as a setup and not a certainty, but universal hatred of an asset is at least the right precondition.

Single names to track.

  • $IREN. Jumped 16 percent on $2.8 billion of new AI-cloud contracts, run-rate target above $4 billion with 85 percent under contract and customers prepaying 45 percent of GPU cost, per the Market list.
  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Reports Wednesday as the referee for the AI-capex debate, carving a bear flag but developing a Frozen V2 chip said to run Gemini ten times more efficiently, per the Market list.
  • $MU (Micron). UBS sees more than $400 billion of free cash flow through 2028 and a buyback of over 40 percent of shares once the restriction lifts, per the Polymarket list.
  • $NVTS (Navitas). The power-semi bottleneck play feeding Nvidia's 800-volt racks, roughly $450 million of design wins but still unprofitable, per this breakdown.
  • ETH (Ethereum). Down 65 percent with the third-lowest weekly momentum reading ever and a bullish ratio crossover, the contrarian setup, per Lark Davis.

Psychology. Watch how fast the crowd flips. This morning the story was oil over $90 breaking the disinflation trade, and by the afternoon oil was under $80 on a ceasefire headline and the neoclouds were up double digits, the same market swinging between panic and greed inside a single session. When the tape moves that violently on headlines, the temptation is to trade every swing, and the cost of doing that is usually your patience and your capital both.

The tell of the moment is the irony nobody is naming out loud. Two weeks ago the market sold every AI stock because a cheap Chinese model supposedly proved the buildout was overbuilt, and this weekend that same model, Kimi K3, had to pause its subscriptions because it ran out of compute, per the Market list. The bear case and the bull case were the same fact read in opposite directions, and the neocloud deals signed today are the market quietly admitting which reading was right. Michael Burry's line that 95 percent of investors have no idea what they own fits a tape where IREN and its peers just proved the demand while their stocks were still being sold as broken.

So the discipline into Alphabet on Wednesday is to let the print settle the argument instead of front-running it with leverage. The neocloud contracts and the Micron cash-flow math say the demand is real and paid for, but Jim Cramer calling tech too hard and oil whipping $10 in a day say the price is going to keep lurching regardless. Own the names whose customers are prepaying, respect that a single earnings report can override every chart on your screen, and keep enough cash that the next violent swing is your entry rather than your undoing.

item.title: [Investing] The whole argument about whether AI spending is about to collapse gets settled on Wednesday when Alphabet reports, and everything trading this week is really a bet on that one number
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Alphabet's capital-spending guide is the referee for a memory complex down 20 percent and a market 2 percent from its record. Korea's stock crisis got worse overnight, oil pushed back over $90, and SpaceX just got a $900 price target the same week its share count starts to explode.
item.content:encoded:
Alphabet's capital-spending guide is the referee for a memory complex down 20 percent and a market 2 percent from its record. Korea's stock crisis got worse overnight, oil pushed back over $90, and SpaceX just got a $900 price target the same week its share count starts to explode.

A Monday that is really a countdown to Wednesday. The market spent last week deciding the AI trade might be broken, and the company most able to prove or disprove that reports in 48 hours. Here is the pre-open picture, then five stories.

Pre-open preview. Futures are flattish into a heavy week. The S&P sits about 2 percent below its early-June record while the Philadelphia semiconductor index is more than 20 percent off its late-June high yet still up 60 percent on the year, per the Market list. More than 80 S&P companies report this week with Alphabet on Wednesday the clear catalyst, Tesla and Intel later in the stretch, and the Fed meeting at month-end. Overnight the trouble was abroad, with Korea's market down another 4 percent, oil back over $90, and gold struggling near $4,000 after its worst week in six, per the Financial Markets list. SpaceX flies its rescheduled Starship test Thursday, not today.

1. Alphabet on Wednesday is the referee for the entire AI-capex fear. The single print that matters is a capital-spending number. Per the Market list, Alphabet reports Wednesday as the first hyperscaler read of the season, and a pullback in its AI capex guidance would ripple straight through the memory and neocloud names that just sold off, while a confident guide would tell the market the buildout is intact.

The fundamentals give the bulls a strong hand going in. Per the Stocks list, Alphabet trades near 22 times forward earnings as the cheapest of the Magnificent Seven, its cloud revenue grew 63 percent to $20 billion with the backlog doubled to $462 billion, and its own chips now sell to Anthropic and Meta. The whole week is positioned around this one report, so the risk is not the number itself but how crowded the bet on it has become.

2. The memory bull case has a cleaner name than Micron, and it is SK Hynix. The trade beneath the AI trade is high-bandwidth memory, and the leader is Korean. Per the People list, Nvidia cannot walk away from SK Hynix because it supplies 70 percent of the memory going into the Vera Rubin platform on co-designed chips, holding 56 percent of the market to Micron's 23, and on Shay Boloor's growth-adjusted screen SK Hynix is the cheapest name in the group at a fraction of Micron's multiple.

The structural case underneath is a cash-flow inversion. Per the Crypto list, Gavin Baker notes that Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom, and Applied Materials are on pace for roughly $430 billion of combined free cash flow over the next year, more than triple two years ago, even as the five hyperscalers' free cash flow falls from around $250 billion in 2024 toward $100 billion by the end of 2026 under an estimated $1.8 trillion of AI spending. The money is visibly moving from the spenders to the suppliers, and Micron itself sits down 30 percent with its memory sold out through 2027, per the Market list.

3. SpaceX got a $900 target the same week its float starts to flood. The most-owned new stock got a bullish number with a catch. Per Lark Davis, Citi set a $900 price target on SpaceX, but the timing matters more than the target, because the public float jumps from about 5 percent now to 60 percent by November as pre-IPO lockups expire, and toward 100 percent by mid-2027.

That is a tsunami of supply regardless of fair value. His framing is the right one, that you do not want to be the exit liquidity for the venture investors who are about to be freed to sell, so the discipline is to let the lockup selling exhaust itself before reaching for Citi's target. The stock is already down about 45 percent from its highs, per the Market list, and the wall of new shares is the reason a great company can still be a bad stock for a few more months.

4. Oil is back over $90 and it is the quiet threat to the whole tape. The move that could break the calm is in crude. Per the People list, Brent jumped back over $90 a barrel as the Iran war entered its tenth day with the Strait of Hormuz still blocked, and gold sold off hard into the strength, posting its biggest weekly drop in six.

The read-through is that the disinflation trade the Fed leaned on is getting more expensive by the week. One rotation call making the rounds is to be long oil from the seventies, move out of semis and software into cyclical financials and healthcare, and stay defensive through the illiquid summer, per the Crypto list. Whether or not you make that exact trade, a crude benchmark over $90 into a Fed meeting is the variable that can override even a good Alphabet print.

5. Crypto is holding its levels while the structural bears sharpen their case. The majors are steady into the week. Per the Crypto list, Bitcoin is back over $65,000 and Ether is pinned to the $2,000 pivot that decides its next move, a close above pointing higher and a loss of it opening a sweep of the lows.

The bearish argument getting louder is Chamath Palihapitiya's. Per the People list, he lays out two structural headwinds for Bitcoin, that speculative liquidity now prefers prediction markets and equities, and that the energy going into Bitcoin mining is worth ten to twenty times more if it is reallocated to running AI models. That is a real long-term question about whether the marginal buyer and the marginal watt both have somewhere better to go, and it is the kind of thesis that matters more the longer the price stays stuck.

Single names to track.

  • $GOOGL (Alphabet). Reports Wednesday as the referee for the AI-capex debate, cheapest Magnificent Seven name near 22 times forward with cloud up 63 percent and a $462 billion backlog, per the Stocks list.
  • SK Hynix. The cleanest memory name, supplying 70 percent of Vera Rubin's high-bandwidth memory at 56 percent market share and the lowest growth-adjusted multiple in the group, per the People list.
  • $MU (Micron). Down 30 percent with memory sold out through 2027, bouncing off its falling-wedge lows on Friday with levels stacked from 806 to 906, per the Market list and Stocks list.
  • $SPCX (SpaceX). Carries a fresh Citi $900 target but faces a float going from 5 to 60 percent by November, down 45 percent from its highs, per Lark Davis.
  • BTC (Bitcoin). Back over $65,000 against Chamath's two structural headwinds of liquidity and energy competition, per the Crypto list.

Psychology. Look east before you look at your own screen. Korea is running the same AI-chip mania the US is, and its market volatility just hit the highest level in its history, worse than the financial crisis, with the index down 30 percent from a record it set only last month, per the Financial Markets list. That is what a crowded, levered version of this exact trade looks like when it unwinds, and it is happening in real time to people running the same thesis you are.

The tell of the moment is how eager the crowd is to call the bottom anyway. The dip-buyers are naming Micron's floor to the dollar and Bitcoin's low to the level, the promoters are quoting Citi's $900 on SpaceX while ignoring the 60 percent float unlock behind it, and everyone is treating Friday's bounce as the all-clear into a week that hinges on a single earnings print. Confidence is cheap the weekend after a scare, and it is usually most abundant right before the scare's second leg.

So the discipline into Alphabet on Wednesday is to hold your size and your patience. The memory demand is real and sold out through 2027, but the cleanest way to own it is the supplier with the lowest multiple, not the leveraged expression that round-trips on a headline. Let Alphabet print before you decide the AI trade is fixed, respect that Korea is showing you the downside of crowding, and keep enough cash that oil over $90 or a soft capex guide is your opportunity rather than your problem. The market wants you certain this morning. The move is to stay liquid and let Wednesday do the talking.

item.title: [Investing] Micron was worth more than Berkshire Hathaway on Wednesday and had shed nearly half a trillion dollars by Friday, and the crash needed no thesis to break, just a rate hike in Seoul and a cheap model out of China
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The memory trade round-tripped an entire euphoria in a single week, and the round-trip is the lesson. The demand behind Micron is still measured in gigawatts and sold out through 2027, but the leverage stacked on top of it is what showed you what it does on a bad headline.
item.content:encoded:
The memory trade round-tripped an entire euphoria in a single week, and the round-trip is the lesson. The demand behind Micron is still measured in gigawatts and sold out through 2027, but the leverage stacked on top of it is what showed you what it does on a bad headline.

This was the week the biggest trade in the market got a real test, and it was not a test of the story. It was a test of how much leverage the crowd had piled onto a story that was mostly right. Here is the arc, the bull and bear cases, and what to do with it.

The arc of the week. On Tuesday the memory blowoff was still going, with Micron briefly worth more than Berkshire Hathaway and the crowd calling for $2,000, while SanDisk printed the highest weekly relative-strength reading ever recorded on any stock. By Wednesday it had round-tripped, with Micron breaking below $900 in a single session and the money that left the chips going straight into Apple.

Then the cause arrived, and it was not the AI thesis cracking. Per Jose Najarro, the Bank of Korea raised its base rate 25 basis points to 2.75 percent, its first hike in three and a half years, which lifted the borrowing cost on the Korean-financed fabs that SK Hynix and Samsung are building, sent the KOSPI down 7 percent, and dragged the whole memory complex with it.

The key detail is that the hike does not touch the demand curve for high-bandwidth memory or the fabs Micron builds with US money, so the sharpest fall was in the names with the local rate exposure, not the ones with the best long-run position. By Friday the momentum unwind had turned historic, with Micron having lost $459 billion of market value in fourteen trading days, per the Polymarket list.

The final shove came from an unrelated direction. A cheap Chinese model, Kimi K3, topped the coding benchmarks and set off a fear that AI spending would slow, and the memory names took the hit even though, as the AI memo this week lays out, the model is not actually the cost bomb the tape treated it as. Two exogenous shocks, a Seoul rate decision and a Beijing model release, took apart a trade that had nothing to do with either.

The bull case, stated cleanly. The demand is real and it is contracted. Per Morgan Stanley by way of Shay Boloor, Micron's gross margins could reach 90 percent in 2027, supported by sixteen supply agreements with floor pricing and high-bandwidth memory that is sold out through 2027, with the HBM4 for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform already shipping since March at roughly twice the ramp pace of the prior generation. The scale behind it is not a slogan, with data-center capacity set to add more than 100 gigawatts by 2030 against over $5 trillion of total spending.

The confirming tell is the calmest company in the chain. Per Najarro, ASML raised its four-year guidance and said its lithography capacity grows 30 percent next year and another 30 percent after, with 2027 already sold out, the bottleneck that stretches the cycle rather than ending it. When the pick-and-shovel supplier at the very top of the chain is booked three years forward while the crowd panics over a quarter-point hike in Korea, the panic is the opportunity and not the signal.

The bear case, taken seriously. The round-trip itself is the warning. A stock that is worth more than Berkshire on Tuesday and below $900 on Wednesday is not being valued, it is being traded on leverage, and the leverage is the problem. The selloff was a momentum-factor unwind from the 100th percentile of positioning, the worst such stretch in 27 years, which means the buyers at the top were mechanical and forced, and mechanical buyers become mechanical sellers the instant volatility turns.

The sharper worry is who is short and what they know. Michael Burry turned bearish on Micron in early July and the stock fell 18 percent, per Stocks with Josh, and the professionals are already shorting the next Chinese memory IPO before it even lists. Per threadguy, CXMT, described as China's SK Hynix, goes public July 27 and is already trading as a pre-IPO perpetual at an implied $470 billion against an $80 billion offering, and the two largest positions are both professional shorts. When the smart money is short the shiny new memory name before its first trade, the supply side of this cycle is not the sure thing the bulls make it sound.

What to do with it. The level is the referee, not your conviction. Per Stocks with Josh, Micron needs to reclaim and hold $861 to confirm the bottom and $805 is the line that breaks it, so let the price prove the thesis rather than catching the exact low on a Monday. If you want the memory cycle, the cleaner expressions are the ones the leverage cannot round-trip, ASML booked solid through 2027, or SK Hynix at 7.6 times forward earnings against Micron's 11.7 if you want the direct exposure a third cheaper.

The discipline is to own the bottleneck and avoid the leverage. The 2x memory funds and the CXMT pre-IPO perps are the instruments that just showed you what they do on a bad headline, and the semiconductor earnings landing this week are the referee for the whole argument. Keep the theme, which stays intact, and refuse the leverage, because the two are not the same thing.

Psychology. Read the week as one emotional round-trip. On Tuesday the crowd owned Micron above Berkshire and was calling for $2,000, and that is euphoria wearing the costume of conviction, and by Wednesday the same crowd was liquidated below $900 on a Korean rate hike it could not have named the day before. Nothing about the AI story changed in those 48 hours. What changed is that the leverage got a reason to unwind, and once it started, the 2x ETFs and the pre-IPO perps did the rest, carrying out the very people who felt most certain at the top.

The tell of the week is who stayed calm and who got carried out.
