  • $CCXI, the first robotics play from a team that called the memory run. Per the Milk Road PRO recap, Melvin bought Churchill Capital XI at $16.87 as a robotics SPAC while the same desk sold $MU at a 145% gain, a small tell that the smart money is starting to rotate the winnings forward.

The bigger rotation to settle: infrastructure, orchestration, or the apps. The single best debate on the tape is where the AI money goes next, and today it split three ways with real money behind each. Aschenbrenner is all-in on the physical infrastructure. Milk Road's AI desk argues the margin moves past the frontier models to the orchestration layer and the hyperscalers who own compute, citing Dylan Patel's claim that Opus 4.8 API tokens run at 80% margins and noting the Mag 7 trade at low-teens multiples with revenue landing in 2028 to 2030. And the Milk Road PRO desk is rotating out of infra into the applications on a profit-per-user thesis, liking $UBER at about $28 of operating profit per user, $NU at $35, and $COIN at $158. You do not have to pick one today, but you should know which of the three you are actually long.

Filtered / Cross-Routed. The Stocks with Josh SPY diamond-pattern call is a clean technical marker, cautiously bearish on a candle close below 740 and cancelled only by a new high, so it stays here as a level to watch rather than a section. The threadguy livestream on trader psychology carried no tickers or levels and was dropped. The Reuters $2.3B Trump-family crypto figure from Trader Mayne went to News as a politics story. The Friedberg immigration test and the Galloway creator-economy segment went to News. The Fable 5 prompting playbook, the free-token weekend, and the Hermes agent tooling went to AI & Tools. Our own kairosllm Daily Tape page in the feed was skipped, since we do not brief our own output.

item.title: [Investing] Bitcoin is sitting on the line it has not lost since 2023, and the two sides have never disagreed this loudly
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Whales bought 270,000 coins into the drop while Citi cut its target and Strategy sold for the first time ever, the memory hike went from forecast to invoice, and the new Fed chair is quietly arguing that AI makes rate cuts easier.
item.content:encoded:
Whales bought 270,000 coins into the drop while Citi cut its target and Strategy sold for the first time ever, the memory hike went from forecast to invoice, and the new Fed chair is quietly arguing that AI makes rate cuts easier.

It is a holiday weekend and nothing trades until Monday, so this is a morning to decide what you believe before the tape can bully you. The loudest argument on the board is Bitcoin at its 200-week average, where the accumulation data and the outflow data point in opposite directions at the same price. Under it sits a regulation story that finally has a real framework, and next to it a memory trade that just turned a price forecast into an actual invoice.

The week ahead, and what to pre-load before Monday's open. US markets were closed Friday July 3 for Independence Day and reopen Monday July 6. Five things to load. First, the FOMC minutes land Wednesday at 2pm ET, and after new chair Kevin Warsh started tearing up the Fed's script, every line gets read twice. Second, the SK Hynix US listing is still on deck for around July 10, a fresh pure-play memory bet in front of American money. Third, $SPCX joins the Nasdaq-100 on July 7 and GPT-5.6 is priced to arrive as soon as Tuesday.

Fourth, the crypto Clarity Act still has a coin-flip shot at a July vote. Fifth, a record $8.3T sits in money-market funds. That is either the fuel for the next leg up or a crowd that likes getting paid to wait.

1. Bitcoin lost its 200-week average, and the accumulation data and the outflow data are screaming past each other. Bitcoin is trading right at the 200-week moving average (the four-year trend line that has marked every major cycle low), the first time it has closed below it since 2023. Lark Davis makes the bull case with on-chain receipts. Whales accumulated roughly 270,000 BTC, about $16B, near the $60K zone, against only $5B of ETF net outflows, and the weekly RSI (a momentum gauge) is oversold for just the fourth time since 2012, with three of those prior four marking bottoms.

His key argument is that the one exception, 2022, only broke because Terra, Celsius, and FTX detonated a leverage chain that no longer exists in the same form. The reclaim line is clean: a weekly close back above roughly $63K puts the trend back on side.

The other side showed up with its own receipts on Swan's World Cup of Money. Citi cut its Bitcoin target to $82K and zeroed out its 12-month ETF inflow forecast, and for the first time in its history Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) reportedly sold Bitcoin, which pokes a hole in the Saylor-never-sells thesis the whole treasury trade was built on. Kalshi bettors now put 55% odds on Bitcoin tagging $50K before $100K. My read: the accumulation is real and the miner-cost floor near $60K still holds, so I am accumulating the dips I already wanted and treating a weekly close under $60K as the signal to stop. The Strategy sale is the single fact that would flip me, so I want it confirmed, not rumored.

2. The ETH short is the most crowded trade in crypto, and that cuts both ways. Underneath the Bitcoin fight is a barbell the whales have all piled onto: long Bitcoin, short Ether. Per the Crypto list, a single 54,200 ETH short worth about $89.2M sits on Hyperliquid with a liquidation price of $1,674, and roughly $95.6M of ETH shorts were already liquidated in 24 hours. When one side of a trade gets this lopsided, the fuel for a violent squeeze is the crowd itself.

The tell to respect is that 33% of all ETH supply is now staked and growing by 50,000 coins a day, which quietly pulls float off the market even while the derivatives crowd leans bearish. I am not chasing the short here.

3. Crypto regulation finally has a real framework, and it is more radical than the market has priced. The positioning story is the Clarity Act, the crypto market-structure bill, and Kevin O'Leary frames its signing as the trigger for the largest capital inflow in Bitcoin's history, with trillions waiting on legal clarity. The substance under that hope is worth reading directly. In the SEC's own "Project Crypto" outline, Chairman Paul Atkins lays out a four-bucket token taxonomy where digital commodities, digital collectibles, and digital tools are explicitly not securities, and only tokenized versions of real stocks and bonds stay securities.

The radical part is a doctrinal shift: an investment contract can end. A token sold under one does not stay a security forever, and once the network decentralizes and the promises are fulfilled, later trades are no longer securities transactions. Atkins wants rules letting those tokens trade on CFTC or state-regulated venues, a "Regulation Crypto" exemption package, and single-license "super-apps," and he states plainly that most tokens trading today are not securities. My read: this is the fundamental case sitting under O'Leary's flood. If the Clarity Act codifies even part of this taxonomy, the compliance box that has kept the largest pools of institutional money on the sidelines finally gets checked.

4. The memory hike went from forecast to invoice, and the trade got fresh receipts. Yesterday this was Micron's record print against Burry's short. This morning it is the supplier sending the bill. Samsung has begun issuing verbal notices to raise DRAM prices (dynamic RAM, the standard memory in every server and phone) by around 20% quarter over quarter for Q3, per the Market list. A price hike you forecast is a thesis, and a price hike your supplier invoices is a fact.

The numbers underneath keep getting louder. Bernstein sees Micron's DRAM gross margins above 90% in 2026 and above 92% in the back half, and Milk Road's Stocks list carries a $4,000 target with Sanjay Mehrotra saying Micron can meet only half to two-thirds of demand and no new industry supply arrives before 2028. SK Hynix just posted a single quarter's profit of $26.15B, which tops its entire 2023 revenue, on 60% HBM (high-bandwidth memory, the stacked chips bolted to AI accelerators) share and a 72% operating margin, and it lists on the Nasdaq next week. Jensen Huang called Marvell the "next trillion-dollar company," with $MRVL guiding FY2027 revenue to $11.5B, up 40%.

The fragility to keep in view is the crowding. South Korea's leveraged-ETF assets hit a record near $45B, up 800% year to date and about 2.9% of free float, so the same names everyone loves are also where the levered money is stacked. When that unwinds it does not ask politely.

5. The new Fed chair's real argument is that AI makes cutting easier. Kevin Warsh is not just tearing up forward guidance (the Fed's habit of telegraphing its next move). Per the Stocks list, his framing is an AI-deflation thesis: frontier inference cost fell from roughly $30 per million tokens in early 2023 to pennies, and AI has added only about 0.3 point to core PCE (the Fed's preferred inflation gauge). He wants a "good family fight" at the FOMC about four weeks out, will not confirm a July hike, and wants a smaller balance sheet, leaning on the Greenspan 1990s analogue where productivity ran hot and inflation stayed tame.

The honest counter is that software prices are going the other way, with Microsoft 365 up 30%, Adobe up 50%, and Intuit up 45% on the year. My read: this is the rates story for the back half, and a chair who removes the script guarantees a wider reaction to every print.

Single names worth a place on the watchlist.

  • $AMZN, the robotics-and-logistics AI trade. On Prof G Markets, Scott Galloway's 2026 big-tech pick is Amazon and Tom Lee agreed "100%." The case: Amazon runs about 1 million industrial robots against roughly 400,000 for the rest of the country combined, and Lee frames it as a logistics company whose addressable market is anything that needs moving, riffing that robots could eventually double its TAM (total addressable market) into housing and offices.
  • The neocloud dip keeps getting cheaper: $NBIS, $IREN. Nebius posted Q1 revenue of $399M, up 684% year over year, on a $27B five-year Meta contract and a $2B Nvidia investment, per the Crypto list. $IREN has now fallen nine straight days into its most oversold reading in a year even as its CEO sold zero shares and analysts carry a $200-plus target. High-beta and not for the faint of heart.
  • $PLTR, upgraded into the open-model shift. DA Davidson moved Palantir to Buy with a $175 target per the People-to-follow list, and the moat argument is that customers can now swap the AI model underneath without leaving the platform.
  • $SOL and the tokenization tape. Securitize tokenized $295M of its own NYSE stock on Solana at its IPO, and Solana's real-world-asset value went from $873M to $3.6B in six months across 291,000 holders, with SOL near $82. This is the cleanest live read on whether onchain adoption is actually happening.
  • $TAO, the decentralized-AI satellite. Milk Road's Bittensor deep-dive frames TAO near $200 with a 21M hard cap and roughly 11.5M in circulation, its top AI-compute subnets already running near $20M of annualized revenue, and Jensen name-dropping it on All-In. Size it as a long-dated option rather than a core hold.
  • $META, buying its way off TSMC. Meta signed a $6.5B deal with Samsung Foundry to build its third-generation MTIA AI chips on a 2nm process, per the People-to-follow list, a real step toward owning its own silicon.

Filtered / Cross-Routed. The "Don't Miss this Move" clip from Stocks with Josh was a paid-Discord funnel, so its only reusable facts (a Micron 861 to 895 fib buy-zone and the Wednesday FOMC minutes) are better sourced elsewhere, and the rest stays out. Four other Stocks with Josh scalps (Nike, a Meta +65% intraday call, Tesla, and a soccer bet) were day-trade clickbait with no durable signal and got dropped. The SCOTUS birthright ruling, the Trump disclosure and Trump Accounts launch, and the Newsom budget went to News. The Fable 5 economics, Hermes agent release, and the DeepSeek and Alibaba price-war moves went to AI & Tools. The robotics-chokepoint names (Harmonic Drive and Schaeffler) are interesting but thin foreign microcaps, so they stay on the shelf for now.

item.title: [Investing] The memory bulls spent all day answering Burry, and Asia already voted with a green tape
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Micron is now the third-largest name in the Nasdaq-100 with record numbers behind it, the AI-capex bear case from this morning got its counterpunch, and Bitcoin's bottom-callers got louder even as the ETF money kept walking out the door.
item.content:encoded:
Micron is now the third-largest name in the Nasdaq-100 with record numbers behind it, the AI-capex bear case from this morning got its counterpunch, and Bitcoin's bottom-callers got louder even as the ETF money kept walking out the door.

This morning the story was Michael Burry leaning on the most crowded trade on the board. By this afternoon the other side had shown up with receipts, and the overseas tape had already picked a side. Markets are closed here for the holiday, so none of this trades until Monday, which gives you the weekend to decide whether the bounce is real or a trap.

The week ahead, and what actually matters at Monday's open. US cash and options markets were shut today, Friday July 3, for Independence Day, and reopen Monday July 6. Four things to pre-load. First, whether the memory names ($MU, $SNDK, $MRVL) follow Asia's Friday bounce or fade it. Second, the SK Hynix US listing: the Korean memory giant plans roughly a $29B Nasdaq ADR (a US-listed proxy for a foreign stock) around July 10 under ticker $SKHY, which puts a fresh pure-play memory bet in front of American money.

Third, $SPCX joins the Nasdaq-100 on July 7, which forces index funds to buy it. Fourth, the calendar is loud into the week: GPT-5.6 is priced to land as soon as Tuesday, the crypto Clarity Act has a coin-flip shot at a July vote, and Bitcoin has to prove the bottom-callers right or wrong at the $62K to $63K line.

1. Micron is now the third-biggest name in the Nasdaq-100, and the bulls spent all day making Burry look early. The counter to this morning's short case is not a vibe. It is a stack of numbers. Micron posted record fiscal Q3 revenue of $41.5B with adjusted EPS of $25.11 against a $20.49 estimate, and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra told Bloomberg the company can only meet "about 50% to about two-thirds" of key-customer demand right now, with no real new supply until 2028. Wolfe Research pegs Micron's DRAM gross margins above 90%.

The structural piece is that this cycle runs on two legs at once. AI servers pull memory twice, once as HBM (high-bandwidth memory, the expensive stacked chips bolted onto the GPU) and again as ordinary high-capacity DRAM feeding the rest of the box. That is why Wolfe calls this "more structural than the usual memory spike." $MU is now the third-largest weight in the Nasdaq-100 at roughly 4.9%, ahead of Microsoft and Amazon, so index money has to own it whether it loves the story or not.

And Asia already moved. On the inbox tape, SK Hynix closed up 11%, Samsung up 8%, and the Kospi up 6% on Friday. My read: I said this morning I still think the durable-shortage story wins, and today's numbers plus the overseas bounce are the bull case answering the bell. Burry short into a $1,000 print can still be right on a wobble, so let Monday's follow-through tell you whether to add, and respect that H1 already ran this group vertical ($SNDK finished the half up 764%, $MU up 301%, $WDC up 278%).

2. The AI-capex bear case from this morning got its counterpunch by the afternoon. At 5:30am the story was three voices calling the buildout a bubble. By the close the other side had answered on every front.

  • Meta's own numbers say the panic is old. The Meta capex breakdown is the sober version. FY2025 capex hit $69.7B, about 35% of revenue, and free cash flow fell 15% to $46.1B. But Meta did this exact thing in 2022, when a capex surge dropped free cash flow to $19B and the stock under $90 before it ran to $790. A discounted-cash-flow model (valuing the stock on future cash discounted back to today) says Meta is worth $659 if the buildout is temporary and $160 if 35% capex is permanent. That gap is the whole debate in one number.
  • The compute-glut story got refuted by the people building it. On the Market list, Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said a model in training, codenamed Watermelon, is already matching GPT-5.5 on an order of magnitude more compute than its predecessor. SemiAnalysis went further and said Meta's data-center spend will accelerate and 2027 capex will be "shockingly high." Bill Ackman called the stock "very cheap." That is the opposite of a company that thinks it overbuilt.
  • Nvidia quietly changed how it gets paid. Nvidia rolled out a revenue-share and credit-support model for the neoclouds (the rent-a-GPU firms like CoreWeave). Instead of a one-time chip sale, Nvidia now takes a cut of the cloud revenue on that capacity. That turns a boom-bust hardware sale into a recurring stream, and it is a direct tailwind for $CRWV, $NBIS, and $IREN, all of which got flushed 12% to 17% yesterday on the Meta scare. $IREN alone is sitting on a $9.7B Microsoft contract and a $3.4B Nvidia one.

The honest close is that both mornings can be true. The bears are right that the trade is levered and crowded. The bulls are right that the buyers keep buying. When a name like $IREN gets sold 17% on a narrative that its biggest customers just contradicted, that is where the dip-buyers live.

3. Tom Lee raised his target to 8,000 and told you to expect a scary autumn first. Fundstrat's Tom Lee lifted his year-end S&P 500 target from 7,700 to 8,000, built on 2027 earnings of $400 times a 20x multiple. His real point is that the market is cheaper now than in January despite being up 9%, because earnings estimates rose faster than price (the forward multiple actually fell from 19.4 to 18.4). The S&P sits near 7,300, so 8,000 is another 10%.

The catch is he expects a "very severe correction" in the fall before that, and he named the triggers. New Fed chair Kevin Warsh is tearing up forward guidance (the Fed's practice of telegraphing its next move), which leaves the market without its usual script. The SpaceX share unlock this fall dumps a wall of new supply onto a stock with only a $90B float. Iran and the Strait of Hormuz keep an oil-shock tail alive. And margin debt (money investors borrow against their portfolios to buy more) is up 55% year over year, the fifth-largest jump in about seventy years, which historically front-runs a drawdown. Take the bull target, but keep some dry powder for the air pocket he is describing.

4. Bitcoin's bottom-callers got louder, and the ETF money kept ignoring them. The chart crowd piled in today. An on-chain "dorito" indicator that last flashed at the FTX bottom lit up again on the inbox tape, the monthly RSI (a momentum gauge, now its most oversold reading ever) is stretched, and Lark Davis notes 270,000 BTC were accumulated near $59K, the single largest accumulation event on record. Standard Chartered is still carrying a $500K long-term BTC target and $40K on ETH.

Against all that, the flows say wait. Bitcoin ETFs have bled for weeks, with BlackRock's fund alone posting ten straight days of outflows totaling $2.24B, and over $11B has left the ETF complex since the peak. The cleanest floor framework came from Charles Schwab, which prices Bitcoin off miner economics: the cheapest, best-run miners produce a coin near $60K, and that production cost has marked the bottom in past bear markets.

Benjamin Cowen is the patient-bear counterweight worth holding in mind, with total crypto market cap near $2.125T and a call for a lower low later this year before the real move into 2027. My read is unchanged from this morning. Accumulate the dips you already wanted, respect the $60K miner floor as your line, and let the ETF flows turn green before you believe the bounce.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $LLY, the AI trade nobody files under AI. Per Milk Road, Eli Lilly is a $1T+ name up 2x in a year, throwing off free cash flow that grew over 100% to about $10B, now pouring it into a $5B data center, a drug-discovery tie-up with Google's Isomorphic Labs, and a direct-to-consumer channel with over a million customers. The thesis is a rotation from AI infrastructure to AI application, and healthcare is the first place that spend actually earns its keep. Even Dario Amodei said he would put his AI-in-biology money here.
  • The neocloud dip: $IREN, $CRWV, $NBIS. Yesterday's 12% to 17% flush ran on a Meta narrative that Meta itself contradicted today. Nvidia's new revenue-share model rewards exactly these names. High-beta and not for the faint of heart, but this is the cleanest oversold setup on the board into Monday.
  • $OKLO, the nuclear-power leg of the AI trade. From two Rick Orford shorts: Oklo signed a fuel letter of intent with Centrus Energy for domestic enriched uranium to feed up to five Aurora powerhouses, with deliveries from 2029. It is a pre-revenue $10B name, so size it as a long-dated option you can afford to lose.
  • $QBTS, the government-blessed quantum bet. D-Wave landed a $100M letter of intent under the CHIPS Act, with the Commerce Department taking stock. It trades at 377x sales, a pure belief stock, but the government validation is real. Analysts carry a strong-buy with targets implying it could double. Satellite-sized position only.
  • Optical, the flush that may be a setup: $LITE, $COHR. Chip Stock Investor flags that Nvidia put $2B each into Lumentum and Coherent. The wrinkle worth knowing: the same research shop that wrote the optical sector down 40% to 60% in June then launched an ETF to buy those exact names. When the bear turns buyer, watch for the V.

Filtered / Cross-Routed. The Standard Chartered $66K-to-$500K BTC and $1,700-to-$40K ETH targets folded into the Bitcoin section. Trader Mayne's meme-coin clip carried one useful stat (under 1% of Pump.fun wallets cleared $10K in profit) and no tradeable name, so it stays a caution, not a pick. The AMD "can it hit $1T" reddit thread was retail sentiment with no fresh catalyst, so $AMD stays on radar off its $584.73 high. The stablecoin distribution war (140 firms backing Open USD against Circle's $CRCL) is a real crypto-structure story but moved slow today, so it sits here as a flag into next week.

The Fable 5 model news, the Etched inference chip, and the Anthropic-profitability report went to AI & Tools. The Hormuz oil tail and the quiet labor-market crack went to News. Trump ringing the NYSE bell next week is noise until it prints.

item.title: [Investing] Michael Burry is short Micron, and the whole AI-capex trade wobbled overnight
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The memory bull wall now has a famous bear leaning on it, three separate voices called the AI buildout a bubble, and Bitcoin's bounce is being sold by whales while the chartists call a bottom.
item.content:encoded:
The memory bull wall now has a famous bear leaning on it, three separate voices called the AI buildout a bubble, and Bitcoin's bounce is being sold by whales while the chartists call a bottom.

Markets are closed today for the holiday, which gives you a full session to think instead of react. Use it, because two things shifted overnight. A brand-name bear stepped in front of the memory trade, and the AI-capex bull case took its first coordinated punches.

Closed today, and what to watch Monday. US cash equity and options markets are shut today, Friday July 3, for Independence Day (observed, since the Fourth is Saturday), and reopen Monday July 6. So there is no session to react to. What is worth pre-loading for the reopen: whether the semis that got flushed Thursday ($MU, $SNDK, $MRVL) find a bid or keep sliding, whether Bitcoin holds the $62K bounce or rolls over toward the mid-$50Ks, and the calendar into next week. $SPCX joins the Nasdaq-100 on July 7, which forces index funds to buy it, and the market expects GPT-5.6 as soon as Tuesday, which would land straight into the AI-bubble argument below.

1. Michael Burry is short Micron, and that reframes the whole memory fight. The biggest new thing overnight is that Michael Burry opened a bearish $MU position, flagged across the Stocks list and four others. He is leaning directly on the most crowded bull wall on the board. The bull case is genuinely strong: Q3 revenue was $41.46B, up 346% year over year and a beat, gross margin ran 84.9%, the Q4 guide is $50B in revenue and $31 EPS, and the stock trades near 6x forward earnings against a CEO target of $4,000.

The bear case is now a person rather than a chart, and it comes with a real risk attached, that $AAPL is exploring Chinese memory suppliers and SK Hynix is pulling price caps off its long-term contracts. My read: I still think the durable shortage story wins over a multi-year horizon, but Burry short into a $1,000 breakdown is exactly the kind of thing that keeps you from sizing up early. Watch how $MU trades on the Monday reopen and let the $4,000 target wait.

2. The flush was a momentum unwind, not a market break. This is the framing that matters for how you play the reopen. Thursday's damage was concentrated and brutal in one place: $AEHR fell 18.3%, $AAOI 17.1%, $SNDK 14.8%, $TER 13.8%, $MRVL 11.2%, and $NBIS ran 30% from its peak. Meanwhile the $SPX finished down just 0.13% and the Dow actually printed a record high, with the $VIX (the market's fear gauge) closing at its lowest in a month and recession odds collapsing from 32% toward 12%. That is high-beta AI names getting sold while the broad market shrugs. Call it rotation rather than a risk-off break. The tell to respect is that it happened into a three-day weekend, when traders cut the risk they do not want to hold blind.

3. The AI-capex bull case took three separate punches overnight. Yesterday the doubt was one bear (Ed Zitron). Overnight it became a chorus, and that convergence is the actual signal.

  • Meta stopped pretending. On Prof G, the read on Meta launching a business to sell its "excess" AI compute is blunt, that the second or third largest compute buyer on earth is walking away from building its own AI products. Zuckerberg's own May line is the receipt: he would not sell "because we think we have a use for the compute, but obviously if we get to a point where we feel that we have overbuilt, then that is an option." In a town hall he added that agent development has not accelerated the way he expected and the stock "would be higher" without the AI spend.
  • China is the mechanism that could crack it. Capital Flows made the sharpest macro case: roughly half the S&P 500 is now an AI trade funded on borrowed money, and the risk is not who wins, it is that the price of intelligence falls faster than the most crowded trade in history can adjust. China runs the Amazon playbook, models one generation behind priced 10x to 100x cheaper and state-subsidized so they never need the API margins US labs depend on. When the US suspended its top model on June 12, a Chinese lab open-sourced a near-frontier rival the next day. The template is DeepSeek in January 2025, which erased $589B from $NVDA in a single day.
  • The unit economics are leaking. Zitron, quoted at length via threadguy, pegs OpenAI's 2025 cash burn at $20.9B with costs that scale linearly with revenue, and notes the IPO reportedly slipped to 2027 after it could not clear a $1T valuation. Nvidia's revenue-share model, confirmed by Bloomberg, hands token credits to AI startups for a cut of future sales. That is vendor financing dressed as demand. And the physical backlash is showing up, with Blackstone abandoning a Virginia data center and 20 Florida counties weighing data-center moratoriums.

The counter is real and I hold it partly: OpenAI delaying an IPO from a position of private funding is optionality, not panic, and none of these bears has been right on timing. But when Meta, a China cost-curve, and OpenAI's own burn rate all point the same way in one night, you respect it by trimming the most levered AI-beta names, not by flipping short.

4. Bitcoin's bottom-callers are buying what the whales are selling. The chart signals are genuinely bullish. On the Crypto list, long-term-holder SOPR (a metric that reads above 1 when holders sell at a profit and below when they sell at a loss) printed 0.615, meaning long-term holders are capitulating at a 38.5% average loss, a sub-0.65 reading seen only at the March 2020, October 2022, and July 2023 bottoms. $IBIT put in its first-ever weekly tweezer bottom and one entity absorbed 270,000 BTC at $59K.

Against that, the whales are handing it to them: an Irish dealer wallet sent 500 BTC to Coinbase Prime with 4,500 ($276M) left to go, a Tim Draper-linked wallet moved 1,000 BTC, and Novogratz keeps saying Bitcoin "lost its sponsorship." Kalshi still prices only 15% odds of $100K this year. Benjamin Cowen is the patient bear worth hearing: total crypto market cap sits near $2.125T, below its 2021 level, and he thinks the whole class stays under its fair-value trend line all year, with a summer counter-rally, a lower low later in 2026, and the real bull into 2027 and 2028. My read: accumulate the dips you were already going to buy, but the flows say the bottom is a process, not this week.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • The on-site power thesis has a small-cap leg now. Yesterday's names ($BE, $CEG, $TLN, $VST) were the blue-chip version. The small-cap version, driven by 3-to-5-year lead times on high-voltage transformers, adds $CGEH (microturbines with an 800-volt "Microgrids 4 AI" product aimed at server racks) and $FCEL (megawatt fuel cells, a 4-gigawatt-plus pipeline), with $POWL, $MOD, and $NVT flagged to research. Size these as high-risk satellites, because fuel-cell and microturbine small caps have a long history of burning cash and diluting holders.
  • $AVAV, the drone super-cycle name. From the People list: AeroVironment printed roughly $642M in fiscal Q4 revenue, a backlog up 65% to $1.2B, and a $500M Defense Department award, with $KTOS getting a JPMorgan upgrade alongside it. Defense-tech is the non-AI momentum pocket that kept working while semis flushed.
  • $TSLA, a defined swing setup into next week. Per Stocks with Josh, Tesla flushed 11% to 12% on its record 480,000-plus Q2 delivery beat, a classic sell-the-good-news move, rejecting $425 resistance and finding support near $381.68 with a $369 pivot below that. His stat: 85% odds of trading above the intraday low within 30 days, 95% within 60. Cathie Wood bought about $40M of it into the drop. A trade with clear invalidation, not a conviction hold.
  • $MRNA, the biotech that quietly went vertical. Fresh two-year high, up about 160% year to date, now the eighth-best performer in the S&P 500. When a beaten-down name reclaims a multi-year base while the hot trade unwinds, it earns a look.

Filtered / Cross-Routed. Trader Mayne's Bitcoin-bottom video and the Market Bubble podcast with Ansem both shipped without transcripts, so there are no levels to pull. Lark Davis's "escape being broke" clip was a generic wealth-mindset piece with no specific calls. The three one-minute threadguy livestream clips (a company "cheat code," Ansem's Solana memecoin, a poker resurgence) carried no tradeable names. The $NXPI post-quantum-crypto thesis is a real secular angle but came from a promotional Substack with no numbers, so it stays on radar, not the watchlist. Trump walking back the OpenAI stake went to News. The Fable 5 usage backlash and the model-release cadence went to AI & Tools.

item.title: [Investing] The crowded memory buy got run over, and $MU closed under $1,000
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Every desk was buying the dip this morning. The tape spent the afternoon proving them early, semis puked to open Q3, and a soft jobs print pulled the Fed hike off the table.
item.content:encoded:
Every desk was buying the dip this morning. The tape spent the afternoon proving them early, semis puked to open Q3, and a soft jobs print pulled the Fed hike off the table.

This morning every desk was buying the memory dip. The afternoon made them look early. The crowding I flagged at the open is exactly why it stung, and it is still the trade to watch, just not at the price the morning wanted.

Where the session landed. Semiconductors led everything lower to start the quarter. The $SOX (the Philadelphia semiconductor index) fell about 4% on top of yesterday's 6% gash, down roughly 10% in the first day and a half of a quarter that just closed its best three months ever. $MU broke $1,000 and stayed under it, a second straight close below the 21-day moving average (the short-term trend line) it lost yesterday, with chart desks now marking 952, 934, 921, and 909 as the shelves below.

The rest of the tape held up better than the chip complex. The Nasdaq and S&P finished red on the chip drag, the Dow was roughly flat, and $AAPL ripped about 4% to the low $300s as money parked somewhere it trusted. The $VIX slipped to a two-week low near 15.87. Nobody was paying up for protection. Crude stayed soft on Iran-talks headlines, the 10-year yield ticked up after Warsh repeated that inflation is still too high, and $BTC clawed back above $62K into the close. Cash markets are closed tomorrow, Friday July 3, for Independence Day and reopen Monday.

The June jobs report, pulled forward ahead of the holiday, is the pin under all of it. Payrolls came in at +57,000 against expectations near 115,000, a clean miss, while the unemployment rate actually fell to 4.2% from 4.3% for the wrong reason, a shrinking labor force rather than more hiring. The market read it as soft but not breaking and did the obvious thing, it pulled the rate-hike risk off the table. Odds of a hike at the July 29 meeting collapsed from around 32% a week ago to under 18%, and a hold now prices above 82%. The regime here is hike-versus-hold under a hawkish Warsh Fed, not the cut-versus-hold everyone traded last year.

1. The memory thesis is durable, but the morning's "smash buy" was a day early. The fundamental case actually got stronger today. On the Stocks list, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said Micron is meeting only 50% to two-thirds of demand, that the shortage runs well beyond 2026 with no new supply until 2028, and that the take-or-pay book (contracts where the customer pays whether or not it takes the chips) is now 16 agreements, with $GM freshly added and 14 of them carrying a $100B minimum revenue floor. He is putting $200B into a US buildout.

None of that broke. The price did. $MU lost the $1,000 line the morning crowd called a floor, kept falling through the level, and dragged $SNDK, $TSM, $AMD, $MRVL, and the rest of the complex with it. My read is unchanged from the open except on timing. Build it slowly, because the tape just told you the buyers were early. Let it base and use a reclaim of $1,000 as your signal instead of catching the knife.

2. Nvidia's new backstop is the reason the neocloud dip got bought. The fresh structural story today, and it was not in this morning's edition, is a revenue-share model where $NVDA rents the unused capacity of the neoclouds (the pure-play AI compute landlords like CoreWeave) and takes a cut of the cloud revenue. The street's line, and it fits, is that Nvidia now sells the shovels, guarantees the loan, and clips the gold on the way out. That flipped the morning's fear into the afternoon's buy: $CRWV, $NBIS, $IREN, and $APLD sold off on $META dumping "excess" compute, then got bought hard by desks treating the selloff as an overreaction.

The bear case is still live, and it is not small. Ed Zitron argued on Prof G that roughly 80% of AI compute is used by just OpenAI and Anthropic, that over 100GW is under construction against maybe 6GW of real demand, and that OpenAI just delayed its IPO after failing to get a $1T mark. But the hard datapoint cut the other way today: AWS raised its reserved GPU rates about 20% on July 1, pushing an H100 from $4.33 to $5.19 an hour, a hyperscaler repricing compute up into the Blackwell ramp.

3. $TSLA beat big and still got sold. Q2 deliveries came in at 480,126, the best second quarter ever and the fourth-best quarter in company history, crushing the roughly 406,000 consensus and even topping Troy Teslike's aggressive 466,000, with 13.5 GWh of storage on top. The stock fell anyway, sliding 2% to 6% intraday, losing its 200-day moving average and pressing toward $400. That is a textbook buy-the-rumor unwind after the number everyone pre-positioned into finally printed. Gene Munster's framing is the one I lean toward: the EV winter that started in early 2024 is ending, and $RIVN raising full-year guidance to 65,000 to 70,000 units backs that up. Own the read, respect the $400 level.

4. Bitcoin bounced to $62K, but the flows never turned. The bottom-callers got loud on the Crypto list, with Bitwise's Matt Hougan "nearing the bottom" and Cantor calling the bear "in its final stretch." Lark Davis stacked the cleaner bull case: Bitcoin has never printed two red years in a row, and the weekly RSI just made a bullish divergence (price at a lower low while momentum makes a higher low, the 2022-bottom setup) pointing at the mid-$70Ks. Against that, the flows are ugly and getting uglier. James Seyffart laid out the damage on Milk Road.

  • Spot Bitcoin ETFs have bled more than $11B off the peak and the pace is accelerating, including a $700M single-day outflow on June 25.
  • Ethereum's ETFs are down to $10.5B, about a third of their flows gone.
  • Three alt products are still taking in cash while everything else bleeds: the $SOL and XRP ETFs (over $1.6B each) and the new $HYPE funds ($192M). That is where the relative strength lives.

On $MSTR, Trader Mayne put the hole at roughly negative $14B and framed Saylor's only real play as survive the bear, then unwind above his cost basis. My read: this is a tradeable bounce inside a bear. Until the ETF bleed stops I treat $56K as the accumulation zone and $44K as the deeper add, and I keep the size honest.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $ZIM, a clean merger arb. The WSB desk laid out the Hapag-Lloyd cash deal at $35.00 a share against a roughly $25 price, about 40% upside, with a second bid at $37.50 already surfacing. The spread is wide because Israel holds a "golden share" approval (a state veto right over the deal), but the precedent there is to negotiate rather than block. Downside if the deal breaks is around $19 to $20, so the risk is defined going in.
  • Energy is the AI bottleneck, and the power names are how you play it. The on-site generation thesis names the tier with revenue today: $BE (fuel cells at data centers now), $CEG (restarting Three Mile Island on an 835 MW deal with Microsoft), $TLN (a 1,920 MW Amazon contract through 2042), and $VST. The SMR pure-plays (small modular reactors, factory-built nuclear) like $OKLO and $SMR are the satellite bet, and $OKLO's 1.2 GW Ohio deal for Meta's data centers is the one to anchor on. On the battery leg, CATL (3750.HK) grew grid storage 120% last quarter and targets storage at half of sales by 2030 on $40B of net cash.
  • $ASML, the chokepoint nobody can route around. Rick Orford walked the case: 100% share of commercial EUV lithography (the machines that pattern every 2nm and 3nm chip), a genuine toll road under the whole industry, up about 130% on the year. The catch is the price, roughly 39x earnings with analyst targets implying only 3% to 33% upside, so I wait for the pullback rather than pay 39x today.
  • $INTC got a real upgrade. HSBC doubled its price target to $200 from $100. In a session where the rest of semis got sold, a doubling from a major desk on the most-doubted name in the group earns a slot on the watchlist.
  • The second-order AI winners, $UBER and $NU. Milk Road made the picks-and-shovels-on-the-demand-side case: platforms the market fears AI will disrupt actually get stronger as AI cuts their cost to serve. Uber is the top pick at 6.1% of the book (202M monthly users, $5.6B operating income, autonomous rides live in eight cities heading for 15-plus), Nubank second at 4.3% ($13.30 monthly revenue per customer against under $1 cost to serve). Waymo self-aggregating demand is the risk to Uber.
  • $RBRK, the cyber laggard with a reason. Chip Stock Investor flagged Rubrik near $70, down about 20%, the one security name that has not recovered like $CRWD did, because AI spend is compressing its margins even as subscription revenue grows near 30%. A reverse DCF (pricing the stock backwards to see what growth it implies) now shows a bar roughly half what it was, which the analyst calls doable but no longer a steal. I want a quarter of stable margins before touching it.

Filtered / Cross-Routed.

  • Context, not news: the $MU-to-$4,000 tweet and the take-or-pay durability story were this morning's material.
  • Dropped: Arbitrage Andy's July picks and cuts, paywalled, no tickers in the free note.
  • Dropped: Joseph Hogue's "60X stock," the threadguy stream, and the Swan Bitcoin show, none shipped a transcript, no names to pull.
  • Dropped: the sector-rotation tweet ($UNH, $HIMS, $OSCR, $LLY, $JNJ, $VRTX), its promised 25-stock bio list exists only as an image, unverifiable.
  • Dropped: the "enablers versus beneficiaries" thread ($ZETA, $RDDT, $NOW, $SOFI, $TEAM), thin and promotional.
  • Dropped: the IBM and quantum shorts, one-minute clips whose only hard fact was $IBM near 47x earnings on quantum dreams.
  • Dropped: Stocks with Josh's $SPCX top call ($176 rejected, no buy under $161), levels but no setup.
  • Noted: Packy McCormick's America's Next 250 deepens the energy thesis above but its names (General Matter, Radiant) are private.
  • Noise: the options-strategy course, the gray-hair longevity segment, the gambling ramble.
  • Cross-routed: Karp's argument, the Fable 5 relaunch, and the Anthropic-Samsung chip to AI & Tools. The SCOTUS spending ruling, Trump's income disclosure, and the AI-driven layoff data to News.

item.title: [Investing] Micron got flushed, and for once every desk is buying the same dip
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The memory pullback is being bought hard, Bitcoin is bleeding under $60K, and Strategy just traded below its own stack for the first time ever.
item.content:encoded:
The memory pullback is being bought hard, Bitcoin is bleeding under $60K, and Strategy just traded below its own stack for the first time ever.

Yesterday was the flush. This morning is the argument about what it meant, and the loudest voices have already answered it: they bought.

Into the open. Cash markets are open today and closed tomorrow, Friday July 3, for Independence Day, so today is a pre-holiday session with thin afternoon liquidity. Two real catalysts land in that shortened window. The June jobs report was pulled forward to today ahead of the holiday, so the number hits a market already jumpy about whether the Fed hikes at all this year. And Tesla ($TSLA) reports Q2 deliveries, where the estimate gap is enormous: the Street sits near 406k against Troy Teslike at 466k, and $425 is the level that matters. Watch whether $MU reclaims its 21-day moving average (the short-term trend line it just lost) and whether the $SOX (the Philadelphia semis index) steadies after yesterday's 6%-plus gash. Watch $BTC and the $60K line. Oil stayed soft with WTI near $68. Size for a holiday tape, not a trend day.

1. The memory dip is the most crowded buy on the board. This is the one to lead with, and not because I am sure it is right. It is because I have rarely seen this many independent desks pile onto one trade at the same moment. Crowding like that either front-runs a real move or marks the top, and here I lean front-run. Here is why.

After the semis got taken to the woodshed yesterday, the Stocks list lit up. Marcos Milla called $MU "under $1,000 equals smash buy" while warning leverage could still shake out 30% in three days. Milk Road Macro is adding with a "$MU to $4,000" target. Melvin booked a 144% gain and is staying long. $MU closed below its 21-day moving average for the first time since April, which the chartists read as a reset, not a breakdown.

The fundamental spine is the strongest part of the argument. In the inbox, Markos laid out the HBM (high-bandwidth memory, the fast memory stacked right next to the GPU) math that matters. Efficiency gains are running around 5% a year and decelerating, so you would need a 25% jump on top of the 30% already priced to flip 2027-28 into oversupply. Cheaper memory tiers add capacity but cannot replace HBM, because the data a model is actively using has to sit next to the chip for speed. His keeper line: no GPU generation has ever shipped with less memory per system, 80GB to 288GB and climbing. That is Jevons paradox in silicon.

CEO Sanjay Mehrotra is selling the same durability story with receipts: 16 take-or-pay agreements (the customer pays whether or not it takes the chips) running 2026 to 2030, 14 of them carrying a $100B cumulative revenue minimum against $22B in customer cash deposits. Even the Reddit desk reads the pullback as healthy consolidation after names ran two to three times, not a cycle peak.

Here is the tell that makes me take it seriously rather than fade it. Kobeissi flagged that retail is now just 6% of Mag 7 volume, a four-year low and down 79% from the April 2025 peak, with the money rotating out of the megacaps and straight into semiconductors. That is not a froth signal, that is a rotation. My read: the dip is buyable, but the crowding is real, so scale in and keep the 21-day reclaim as your confirmation rather than chasing the first green candle.

2. Marvell is the "next bottleneck" everyone is pre-positioning into. Milk Road's follow-on to the memory trade is $MRVL, and the thesis is clean: the bottleneck arc runs compute to memory to connectivity, and Marvell owns the connectivity leg. The CXL memory-fabric market goes from $1.3B to $7-10B by 2030, Marvell bought XConn for $540M to lead it, and management guides CXL revenue to $1B in FY27 and $2B in FY28. Custom silicon is the bigger number: 18 programs, 12 of them at top-four hyperscalers, an FY27 guide of $11.5B up 40%, and a path to $10B-plus by FY29. The risk is not the story, it is the price and the concentration, Amazon is 30-40% of revenue and $AVGO is coming for the same sockets. This is a position-builder's name, not a chase.

3. Bitcoin is risk capital squared, and the AI vacuum is the reason. $BTC is grinding lower, closed below its monthly 50 and weekly 200, and keeps refusing to hold $60K. The datapoint that stops you cold is on the Crypto list: Strategy ($MSTR) just traded below the value of its own Bitcoin for the first time ever. Michael Saylor holds more than 800,000 BTC and the stock is down about 80%, and he is out talking his book with a coherent story, that the "AI black hole" pulled $10-20B out of crypto and $500B into the AI IPO complex, that Bitcoin's dominance (its share of the total crypto market cap) is back near 70% from 41% in 2021, and that Bitcoin is now undervalued. The bears do not disagree on the mechanism, they just are not waiting around: Novogratz says crypto "lost its sponsorship," and David Hoffman sold his $ETH as Ethereum's smart-contract dominance fell from over 90% to 60%. Levels: $60K is the line, a final flush to $50-55K is on the table, and you do not get a confirmed bottom until a higher high above $67K and a reclaim of the 200-day. Stocks with Josh is buying that fear with a weekly death cross (the 50-week average slipping under the 200-week, classically bearish) as his signal, a $56K target zone and a deeper add near $44K. The one alt with a real bid is $SOL, where Ignas (the SIMD-547 base-fee burn turning it deflationary), andyyy, and Nebraskangooner independently called a bottom. If Bitcoin pukes again, Solana goes with it. Own it for the upside, not the protection.

4. The macro regime quietly changed, and almost nobody is pricing it. The sharpest macro take of the morning came from Eric Wallerstein: the Warsh Fed kills "kangaroo macro," the print-to-print obsession where every data release is a trade. Warsh pledged 2% inflation eight times in one press conference and bond yields fell, and the new game is cycles and trends over reacting to a single jobs number, especially with post-Covid data reliability degraded. That reframes today's jobs report as noise inside a trend, not a verdict. The risk-off tells are still worth respecting: Kalshi prices a 50% chance of a Fed rate hike this year, and Bank of America's peak-indicator model has 7 of 10 triggered. Watch funding and liquidity conditions as the accelerant, not the headline number.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $IREN, a two-sided setup, name both sides. The governance red flag first: the markets desk flagged the Roberts co-CEOs granted 18.2M RSUs combined, roughly $400M and 5.09% dilution, with the performance hurdles removed, against a share count that went from 100M to 357M and a $6B ATM (an at-the-market program that keeps selling new shares into the open market). That is the kind of thing that caps a multiple. The other side, from Chris: the 4-hour RSI is the most oversold in a year, and the prior two times it got here the stock rallied roughly 90% and then 130%, with price now backtesting broken downtrend resistance as support. A trade, not a marriage.
  • $PLTR, the anti-frontier-lab bet. Palantir was up around 7.5% expanding its Nvidia partnership for US-government AI systems. Alex Karp's pitch, quoted at length on the Financial Markets list, is that enterprises "pay for tokens that create no value" and are training their own replacements by running confidential data through frontier models, so the winners are the ones who let you own your compute, weights, and alpha. Whatever you think of Karp, that narrative is a real tailwind for the on-prem, data-sovereignty names.
  • $META, treat the "compute pivot" with suspicion. The bullish frame is Meta selling excess AI capacity like a neocloud. The skeptical read, which I lean toward, is that Google throttled Meta's Gemini compute, Meta is burning around $261M a month and just locked $40B across $NBIS, $CRWV, and Cursor, so "excess to sell" and "compute-constrained" cannot both be true. Reconcile the CoreWeave-scale contracts before you trust the story.

Filtered / Cross-Routed. Yesterday's session recap (the semis flush, Meta's pop, the neocloud drop) was last night's story, so it is context here, not news. The All-In clip on SpaceX's valuation named no fund manager and no hard numbers, so there is nothing to trade in it. The quantum executive order is real but the loudest video on it named zero tickers, so it sits in News until someone attaches names. BowTied Bull's update is paywalled with no extractable specifics. Karp's full argument and the AI-access tightening are cross-routed to AI & Tools. The Senate-control shift and the Fed-personnel angle went to News.

item.title: [Investing] The memory trade cracked and Meta became a cloud company in one afternoon
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Chips got dumped while $META ripped 11% on a compute pivot, and Bitcoin printed a fresh low under $58K right on Ben Cowen's 2018 script.
item.content:encoded:
Chips got dumped while $META ripped 11% on a compute pivot, and Bitcoin printed a fresh low under $58K right on Ben Cowen's 2018 script.

Today was the rotation, live on the tape. If you have been waiting to see what "the leaders get caught offside" actually looks like, you just watched it happen in real time.

The close. Chips got taken to the woodshed while everything else held up. The semis led the drop, with the $SOX (the Philadelphia semiconductor index) off as much as 6.7% intraday:

  • Chip decliners: $MU down 6.7%, $ARM off 4.6%, $INTC down 4%, $AMD down 3.5%, $TSM off 3.4%, and even $NVDA down 2.3%.
  • The other side of the boat: mega-caps went green into the bell, $MSFT, $AAPL, $TSLA, $AMZN, and $GOOGL all near highs of day, and software ($IGV) up 4%.

Charlie Bilello's stat of the day: semis are up 237% in fourteen months, which now exceeds the dot-com-peak surge.

Under the tape it was a disinflation print. ISM Manufacturing landed at 53.3 (below the 54.0 expected but a sixth straight month of expansion), and prices-paid collapsed from 82.1 to 73.0, the biggest four-month drop in four years. ADP private payrolls came in soft at 98k against 118k expected. WTI crude slid under $68.50, a four-month low, with the entire Iran-war premium now gone.

Heads up on the calendar: US markets are closed Friday July 3 for Independence Day, so the real catalyst is Thursday's jobs report, pulled forward a day.

1. The memory air pocket showed up. For weeks the loudest trade in this book has been memory, and today it finally coughed. $MU gave back 6.7% on a day the whole complex bled. Do not confuse a shakeout with a top. The bull case is still intact and it is a good one: on Prof G Markets, Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon put roughly 70% of the semis rally down to actual earnings growth, not multiple expansion, and laid out why memory is the real bottleneck. HBM (high-bandwidth memory, the stacked chips that feed AI accelerators) eats four times the wafer capacity of standard DDR5, so adding wafers does not add bits, and clean-room shortage caps supply into 2027 and beyond. His read is the upcycle has duration and the "air pocket" is a 2028 problem, not a this-year problem. Milk Road Macro reminded everyone how far this has run: $MU +150%, Nebius $NBIS +124%, Hyperliquid $HYPE +114%, Bloom Energy $BE +110%, SK Square $SKSQ +63% over the stretch. When a trade is up like that and everyone can recite the thesis, days like today are the tax you pay. I am watching $MU into the high-70s gross-margin story, not selling the shakeout.

2. Meta became a cloud company, or the market decided it did. The single biggest move today was $META up 10 to 11% on "Meta Compute," reporting that it will sell its excess AI capacity AWS-Bedrock style and rent raw compute like a neocloud. Jim Cramer slapped a "$100 a share" on it. The bull frame is a capex-to-revenue bridge on a name trading around 9x earnings near a two-and-a-half-year low versus the $SPX. Here is the tell I would not ignore, flagged across the Financial Markets list by Jeff Pu and others: Meta just signed a $21B CoreWeave deal and Google is throttling Gemini compute, which makes Meta look compute-constrained, not oversupplied. So which is it, excess capacity to sell or a shortage to cover? You cannot be both. The neoclouds voted on the read: $CRWV fell 9.7 to 12% and $NBIS dropped 13% on the same headline. On the Market list, Amit Kukreja bought that $NBIS dip at $232.49 and called it an overreaction, noting AWS just raised GPU rents 20%. Reddit had the same instinct earlier, framing it as Zuck choosing violence against the neoclouds. My take: the pop is real, the "$100" is a meme, and the CoreWeave contract is the fact that has to be reconciled before I trust the excess-capacity story.

3. Bitcoin printed the low, right on schedule. $BTC made a fresh cycle low near $57,700 today, and two independent chartists I track called the same thing without talking to each other. Benjamin Cowen says 2026 is tracking 2018 almost tick for tick, the June 2018 low was $5,743 and today we tapped ~$5,770-scaled at $57.7K, hence his "simulation confirmed." His plan is unglamorous: ignore Bitcoin in the first half of a midterm year, DCA through the second half, and assume the bottom lands somewhere between $30K and $60K. Crypto Currently is looking at the same chart from the bull side: price is below the 200-week moving average (a once-every-four-years event), and for the first time since the 2022 bottom the weekly RSI printed a bullish divergence (lower low in price, higher low in momentum). Realized price (the average price at which every coin last moved, a proxy for the network's aggregate cost basis) sits at $53,500, and Tether ($USDT) just flipped Ethereum ($ETH) by market cap for the first time ever, which is the kind of thing that happens at washouts. The flows back the fear: Degen Sensei notes US spot BTC ETFs just booked a record $4.5B of June outflows, the worst month on record. Kalshi has only 12% odds Bitcoin hits $100K this year (an all-time low) and 70% odds it trades below $50K. Both creators are DCA-buying under $60K and neither is going all in. I am doing the same. This looks like an oversold bounce setup, not a confirmed trend reversal. Watch for a weekly higher low to confirm a July relief rally into the 200-day, and watch ETF outflows flipping positive as the real bottom signal.

4. Solana is the relative-strength name in crypto. If you want the coin that is acting best, it is $SOL, holding around $77 to $79 while Bitcoin makes new lows. Lark Davis gives the actionable level: a daily close at or above $76 opens a run at $97, roughly 28%. Two well-known traders (Psycho, who publicly bought the $15 Solana bottom last cycle, and OSF) are both accumulating spot here and calling it a "lock in now" zone. Just respect that if Bitcoin pukes again, Solana rolls over with it, so you are buying leveraged beta on a Bitcoin bounce here.

5. Tomorrow is a Tesla day. $TSLA reports Q2 deliveries pre-market Thursday July 2, and the gap between estimates is enormous: the Street is around 406k, Troy Teslike is at 466k. The stock is up 16% since Friday and pinned near $400, which happens to be the level where Michael Burry's short sits on the wrong side. Reclaim it cleanly and the momentum crowd targets $440 then $520. This is a binary, so size it like one. The read-through worth noting: $GM's US EV sales fell 41% year over year in Q2, so the EV pie is not the story, Tesla's own number is.

Single names worth your watchlist. A few high-conviction ideas landed today that fit a position-builder better than the day's noise:

  • The BEDS trade ($GEO + $CXW). The detention-bed thesis is the cleanest catalyst setup I saw. Federal agencies need roughly ten turnkey facilities, GEO Group and CoreCivic each sit on 20,000-plus idle beds, and both trade at $3 to $4B caps against a $70B funding backdrop. $CXW around $30.50 and $GEO around $29.50, both already up 30 to 45% since June. Benchmark puts 80% odds on a two-facility sale with price targets to $36, Northland sees $40 on both. Both just beat on EPS and raised guidance. Call-to-put volume is running 30-to-1. Risk is a policy-shutdown headline, which knocked them 20% earlier this year.
  • BlackBerry ($BB). The least-covered name with the strongest fundamental turn. QNX is the safety-certified OS in 275 million-plus vehicles and the foundation under NVIDIA's DRIVE and Thor platforms. Revenue up 26%, adjusted EBITDA up 144%, and the first positive operating cash flow in a first quarter in nine years. A real physical-AI edge-OS play, not a meme.
  • Figure ($FIGR) and Ouster ($OUST). Two fresh IPOs riding structural themes. $FIGR is Mike Cagney's blockchain-native lending marketplace, 55% EBITDA margins, HELOC origination costs of ~$800 versus an ~$10K industry average, ran from $40 to $78 on preliminary results. $OUST is a digital-lidar and perception platform for physical AI, Q1 revenue ~$49M up 49%, $175M cash and no debt, around $42 with a 12-month base case of $60 to $75. Both are swing-to-position candidates, not day trades.
  • The beaten-down mega-cap dip-buys. Invest with Henry is buying $SOFI under $18 (net income +134% year over year), $PLTR around $100 (half off its peak), $NVDA around $200 (target $300), and $MSFT at $373 (down 17% in a month). Fade the affiliate pitch, keep the names on the list.
  • Real-cash-flow crypto. With momentum bleeding, Milk Road is paying up for revenue: Galaxy Digital ($GLXY), whose "Helios" site is a 1.6 GW campus leased to CoreWeave for fifteen years at $1B-plus a year, and Sky ($SKY), the USDS stablecoin issuer that just did its best quarter ever at ~$124M revenue while the token fell 25%. The Milk Road Pro desk is adding $GLXY on the dip and rotating Micron profits into Marvell ($MRVL) as the next bottleneck link.

Filtered / Cross-Routed. The threadguy and "Fable tokens" livestreams had no transcript, so nothing to mine there. Trader Mayne's zero-tax-country monologue and the a16z summer reading list were lifestyle and books, dropped. The energy-and-photonics bottleneck ($BE, $LITE, $GLW, $NBIS, $MRVL, and the 80-to-150 GW data-center power ramp) is a genuine investing theme but I routed the detail to AI & Tools this edition since it rode in on the AI-compute story. The rare-earth choke-point angle went to News.

item.title: [Investing] The memory trade ate the first half, and now Burry is shorting the melt-up into July
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Stocks closed the best six months in years on a record-narrow semis bid, Michael Burry stacked shorts on Nvidia Tesla and Caterpillar, and Bitcoin lost its 200-week line as the forced-seller math around Saylor got real
item.content:encoded:
Stocks closed the best six months in years on a record-narrow semis bid, Michael Burry stacked shorts on Nvidia Tesla and Caterpillar, and Bitcoin lost its 200-week line as the forced-seller math around Saylor got real

Half the year is in the books and it was a monster. The Dow finished H1 up 8 percent, the S&P 500 up 8 percent, the Nasdaq up 11 percent, and the Russell 2000 up 21 percent for its best first half since 1991 (Financial Markets list). Q2 alone added roughly $8 trillion of market cap to the S&P, the best quarter since 2020 (Market list). Great number. Now read who carried it, because that is the whole story heading into July.

The only trade that mattered was memory, and that is both the bull case and the risk

One group did the work. H1's S&P leaderboard: $SNDK up 857 percent, $MU up 303 percent, $INTC up 278 percent, $WDC up 271 percent, $MRVL up 250 percent, $DELL up 243 percent, $AMD up 171 percent (Financial Markets list). The semis index $SOX ran 83 percent in Q2 against 9 percent for the Mag 7, a full rotation out of the mega-cap generals and into the picks-and-shovels (People to follow list). Three of the new members of the $1 trillion club this quarter were memory names. Semiconductors are now a record 19.7 percent of the entire S&P 500 (Polymarket list).

That is roughly a fifth of the index riding on one theme. Jim Cramer is out saying $MU "tells its story better" than $NVDA, and Traderstewie has $MU as his IBD Top 50 number one with a $1,400 to $1,500 target (Market list). When the leadership is this narrow and this loved, you own it and you respect it at the same time. SK Hynix just filed to list in the US under $SKHY, one more sign of how crowded this memory trade has gotten.

Michael Burry just shorted the melt-up

Michael Burry is now short $NVDA, $TSLA, and $CAT, the first time he has been on Caterpillar, confirmed across multiple lists (Market list). Burry is early and often wrong on timing, so this is not a sell signal by itself. But shorting Nvidia, Tesla, and the single most cyclical industrial name in the market at once is a coherent bet that the melt-up is late-cycle. Pair it with the accounting story running underneath the tape. A University of Florida study says roughly 12 percent of Q1 S&P earnings were unrealized markups on OpenAI and Anthropic stakes rather than real operating profit (Prof G Markets). Strip the paper gains and earnings growth falls back to the five-year average. The melt-up is real. The quality underneath it is thinner than the tape suggests.

Bitcoin broke, and the Saylor math is the story now

Crypto is the opposite picture and it is ugly. Bitcoin closed below its 200-week moving average (the four-year trend line that has floored past bear markets) for the first time since 2023, down about 20 percent in June and 53 percent from its all-time high, trading in the high $50Ks to low $60Ks (Kalshi list). Whales are pressing it. On Hyperliquid there are three separate leveraged shorts worth more than $100 million combined, including a 20x position of 1,100 BTC with a liquidation up at $67,914 (Hermes list).

The bottom-callers cluster lower. Trader Mayne wants $49,500 to $50,000 first and would not be shocked by a flush to $38,000 to $40,000 into Q4, and he is only a buyer heavy in the high $30Ks to high $40Ks (Trader Mayne). His cycle model caps the next bull run near $180,000, not the $500,000 everyone spent last year screaming about. Kaleo says low 50s into the 40s. Polymarket treats sub-$50K as almost a certainty.

The variable that could actually mark the low is Michael Saylor. Strategy ($MSTR) is now something like $14 to $16 billion underwater on its stack with an average cost far above spot, and it owes roughly $1.7 billion a year in perpetual preferred dividends it can pause but not stop (threadguy). Kaleo is arguing Saylor should proactively sell $1.25 billion of BTC now (Hermes list). If a new monetization program forces Saylor to actually sell Bitcoin to fund those dividends, that is the FTX-style forced-seller capitulation that tends to print the bottom. Watch it.

The bull who is buying the knife

The other side has a name and a balance sheet. Ben Werkman, CIO of Strive ($ASST, the Vivek Ramaswamy-founded treasury firm run by ex-CalPERS bond chief Matt Cole), is buying, close to 20,000 BTC on the books after picking up 2,500 then 1,500 coins in the $60Ks (Milk Road). His pitch is the 200-week and power-law floor as an entry, fiat debasement at 6.7 percent M2 growth, and a sovereign bearer-asset thesis. Strive's preferred $SATA pays a 13 percent dividend daily and trades around $90 against $100 par, and Werkman blames the discount on a leverage unwind in Strategy's STRC paper, not credit. He held an 18-month dividend reserve and sat out last week's mess. If you want the bull case articulated by someone with skin in it, that is it.

Names on the tape worth a look

  • $UWMC (UWM Holdings) is down about 80 percent from its 2024 high to around $2, at capitulation volume, and tomorrow July 2 there is a Two Harbors merger vote that would improve its leverage (r/UWMC). It holds 44 percent wholesale market share and originates 10 to 12 percent of all US mortgages, trading at a base-case P/E under 5. The risk is CEO Mat Ishbia, who pledged more than half his stake (805 million shares) to JPMorgan and has pulled $4.4 billion out of the company since 2021. He also stopped selling, last hitting the tape at $3.39 in May.
  • $NOK (Nokia) is a stealth AI-networking play. Nvidia put $1 billion into it, it bought Infinera for optical, and connecting tens of thousands of GPUs is exactly its lane (r/Nokia).
  • $RKLB (Rocket Lab) is acquiring Iridium ($IRDM) in a roughly $8 billion deal (Market list). $AMBA popped 22 percent on edge-AI silicon. $NBIS ran 175 percent in Q2. $EOSE (Eos Energy, zinc-based long-duration storage) is moving from proving the tech to proving management can execute (r/Eos). $IONQ stays the leading pure-play quantum bet with the valuation priced for perfection (Rick Orford).
  • $SOL has two independent bulls. Market Bubble sees a run from $60 to roughly $600 this cycle on a break of the prior all-time high (Market Bubble), and Trader Mayne is long from about $67. ETH at roughly $1,570 gets a $6,000 fair-value case from DeFi Dad, who values it as the cost to attack the network securing $160 billion in stablecoins and $200 billion in DeFi (DeFi Dad).

Levels and the trader tape

Stocks with Josh has SPY confirmed bullish above 743 and pushing 757, with a summer flash-crash near 19 percent the dip he actually wants to buy (Stocks with Josh). Tesla lives and dies at $411, reclaim it and 425.50 then 450 open up, lose it and $370 is in play (Stocks with Josh). His Microsoft call already hit the 3624 target. And over in the casino, an r/wallstreetbets trader is calling $NVDA "free money" into incoming VIX volatility to kick off a $1,000 account challenge (Nightcrawler). File that under sentiment, not analysis.

Market context: what to watch into the open

Q3 opens on the back of the best first half since the early 90s, and July is historically kind. Ryan Detrick notes the S&P has been higher in July 11 straight years for a 2.9 percent average, and 5 for 5 under Trump (Financial Markets list). The Dow closed above 52,000 for the first time. The catalyst that matters this week is Thursday's jobs report, and after JOLTS openings ran hot at 7.594 million versus 7.296 million expected and Fed's Hammack called the labor market "right around full employment," a softer payrolls print is the good outcome that eases the hawkish worry (People to follow list). Also on the radar: the Two Harbors and $UWMC vote tomorrow, whether the SK Hynix $SKHY IPO adds fuel to the memory bid, and the reaction function under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. Key level to hold is SPY 743. The tape is strong, the leadership is narrow, and the smartest bear in the room just shorted three of the biggest names at once. I stay long the memory trade and keep the stop tight.

Filtered / Cross-Routed

  • OpenAI and Anthropic IPO mechanics, the AI-bubble earnings study, and the Anthropic export-control news are led in AI & Tools, with the market read kept here.
  • Trump's $1.4 billion crypto disclosure and the Colorado primary results route to News, with the $DJT and stablecoin angles noted here.
  • Dropped: a promo-heavy live MSFT/TSLA options call and the "how Camilla Araujo invests $30 million" clip (real estate, not a market call).
